Written in the customer’s language, in their branding. (Not a deck slathered in your branding, with a buncha product speak.)

Simple, clear, easy to forward around.

content:
A customer's CEO, Pat, said something at an onsite that's stuck with me, and I think it's something all AE's should read before an exec-level meeting:

"My EA sets external calendar invites for 20 minutes, but she actually holds 45 minutes free on my calendar. So, if whoever I'm meeting brings me something interesting, I give them the full 45 minutes. 

Otherwise, I just wrap things up at the meeting at the :20 minute mark.

Now, if it's a *really* good conversation, I text her, and she pushes out my next meeting, so I can end up spending a full 90 minutes on the topic."

They've done lots of acquisitions over the years, so this was in the context of vendors, partners, investment bankers, anyone "pitching."

And it's a great question to think about in prep for an exec meeting:

→ Is your point of view* so good, you'll make them late to their next meeting?

_____

*A point of view in "soundbite" form has 4 main parts, in my opinion:

1. Because of [ a major shift / change in their business]
2. Now’s the time to [ respond with this approach ]
3. When you do, [ you'll unlock good outcomes ]
4. While avoiding, [ the cost of bad outcomes ]

Which brings together: 

1. Something that already has built-in momentum / exec mindshare. So you're not trying to manufacture something new for them to focus on, you're "hyperlinking" your convo with what they're actively working on.

2. But, you're introducing some type of non-obvious or hard-won take on *how* to respond to that. Every exec wants to know, "What are others doing, that I'm not, but should consider?" With a degree of specifics.

3. Contrast in the outcomes: value = good - bad outcomes, so, the wider that gap, and more believeably you can describe it and give examples, the more likely you are to build interest in the convo. 

_____

Your turn too: if you're talking to a new AE who asks you: 

"What's the # 1 tip you've picked up over time, for running a solid exec-level meeting?" 

What would you tell them?

How do you attribute the outcome to their work, vs. the human sellers?

That's the harder question, and the unsolved one right now, so that’s exactly what we’ve been working on: tying what an agent did, to the outcome it helped create.

content:
I've read almost everything from OnlyCFO (the anonymous CFO blogger) ever since a 1:1 with him last year (video off, of course). His write-up last week is wildly practical for every seller / account manager right now:

His first take is that a software purchase is 1 of 4 things.

1. Increases revenue
2. Mission-critical
3. Improves efficiency
4. Candy (nice-to-have)

(His name for # 4 is kind of perfect because of all the AI "wrappers.")

He's got just 1 question for *new vendors*:

"Why do we need [X] tool now? We were fine before."

And A LOT of questions for *renewals*:

→ Budget Q's

1/ Is the spend in the budget? If not, how will we make up the difference? You’ve got two choices…1) people or 2) software/AI.

2/ Could we build all or some of this internally? (Some features are not only cheaper to build, but more customizable)

3/ How much do the alternative vendors cost? 

4/ What tools do we already have with overlapping functionality? (Note: more vendors are going multiproduct, so it's more common this year)

→ Agent/AI Q's

1/ Do you have an MCP / are you easy for agents to work with? 

2/ Ask the seller, “How is your AI stuff different from what I can do with Claude/ChatGPT?" (Maybe the base models are fine to use instead.)

→ Pricing

1/ What are the implementation costs?

2/ Will we need to upgrade plans soon to enterprise or some other tier?

3/ What does the cost look like this year and how does it scale next year?

_____

My added notes: 

A lot, if not all of these questions, are coming to your champions this week during internal convo's happening without you in the room. 

So, to what extent have you already asked these same questions to your champ?

Or scripted the answers in their voice, in a thoughtful memo or exec summary they can forward to their CFO? 

(If neither, how can you be confident that convo's going to go well?)

If you're a seller who's only learning from traditional sales blogs, switch it up this week. Check out OnlyCFO, read all you can, and I think you'll be glad you did.

content:
I was flying back from a customer onsite this year, and their CEO sat down next to me on the plane. Without realizing that, he asked one of their VP's who was sitting in the row in front of us: 

"How was the keynote? I had to miss it, was it any good?"

(I was sitting directly behind the VP, so she didn't see me either.)

I was wrapping up a phone call so I didn't chime in then, I just kinda eavesdropped on their conversation about me. (Without them realizing I was literally right next to them.)

It was amazing. Because for as often I write about shaping "internal conversations" in the sales process, I got to sit in on this one.

The 3 things she said:

1. “People laughed a lot, that was good”
2. “The soundbite framework was solid”
3. “Everyone was asking for the slides after”

Then we laughed when I (very awkwardly) said soon after that: 

"Umm, hi, sorry I couldn't say this sooner, I'm that guy from kickoff..."

My takeaway from this for you is pretty simple too. 

If you’re running a demo, a POC readout, an exec conversation, a discovery call, whatever it is this week:

If people laugh, if they remember 1 practical thing, and they walk away saying, “I want to do something different,” that's a job well done. 

So I'd ask: 

1. Do you have a story to tell them? 
2. Do you have a shortcut to give them?
3. Do you have something to leave behind for them? 

If so, you've got this! It's going to go great.

AE's, got a group meeting on the calendar this week? Here's an underrated tip we use in deals to avoid the whole "let us sync internally" dead end:

Send a second cal invite for just you + your main contact, for 10 mins after. 

Like this:

- Group invite: 10:00 - 10:30am
- You + 1 contact: 10:30-10:40am

Set it up with your main contact (ideally a champion) like this:

"No doubt you'll want to sync with your team after [ meeting ]. So I've found it helpful to hold 10 mins right after, for just us to debrief. 

We'll let the group jump, nail down next steps, and I'll send you a forwardable summary with it all after. You up for it?"

Then, once you're in that 1:1 debrief after, ask:

"I'm guessing you were getting some Slacks / Teams messages during that, what'd the group think?"

9 / 10 times, they'll give you the insider's take. 

Assuming the call went well, you'll get intel you'd typically never hear.

(Which you can put right into your exec summary and follow-up.)

content:
Here's how I've been running our AE interviews, with an approach you could adopt and use at your company too:

(1) Pick an actual customer and why they bought.

(2) Send your candidate a couple call clips to watch before your call. Actual prospects, actual objections, real messaging live. 

(3) Have them run a 5-7 minute discovery, paired with a bite-sized demo (think 60 seconds). And you're interacting as the customer you picked.

(4) Hit pause. Then I break down feedback for them. Nuance they missed, what they need to switch up and change.

> Now this is where the process comes to life:

A top hire is testing YOU at the same time. 

So you want them walking away feeling like, "Dang! This is way more helpful than anything I'm getting right now..." and you're giving them something they can use, regardless of whether they're hired. 

(5) Have them the exercise again while you play a new customer. 

>> This is the second key: 

You're looking for the change between the 1st and the 2nd run. 

Can they adapt quickly? Are they coming alive with the critique / feedback? Did they shut down and stay same-same in the 2nd? 

It'll signal how quickly they'll ramp. So it's more about their "rate of change," not just their baseline. 

(6) Finally, have them apply that discovery to follow-up in writing. 

Can they craft sharp, tailored messaging that'll get forwarded by buyers?

Do # 1 - 6, you'll find your person. 

Any other way you runs "tests" in your hiring process that works well?

content:
A'lotta sales leaders make deal reviews about what they need to get, like, "Help me forecast this deal, so our execs trust I'm on top my stuff."

But a deal review is actually about what we *give* our reps.

So done right, the rep is our customer, and our "deliverable" is a creative idea / insight / intro that they couldn't have gotten without us.

And, it doesn’t count if you just say, “Here’s an idea for you…” good luck. It only counts as a deliverable if you give them a headstart. Like, you actually: 

- write the intro
- send the text
- edit the deck

One of my favorites, that works every time about 80% of the time, helps reps help their buyers get a job done (and get re-engaged in the deal):

Courtesy of a tag team with Will *The* Email Guy.

____

Email:

[1] Recall a past topic.
[2] Align it with a tool or idea.
[3] Confirm this is still a priority.
[4] Give proof your idea is helpful.

Subject: Idea, [ Job To Be Done ]

[ Prospect ], last we spoke, [ 1. their challenge in their words ] was a focus.

content:
AE's making the jump to Enterprise: "Price's Law" is often the difference between getting $1M+ signed faster than a mid-market deal, or, not at all. So here's what it is, and how to use it.

Price's Law says: 

"The square root of people perform 50% of the total work." 
(image credit: Devon Nall)

Which means:

- In a 1,000 person company, 32 do 50% of the work
- In a 10,000 person company, 100 do 50% of the work

You catch that? 

→ Headcount jumps 9,000 people. 

→ But, the people who really make a difference only goes up by 68. Leaving with 8,932 more people to filter through and get distracted by.

Then, if you take those 100 people who "matter," and spread them across 15-20 business units, really, this means ~5-6 people out of every 500-600+ can truly get something done — and that's who you want to sell with.

They're hard to find, in short.

So here are a few things I do, to figure out who to build into a champion: 

1/ Look for VP's/Directors an executive's consistently brought with them across multiple different companies

2/ Throw out a general question to nobody in particular in a group meeting, then watch to see who everyone waits to hear from first, before voicing their opinion

3/ They know their numbers. I show them a problem statement, they can put specifics on it, without having to "call a few meetings to run some reports."

4/ Or, they'll challenge you on it with simple, direct language, "No, that's not right. It's actually X, because Y. Update that." 

5/ Other small tells, like, they edit an exec meeting agenda directly as you talk, or they'll put a meeting directly on an exec's calendar, for tomorrow. 

(^others will get in line, writing a request to an EA, or a "suggestion")

6/ Just ask: "If you actually want this project to move forward without stalling out, who's the # 1 person you'd trust to make it happen?"


What other "signals" show you someone's got the juice?

content:
It’s easy to think you need to have “smooth” conversations to sell, but our standout reps have always done the opposite. Creating "thoughtful friction." So here are 3 questions you can use to do the same:


1/ “What about experimenting with this [ give them a DIY solution ] first? Seems like this [ workaround ] could be good enough?"

Beware the “problem” nobody’s already trying to solve with a workaround. It’s probably just irritating, not a true problem. 

Because if it’s not costly enough to create a hacky solution for, is it costly enough to create budget for?


2/ “I’m guessing [project] isn’t your full-time focus: which projects would your team prioritize before this in your next meeting agenda?”

Your contact’s first priority isn’t always their team’s. 

So this assumes there are other, higher priorities. And lets buyers either: 

(1) correct you
(2) give context on other projects

(Referencing meeting agendas makes it practical too.)


3/ "Gotcha, so were you thinking going live by [ end of year / long timeframe ] or later?"

You can’t really manufacture urgency. It’s always internal. So do buyers accelerate your timeframe if you slow it down?

- If they don’t, the deal will often stall or push
- If they do, why are they pulling the timing up? (Share that later if momentum slows.)

Each question builds on the last, so you can layer them together.

Then you’ll know for sure if you've got something together 🙌🏼

My fam’s been on the Big Island this week, spending down some of the miles I racked up during Q1 onsites / kickoffs. Last year, we did Oahu, and there was this moment on that trip where we were on the beach at sunset. 

Naturally, my wife wanted a picture of her and my daughter.

(Somehow we always comes back from trips with 1,001 pictures of me and my daughter, and I end up taking like 7 total of her.)

So, I run up to my backpack, grab my phone, and see an email pop up.

At the time, we’d just kicked off a fundraise for Fluint, and it was an investor saying something that, for whatever reason, I got sucked into and couldn’t help but start replying to.

“Family can wait… this is important…” was basically my thought.

By the time I snap back, the sun had slipped over the horizon. And if you haven’t seen this happen before over the ocean, it’s literally there, then gone in an instant.

So I missed it, and I remember this look I got from my wife, like, “You couldn’t put the phone down just for a minute?” and feeling brutal after.

Fast forward to this trip:

As we’re flying out last week, I’m walking through the airport (basically my natural habitat during Q1), and I see this post from someone:

“Young parents, you only get:

- 1 Summer with your baby
- 3 with your toddler
- 9 with your child
- 5 with your teenager.”

I forget who shared that, but man, it came at the right time. So this trip, I've been trying to do it differently. And it’s been pretty simple: 

I just leave my phone/laptop and don’t bring it with us.

After a week, I’ll say, it’s pretty wild how much more brainspace I have: 

- When I’m working (ps, we have some MAJOR updates I can’t wait to share), I do it early or during naps. Family knows, so I don’t have to “hide” or “sneak” it.
.

I got to crash a QBR with Okta's Strategic team, and this example from a Fortune 20 account is a must-hear for enterprise sellers.

We spent 4 hours writing exec-level messaging together.

The goal was to shrink dozens, sometimes 100's, of pages of account research, customer history, conversations, etc... into short "soundbites."

Something simple but powerful to pass along to the exec at each account.

One of their sellers (they're a smart, thoughtful crew, built by the legend Doug) shared an example with the group from a recent meeting. 

He was meeting their CTO, and just consider this for a second: 

< 30 minutes to engage THE TOP exec, leading 1,000's of people. 

What do you say in that kind of meeting?

Well, what he didn't do was show up with a 50 or even a 15 page deck. 

Instead, can you guess what he presented? 

2 slides. 

That's it, because it's all he needed. 

Strategic reps are crazy good at this too: they deliver their core message in 2 - 3 sentences, max. 

Think of it like compressing a 100 MB file down to 1 MB. You can send it over email, without losing any context, quality, or clarity.

The message gets delivered, without getting lost or bounced.

So think about it:

If you had to "compress" your entire deal down to 2 - 3 sentences, what would you say?

TL;DR: the higher you sell, the shorter the message.

content:
Here's a legendary case study from Expedia, about solving $100M+, enterprise-scale projects by framing up a sharp problem and attaching it to an exec priority. 

Their former Head of CX, Ryan O'Neill, was looking at call center data:

- For every 100 customers, 58 contacted support
- So support was fielding 20M customer calls/year
- They cost $5 each, creating a $100M/year issue
- And growing over time.

So, support leaders were asking: 

"How do we cut time-to-resolution from 10 to 2 minutes?"

To cut cost-per-call from $5, to $1, and create a more efficient call center.

→ But what if that wasn’t the problem? 

The actual question to solve:

*Why was Expedia getting so many calls in the first place?*

The challenge is nobody actually owned that problem. (O'Neill gives the full breakdown on this in 'Upstream' by Dan Heath, great read.)

So he took it to their CEO, Dara, who attached *preventing* customer calls to his top priority. With a new project team, he looked at what drove call volume:

People needing their itinerary. It wasn’t getting through to their email.

Which reframed things entirely:

(Problem 1) Slow resolution = high cost-per-call
(Approach 1) Faster call resolution reduces costs

Versus:

(Problem 2) High call volume for itinerary requests
(Approach 2) Cut call volume by making itineraries accessible

After reframing the issue and making itineraries visible to customers in their account, call volume dropped from 58%, to 15%. 

This is EXACTLY what enterprise sellers do: 

→ Find & frame high-cost, high-priority problems. 

So, here are two points on this:

(1) How to write a sharp problem statement:

"Every [ frequency ], at least [ reach ] are experiencing [ pain ], costing [ loss ]. If it’s not addressed by [ timeline ], that means [ consequence ]."

Applied to Expedia, this reads like: 

"Every month, at least 1.67M customers can’t find their itinerary and have to call support, costing $8.35M to resolve these requests. 

If it’s not addressed by end of year, we’ll see another $500M in lost, repeat purchase revenue from frustrated customers opting out of our loyalty program."

(2) "Layering" problems:

- 1st Level: “We’re paying $100M per year in support costs.”

- 2nd Level: “Angry customers aren’t enrolling in our loyalty program."

- 3rd Level: “Customer lifetime value (CLTV) increases with loyalty members making repeat purchases, so now, we’re missing $500M in future revenue.”

You could even say marketing spend inflates CAC, spent for more first-time customers to offset lost loyalty revenue. 

So Expedia dropping call volumes to 15% of bookings: 

- Saves almost $75M per year in support costs 
- Saves an estimated $500M in future revenue

That's huge. 

So a question for you: 

What % of your deals have a written problem statement? With edits or data from the buying team?

"The 0.5+ Page Business Case" has been one of my favs lately, and it's landed us multiple, multi-year deals with public companies over the past year.

It's based on this idea from David Ogilvy: 

"The longer your memos, the less likely they are to be read by those who have the power to act on them."

Which led me to ask: 

"Can we cut our 1-pagers down to just 0.5 pages?"

Our most widely-used framework is The 1-Page Business Case.

→ 0.5 pages:

A summary strong enough to stand alone for execs who skim.

And, here's the key: 

Leave lots of white space to create a "short and easy" feel. Which gets you past a "that's a lot of text" reflex, so execs naturally move to the next page: 

Drawing them into a second layer of detail, for more overall context.

content:
You ever get those emails from a buyer saying, "Hey... can we push this to next month?" Us too. Even when our AE's find a truly costly problem. So here's a little formula we use to check if we've built (genuine) urgency in a deal.

Urgency = [ D x FV x FS ] /  P

Where:

-D = Dissatisfaction with the current state
-FV = Vision of what’s possible with you
-FS = First steps to move towards the vision
-P = Customer priority level

Notice a couple things here:

1/ It's multiplication vs. addition.

So if any single factor is zero... the whole thing goes to zero. Doesn't matter how strong the other three are.

2/ Priority = the denominator.

So if you're item # 5 on the exec's list, allyour value just got divided by 5. You need to be attached to # 1 or # 2. (Or you'll get ignored)

Now, here's one thing you can do on each factor:


1/ Dissatisfaction:

People sometimes hear what you tell them, but they *feel* what they tell themselves. So you can present the numbers behind something, like: 

"Your patient ratings dropped from 3.9 to 3.2." (Good information) 

But if you can ask, "What does that mean in $ of insurance reimbursements?"

Then help them go find out. When they do the work with you, it builds that, "We gotta change this" type of conviction.


2/ Future Vision: 

One of my fav things nobody does, that a customer showed me recently: 

Get the customer's brand kit from their site, mock up a press release from *their* point of view on what *they'll* able to announce *because of* the project you enable.  Then loop in their feedback: 

"Hey, here's an example of what [ exec ] would be sharing with [ customers / market / investors ]... think we could get their take on it?"

It's fun, and the narrative makes it feel real (vs. just an ROI number).

3/ First Steps: 

Our team's been building "SLIP" kits (security/legal/IT/procurement) on our biggest deal,s with copy/paste snippets + internal docs our champs need. 

Combined with the above, it makes movings things forward concrete/easy. 


4/ Priority: 

I've said this many, many times: 

When something's important to an exec, they'll have a catchphrase / codename internally for it. So, have you found it? And built your message around it?

e.g. "make the mail move", it's usually very specific. 

And it's a shortcut that'll hyperlink your product, to their project.

content:
One thing we've been doing lately is shifting from "future" to "past" discovery Q’s. Example: if you asked me, "How will you get your daughter to school today?" I'd say something like: 

- Well, first we wake up and get dressed
- Then we go downstairs and have breakfast
- Play with cars / blocks / read books
- Then we get in the car

But if you ask, "How did you *actually* get your daughter off to school *yesterday*?" I'd say: 

- Tried on and tore off 3 different outfits
- Cleaned up pear juice and avocado from the floor
- Ran around the block on a horsey ride as bribe for getting in the car

So my point is: 

Whenever you're asking "process" questions, or trying to figure out internal dynamics in a buying group, you have to ask about the past. 

Which is where the actual evidence of what people *do* vs. what they say is.

(You get far more "texture" in the answer.)

For example, instead of:

"How do you typically make a purchase like this? Can you walk me through the steps and who would be involved?"

Try asking: 

"How did you actually get [ past project ] from idea to implemented? Can you walk me through who / what surprised you along the way?"

Small thing, but man, you'll get such a different level of discovery done.

You know what I mean?

PS: it's a snow day in Denver, in May. Wild.

content:
Some classic sales advice that's aged like the yogurt pouch my toddler left in my backpack this week: "Don't talk to execs about features! Sell the outcome!" 

I mean, kind of. 

You've got to connect your message to a topline metric. 

But what happens is reps end up *avoiding* any talk about what makes them unique, right when every exec (at least those in my orbit right now) are craving more specifics and in-the-details types of learning. 

(The number of CMO's who are learning how to self-serve from a CLI, or COO's experimenting with creating their first agent, etc... is jumping in a big way.)

So, most meetings end with an exec thinking: 

"...so what exactly do you do?"

"...you increase our revenue, and decrease our expenses?"

"...umm, yes, very cool."

So here's a different flow you can test this week. 

____

(1) What's changing?

Start with a shift in the exec's environment (internal or external). Something that has mindshare to create an, "Oh they get it," moment.


(2) What's the right approach? 

A *specific* recommendation on how to respond to the change, that only you can say, because of what your product enables. To create a, "Oh tell me more."

SO THAT THEN YOU TELL THEM MORE.

And can get specific on *how* you do what you do.


(3) What's the good / bad? 

Now this is when you talk about outcomes. Because it'll land, and there's credibility and context wrapped around it. 

____

Here's an example:

(1) Shift: 

"Chipotle, you're rolling out a new catering division in major urban markets: where 1 customer could spend $10K on burritos, not just $8.99 per order."

(2) Approach: 

"But that means rebuilding your loyalty program, where you've got to find the right mix of, (a) keeping margin and giveaways for repeat orders; (b) the notification and comms channels the corporate needs. Here's how..."

(3) The good/bad: 

"Brands doing this see B2B loyalty customers delivering 25X the revenue per signup, and, end up converting ~10% of them to their consumer program too."

content:
Here’s a $0, 5-minute exercise you can run with your AE's, to show them just how much of their messaging gets through to executives (or not). 

Executives out there, is this not spot on? 

I ran this for Workday’s enterprise team as part of a program Andrew Barry designed for them, it was a total hit.

Step 1:
Have each AE pick a topic they absolutely love. Their thing. 

Step 2: 
Have them present on it for 5 minutes to a group of 3 - 4 AE's. 

Step 3: 
Meanwhile, other AE's in the "audience" try to get some emails sent during it. 

Step 4: 
At the end of the 5 mins, ask the AE's in the audience: what stuck? What do they remember?

The point is to replicate what it's like to work with someone who has so much going on, so much flying at them, their meetings are an exercise in mindshare.

So you're always starting off with "continuous partial attention." 

And your job is to insert small phrases: 

- "The reason I'm telling you this is..."
- "Given your focus on X..."
- "You might think... but actually..."

Try it out. 

You'll notice each AE gets better and better at reeling a distracted group back in. 

Finding short phrases that keep them stuck in the present. Like honey for the brain 🍯

content:
Classic sales advice is to end meetings with clear next steps, but, how often do we "stick the landing" with clear messaging? Which is a simple formula: 

Sticking the Landing = 

(1) Grab Attention + (2) Highlight The 1 Thing + (3) Stop Talking

(If you don't follow Paul Stansik, you should, this is his catchphrase, and he's given me great, great feedback on this topic over the years.)

___

(1) Grab Attention = 

A short phrase like this, with strong emphasis: 

- "If you hear *nothing* else today..."
- "If you forget everything, *don't* forget..."
- "The *one* thing I wanna make sure you hear..."

Here's a screenshot from when I joined one of our reps' calls. 

It's a late-stage deal, we're head-to-head with another vendor. 


(2) Highlight The 1 Thing = 

Your differentiator, that matches your customer's goal.

In ~40 minutes in this call, we probably covered 12 different areas of comparison with their buying group. But I know this 1 thing in the screenshot is where we win, and the other vendor can't deliver on it.

(And if the buying team doesn't believe this differentiator matters, they're not a great fit for us / we're not a great partner for them long-term anyway.)

So that's what I picked.


(3) Stop Talking = 

It means exactly that. So that your 1 thing actually sinks in.

___

So keep a mental visual of a gymnast sticking the landing this week while you close out your meetings 🤸‍♂️

I think you'll find it's a small thing, that makes a big difference.

content:
AEs: pay close attention to what your leaders do on customer calls, but never coach you to do. It's where the high-value/hard-won advice lives:

It’s called "tacit" knowledge:

(1) Patterns that took years to build up
(2) Things they don't realize the do, and couldn't articulate if you asked

A few examples:

- How do you avoid getting steamrolled by execs?
- How do you plant an idea with a skeptic?
- How do you compress a deal into 2 minutes of framing for a group? 

All of it's kinda like skiing or cycling. 

They just seem to… do it.

So, here’s 1 way to quickly find these specific to your deals, and examples.

____ 

(1) Give your favorite AI this ask:

"Look at the last 3 months of customer conversations [your exec] joined me on. Break down the subtle decisions they made to guide each one, and identify patterns across calls.

Make their tacit knowledge explicit, step-by-step, so I can use it. Then compare my calls against it. Score me 1–5 in each area, with specific moments where I went against what they'd have done."

_____

(Olli from Fluint does this differently, but, the copy/paste will get you started with your AI of choice)


(2) Some examples our AE's found from me:

→ Opening convo's with new people:

I use a pattern of Frame the Situation → Add Friction → Drop a Question. 

e.g. “Your goal is X, but Y is also true, so how are you thinking about X/Y?”

Get them talking early, we'll know where the newbie's coming from.

→ When 1 person in a group goes into too much detail: 

I'll jump in and quickly summarize where I think they’re trying to go, so they feel heard vs. cutoff, while using that window to redirect the convo.

→ With skeptics: 

The bigger the skeptic, the more I'll direct an “angled” question to friendlies on their team, to let them speak vs. us convince.

“…[Champion], how are you thinking about balancing X against Y?”


What’s one thing you've picked up from your team that's stuck?

content:
AE's, here's a simple way to nail your next exec-level meeting: 

Give'em options. 

Because first, if we outline what the job of an exec actually is, it's:

(1) To get an outcome
(2) By making a decision that carries tradeoffs
(3) And involves a judgment call in a gray / ambiguous situation  

That's pretty much an exec's week. 

Matching up their experience and a set of patterns they've built up over time, to a new scenario their team's facing. 

Then once you've framed that up the situation, give them 3 paths, with a recommendation based on your point of view. Deliver it upfront, then let them unpack the recommendation and ask questions.

Watch how they work through the problem out loud, and as you hear how they break it down, you'll gain a LOT more context from their world. 

Vs. the mistake most sellers make:

We come in with 1 pitch, and think the meeting is about them agreeing to it. 

Like, "Hey, isn't this a great idea? Give us budget now, please?" 

But that's not actually allowing the executive to do their job, and it assumes we have all the same facts and context they do. (We don't.)

So, instead, by bringing options, you're saying: 

"I *think* this could be the way, but I want to understand what you know that I don't, to decide if these alternatives have merit." 

This way, you're working *with* them to get an outcome you both need. 

In short: 

(1) What situation are we in? 
(2) What are the options, with pros and cons?
(3) What's the recommendation? And after, the decision? 

That's an exec-level meeting well run.

Hey AE’s, if you’re new on the job, here's something I tell our AE's when they're ramping up and feeling stuck in a conversation. You can just say:

“There’s so much I want to tell you about [ your product ]. Let me just think for a second about the best place for us to start.”

And then you can just sit quietly for 10 - 15 seconds. 

(It's totally legal.)

Because what comes after this is typically a far more clear point of view. A POV where your buyer will want to lean in, and listen to what you say.

Otherwise, it's so easy for us to just "think-talk" our way to what's next. 

Rambling through a few muddy sentences to buy ourselves time.

But if you trust it's cool to take a breath when you need it, you can:

1/ Actually listen to what the customer needs.

(Instead of spending all our time thinking about what WE want to say.)

2/ Focus them on the 1 thing you do that's most valuable to them.

(Instead of falling back on whatever script is easiest for us to remember.)

content:
I've been at 15 customer onsites since the start of Q1, and here's a simple analogy I've used at all of them, to describe what AI in GTM is right now:  

Remember that old cartoon The Flintstones? And how Fred traveled around? 

(A pedal car, powered by his feet. Just pure leg day every day baby.)

Now, remember The Jetsons? 

They had hovercars, which was a fundamentally different technology vs. the Flinstones. But... what'd they do with it? Well, they drove their hovercars down floating roads with stoplights, cross traffic, lane markings etc.

They took their new tech, which unlocked entirely new planes of travel, and bolted it onto what they knew: roads.

Which is where I think GTM teams are today: 

Running the same motion we've always run, just with AI to go a little faster. 

You can take run all the "AI Maturity Assessments" you'd like, but I think you really only need 1 question to know the extent to which you've built a truly "AI native" GTM: 

*If you killed all your AI contracts and ripped AI out of your GTM tomorrow, what would stop working?*

Not "go slower," or "be less convenient." 

What would break?

To the extent things do break, you've built an AI-native GTM. To the extent it all keeps humming along, just a bit slower: you've got a "floating highway."

Two of my favorite examples we're building around, that just couldn't have existed 18 months ago:

1/ A "living" sales playbook that rewrites itself. 

Instead of the big PDF that enablement & revops unveils during SKO, then updates it once or twice a year, something that learn and adapts. 

It helps execute itself, then takes the new GTM data it creates, and adjusts based on new patterns. Creating more "flywheel" than playbook.

2/ "Ideas" vs. interrogations. 

Deal reviews = scheduled calendar invites (which may or may not be a meaningful time in that deal), so leaders can "interrogate" those opps.

But a rolling update that's prompted from system to leader, exactly when that specific deal needs it, so the leader gets a briefing on what's happening and cut right to giving their rep a new *idea*, "Hey, here's what I'd do next."


What's another AI use case your team's been jammin' on right now?

content:
I've screwed up my fair share of exec-level meetings over the years. So here's a minute-by-minute outline I built to keep you on track:

1. Deliver a "Non-Obvious Insight" (:00 - :05)

Execs decide whether you're more or less interesting than the other priorities on their mind during the first few minutes.

The fast way to earn attention is to deliver a different, non-obvious take on a topic they care about. Here's an example structure: 

"Most people believe _________, but actually, ___________."


2. Adapt to Their Quirks (:05 - :10)

Every exec is a little odd in their own way, so your job is to adapt. 

For example, I've had meetings with execs who:

- Cut me off, constantly, to show he was engaged.
- Sat with her back to the screen and refused to look at slides.
- Objected to everything, even if he agreed, just to test us. 

So if it feels like you're off the rails, every meeting may go that way, and you can just ask your champion a question then follow their lead to help adjust.


3. Confirm or Correct Your POV (:10 - :20)

Now you're deep enough to start figuring out what from your initial POV they'll confirm, and what they'll correct. Either is a win. 

And you can literally just ask, "What are you seeing that I'm missing?"


4. Frame Up the Decision Path (:20 - :25)

At this point, the exec is considering:

- Does this help or distract?
- Is it important enough to trump a current priority?
- Who do I delegate this to?

Execs think in choices and tradeoffs. If the goal is "increase revenue," there are a 132 ways to do that. The higher the metric, the more options that exist.

Which means your main competitor is the risk they prioritize an altogether different project / approach over yours.

So you need to understand if they believe the cost of the problem you solve (and payoff you unlock) is > than the cost / upside of every other priority.

To find out, frame up a choice:

"If you were to stack rank this convo against other projects your team's already working on, what would this need to take a backseat to?"

(Assume there are higher priorities, then let them correct you.)


5. Confirm Owners & Outcomes (:25 - :30)

The most likely outcome is an internal referral, which is worth its weight in gold. It basically says:

"Do this, it matters."

But the key is to get a specific name, not a generic action item.

→ Bad: "We'll need to make sure you pass our infosec." 

→ Good: "Jon Clark is VP of InfoSec. He'll send you our vendor portal."

Related tips: 

1/ Pre-meeting: attach a 1-pager to the cal invite so they have context. 
2/ Post-meeting: send a forwardable email they can use for next steps.
3/ Send a no-reply-needed update a week or two out with progress.


What would you add?

content:
We signed up our first paying customers 2.5 years ago. 2 weeks before that, my daughter was born. Which put me right into founder + father mode at the same time, and it’s been nonstop sense. 

A lot of what I see written about working parents is something like, “I value my time a lot more, so I prioritize and manage it better now.”

Which I think is true for a lot of people. 

But for me it’s been a different battle in my head:

GTM tech is moving SO fast, and our process for shipping product, content, etc… can compress hours of work into minutes, that it’s hard to break away from. Even 5-10 minutes with Olli means I can get something to a customer and see the reaction / revenue fairly soon after. 

In short: the work is fast, the return is fairly immediate, and that’s addicting. 

Meanwhile, my life as a dad though isn’t like that. 

At all. It’s the opposite in a lot of ways. 

Have you ever watched a toddler try to put on shoes? It’s very slow. Now throw in a love of extra thick Bombas socks (the only ones my daughter will wear) with a *need* to wear the shoes she grew out of 3 months ago. Which, of course, have to be on before we’d even consider standing in our toddler tower for breakfast at the counter. (You need shoes to climb the tower at the park, so it makes sense.)

So, forming a little human takes a lot of time, it’s pretty inefficient, and my prompts don’t always get a direct 1:1 response. 

Because she’s a toddler. 

So on a Saturday when I’m coming down from the high of a week, fueled by speed as an AI founder, it can be a little jarring. 

There’s a big contrast between:

- Fast, immediate, linear (founder)
- Slow, delayed results, wandering (father)

And that juxtaposition is very real in my mind, as a voice often whispers, “Sure, you could go stack the 100th magnet tiles, that are only going to get smashed again… or you could sneak away and get a 5 min Slack session in that means…”

I think I’m doing a decent job fighting back against those whispers. Because that little glasses-wearing, 36” ball of delight creates these little pockets of time, where when I’m just sitting there listening to her say, “Again daddy! Again again!” I can feel my soul catching back up to my body. (The soul works at the speed of a toddler, not like AI.) Which I think I carries into my work after. 

So, no, I don’t think being a father has made me somehow better at prioritizing and managing my time as a founder. But I do think I’m a better human with the time that I do have. 

(Can’t wait for even more chaos when # 2 joins our little family this summer ❤️)

content:
Most sellers know they should "quantify" problems, but only a handful "frame" problems (which is a big miss). 

Because how you frame a problem will completely change how buyers look at a solution (yours, or a would-be competitor's).

Here's the most famous example of this: 

It's from HBR’s "Are You Solving the Right Problems?"

(TL;DR: join the crash course on problem statements this Thurs: https://lnkd.in/gUksHQ9Q )
 
______

Let's say you own an office building, and your tenants hate the old and slow elevator. So much they'll cut their leases if you don't fix it.

So, what's the problem here? 

A slow elevator. 

But is it really? That intro framed the problem in a certain way. 

Which sets you up to browse a specific "solution space."

1/ Problem: slow elevator.
2/ Requirement: speed it up.
3/ Solution: new motor, upgraded lift, etc..

BUT, what if the problem is actually the fact people hate waiting?

How would that change the solution?

1/ Problem: bored tenants.
2/ Requirement: entertain them.
3/ Solution: Install mirrors in the elevator. 

A different and far cheaper solution works, because people love to look at themselves. (Which is a real thing. Look for mirrors in old buildings.)

______

So here's the point for sellers:

Problems are entirely *subjective.*

So as a buying team expands, so will the number of problems, and 10 buyers can easily come up with 5+ "root causes."

Which means you'll never know if you're on the same page... 

Until you're *literally* on the same page. By:

1/ Framing up the problem *in writing* 
2/ Attaching that problem statement to a pre-read
3/ Making agenda item # 1 "What are we solving for?" 

One legendary leader, Keith Weightman @ Bullhorn made this the # 1 focus with his team, and no surprise, they were top of the company last year. 

So we're doing a 25-min, live crash course breaking down how to write sharp problem statements that sell, this Thursday: 

Come hang! 

→ https://lnkd.in/gUksHQ9Q

content:
Here are 5 *slightly-awkward* discovery questions I like, that signal you're different than the typical AE who's never thinking post-sales. And you're up to dig into what happens after the contract's inked.

Especially key if you're selling complex / enterprise deals.


1. Past Failures 

"Could you walk me through a time your team invested in something that technically worked, but didn't deliver the outcome? What happened?"

→ Finds their real definition of success, internal change management / political dynamics, and what metrics actually matter.


2. Unexpected Outcomes

"[ Target outcome / use case ] is the goal, but if our biggest win came in a totally different area we didn't expect, what's the next place a win might show up?"

→ Start it off with a win scenario, and get them thinking past the first use case into (potential) expansion areas.


3. Resource Check

"If this gets approved, what's one resource your team will have to 'borrow' from another team to make it successful—and how comfortable are you having that conversation?"

→ Cross-department dependencies are very real. Best to call out delivery roadblocks now, they haven't planned for later.


4. Executive Sponsorship

"When you show this to [ exec sponsor ], what's 1 question they might ask, that you're hoping they don't... and what would your honest answer be?"

→ Often, what someone's telling you and what they know internally about an exec's concerns / skepticism are different things.


5. Six Months Later:

"Let's say it's 6 months from now and you're in a QBR. Someone asks, 'Was this worth it?' What do you pull up on your screen to prove it was? And what would make you nervous about showing that?"

→ Helps you define real success metrics, and how they'll be tracked.


Could you see yourself testing one of these?


And, Olli from Fluint is crazy good at crafting disco questions for you. Because he's studied what works in 150K+ deals. So every doc he writes, he lists 5 gaps and his top 5 questions you can ask the customer to strengthen it.

content:
AE’s walk out of the typical enterprise deal review with… the exact same deal they walked in with. (Womp womp.)

Part of the rub is there’s a mismatch between: 

- Leader’s trying to get *information*
- AE’s trying to gain *traction*

Said another way, “reporting the weather” vs. "changing the forecast."

So, here are 3 habits I started using in our deal reviews. All built on getting to the “3rd level” in a convo:

L1: Finding a gap: "We haven't engaged Jamie the EB."

L2: Giving direction: "Here’s how to bridge this to Jamie's data initiative..."

L3: Action: "Here’s a forwardable framing the initiative for Kara, our champ, to ship to Jamie before their 1:1 this Friday."

And I’d argue Level 3 ("action") isn’t the rep’s job. It’s our job as a leader to model what good looks like + create momentum the team can't on their own. 

(Set the standard → hit the standard)

So, the 3 habits:


> Habit 1: Use pre-reads to skip the recap.

It feels like extra process at first, but have cal invites attach a brief with context, to skip the preamble. You can read WAY faster than reps can talk.

Which (of course) reps can do with AI assits: 

- Stack ranks top risks to focus on important
- Living docs that updates based on new changes

One thing I love about how Peter Sheehan does this at Informatica: set invites for :05 after the hour, he reads, they get into it. 


> Habit 2: Surface what's working & replicate.

You've seen hundreds of 100's of deals across reps and segments. A new AE's seen, maybe.... 10. So we need to use that prescriptively. 

Example:

"Shawn’s deal XYZ is a lot like this one because 1, 2, 3. So we sent a 1-page biz case tied to their CFO's cost mandate vs. the data route, procurement approved in 8 days.  Let me pull up what she did, we'll build something similar."

(Also why we built Olli at Fluint as a single agent across your pipe, to pattern match vs. a bunch of disconnected workflow bots.)


> Habit 3: Do at least 1 thing *during* the meeting.

My old CEO would do this all the time: he’d stop our meeting after he picked out one thing that mattered, and he'd just start doing it.

It annoyed the heck out of me at first, b/c I never finished my update. 

But I found it was a gift, and I started to frontload things if I needed:

- A blocker cleared
- An intro made
- A decision, etc.

And the best leaders do that to create momentum: 

- Write an exec-to-exec email for a stalled deal
- Edit a POV before an upcoming onsite
- Make a warm intro to a new account

Which is where all 3 habits connect:

With a pre-read that's oriented you + patterns on what works, the "1 thing" to do next becomes obvious. So then, GO DO IT  to change the outcome.

(Nike sign baby ✔️)

Your team will feel the difference, and I promise, they'll start bringing you their hardest deals instead of hiding them.

content:
In my last 5 on-sites, I asked each CRO in front of their team: 

"How many times did an AE ask you for a warm intro, give you a forwardable email, or add a customer call to your calendar last quarter?"

Out of the 500+ AE's those teams represented, there were ~10 examples total. So about 2% of the time. 

Which is something I see too often (and most often with early career AE's): 

They try to protect their internal leaders' time (their VP, CRO, other cross-functional leaders), instead of using their voice to get as MUCH of that time for their customers. 

Generally it comes from a good place of assuming everyone's busy, and focused on important things.

But a (maybe the?) core skill for senior leaders is an uncanny ability to map time to what matters. And you elevating an ask to them is a gift. Because execs WANT to absorb a high volume of inputs from the field, so they can turn that into 2-3 high-quality decisions and meaningfully influence an outcome.

But if you never speak up to make the ask, you take that choice away.

So, you might think top AE's get their exec's attention because of their revenue.
But, they create that revenue *because* they've started to command time and attention from them.

And it's actually pretty simple to start doing: 

1. You actually have to ask. 98% don't (see above).

2. You match your ask to their job. 

(e.g. put your CTO on a call with a heavy technical detractor, vs. your SVP Sales on a call with procurement trying to make commercial decisions)

3. Be specific. 

Not, "hey can I get 15 minutes to pick your brain?" It's: 

"I'm working on a $250K land deal, and know you're connect with [ warm intro path ]. So I wrote up a short email in your voice — can you send it to [ contact / email ] by 10am tomorrow, to help us get an onsite with them calendared?"

Which is you giving them the chance to do their job 

(Which is to help you and your customer win.)

content:
AE’s: when a sales leader says “build a POV” (point of view), here’s what they mean, and how to do it.

(I've been running through this idea a LOT during onsites lately, and it's worth replaying for you.) 

To start, you're looking at a “driver graph” here. 

It comes from the FP&A world, and models the cause-and-effect in a company’s core metrics. So you'll look at the left side and ask:

1/ What’s the highest-level metric your buyer (the “EB”) owns?

2/ When they stand up at their next board meeting, which path down the driver graph are they prioritizing?

e.g. if revenue’s down inside an e-commerce business, is that because:

- customer base shrank year-over-year?
- same base, but they’re spending less?

3/ If they're spending less, and the exec talks with their VP's about why net-sales/customer is down, let's say they find declining order value (AOV).

What’s trending there?

4/ Let’s say it's a drop in cart volume (# items / order). 

Well, the question is, how are they gonna fix it?

That’s where your POV comes in (see the last visual, Venn Diagram).

Let’s say you sell a code snippet that looks at website/purchase behaviors, and recommends product bundles, to drive more cross-sell at check out.

Then, your POV = the intersection of what’s changing + what you do differently/uniquely to fix it.

It's a “think big, act small” approach, as my friend Brandon Fluharty says:

- Big impact at a high level
- Grounded in specific actions

To help you build a credible storyline between:

- Left side: what metric you’ll influence
- Right side: how you plan to impact it

Do this, and you’ve built a point of view that's credible across the entire buying team. Plus, you've got the foundation for:

1/ A full biz case that resonates at an exec level
2/ Framed around a high-priority problem
3/ With a believable approach to fix it
4/ And a clear way to measure it

Two resources if you want to go deeper: 

- Olli from Fluint can guide you through this (signup below my name)
- My 2nd book "Brief & Brilliant" on Amazon has more examples 📖

Complex deals generally come down to 3 main ingredients. If you've got all 3, you're cooking, and I'd be 80% certain you'll get that deal done:

→ Names, numbers, dates.

(1) Names

What's the internal "codename" for the project you're aligned with? 

Don't have a specific, named initiative you're rolled up into? That deal's probably going to stall in a big org without it. 

But if you do, next question:

Can you pull up the names of who's backing that project as contacts in your cell? Do their names show up in recent text threads?


(2) Numbers 

From inside the buying team, detailing the *problem.* 

(Not a "guess" at the ROI.)

To turn something vague like "churn" into something more vivid, e.g: 

"Our customer LTV fell below $1,000/shopper this year, down from $1,350, since only 40% of loyalty members make more than 2 purchases/year..."


(3) Dates

No exec sets a priority without a target date/deadline. 

If it's meaningful, trust me, it's time-bound. 

So what's the date coming from inside the buying team? Did we break it out into a series of milestones? How are we pacing toward each?

________

Trying focusing the first ~60 seconds of your next deal review here. 

Even better, pull up the exec summary you wrote. Which should be a 1-page brief with names, numbers, dates, in the customer's language.

(2) The skill to back it up

If you have 1 but not 2, people stop believing you.

Then he left, while that optimism stayed with the team.

Which was a choice he made. Not because he’d slept 9.5 hours and had extra energy to give. He just did it anyway.

Now here’s part 2:

Four months later, the team came off their best year ever. They delivered, and put up the numbers.

Which feeds point 1 going into 2026. 

Magnetic leaders who makes you 10 feet tall and bulletproof: you know what I’m talking about, right?

If you have that type of leader right now, they’d probably love to hear a thank you today.

content:
I chased my toddler around a giant IKEA store last night. 50% because they’ve been my go-to example for sales workshops and demos for the last year.

The other 50% is because my wife’s in nesting mode before a new little one joins our family soon. So when we decided to redo our basement, I mean, heck, why not remodel the kitchen too?!

Makes sense.

Now, IKEA wasn’t my first choice for a remodel, but there’s something happening in their business today that makes them an obvious case study.

So I was kinda curious to experience it live, firsthand.

You know their massive warehouse stores, right?

Well, they’ve moved to this new business model where, (1) we had someone come to our, take measurements, talk about ideas, (2) a designer then met us on zoom with a 3D model; (3) we went to the store to touch / feel the options; (4) now we have a follow-up zoom with a designer.

If you caught that, it's a MASSIVE change from what IKEA was:

They’ve been re-skilling coworkers (their word for employee) into interior designers. With other customer support tasks handled by their AI, “Billie.”

Which has a $1B+ revenue target from services, not furniture, attached. That was never part of their revenue model before now. And it's all because they’re trying to capture a new segment that's urban, likes things custom-made, and white glove (vs. DIY).

Setting up all 4 major parts of what a good "soundbite" in any deal is:

1. Because of [ a major shift / change ]
2. Now’s the time to [ respond with this approach ]
3. When you do, [ good outcomes ]
4. While avoiding, [ bad outcomes ]

It’s the 4 elements you need in any deal you’re working on.

So for example, if we’re selling a learning platform, we might say:

_____

→ Shift: Because you just bet your 8,500 call center coworkers can become interior designers (with Billie taking all routine calls):

→ Approach: Now’s the time to turn training content into “behavioral nudges” delivered in the flow of work, so your re-skilling investment actually sticks.

→ Good: When you do, you'll make sure the AI + human model delivers your target 10% of ‘26-’28 revenue from interior design services.

→ Bad: While avoiding the silent cost of co-workers completing trainings, but never delivering on the customer's experience (the gap where your $1.4B growth bet dies).

_______

Which is my whole point of telling you this:

SHOULD WE BUY AN IKEA KITCHEN?

(Okay not the point, but I never thought we’d be entertaining it, so anyone remodeled their kitchen? Tips for us?)

My real point:

If you can tap a major exec initiative, describe it in their language, while guiding a unique response, with specific metrics attached to it…

That’s your deal.

Sure, you’ll have to chase some people around and try to get them aligned (like me trying to wrangle my daughter in a room full of couches to jump on).

But that’s the heart of every deal you do.

Got one for my RevOps crew and AI builders today: why most AI in sales is built wrong for the problem it's trying to solve, and why we went with a single agent architecture. Vs. what most vendors + builds do: 

Deploying "specialized" agents for each sales workflow. 

Which looks like this: Research agent. Meeting prep agent. Email agent. etc.

String them together, call it an agentic platform.

^that's 95% of the market right now.

But the problem is workflow agents are "stateless." They run, produce some output, and disappear. So they never build a continuous understanding of the deal, and can't compare what's working across deals. 

(They don't persist long enough to see the pattern.)

The alternative is 1 "super agent" per deal, but it creates a new problem: 

Thousands of isolated agents, each learning locally, vs. sharing what works.

So when we built "Olli" at Fluint, we went a third direction: 

Single agent, full deal context, across your entire pipeline.

And here's why I think that matters:

The most valuable thing AI can do for a rep isn't summarize a call, or draft a prep doc. It's answer 1 simple question: 

*What actually works in situations like mine?*

Which requires comparison, by looking across deals, to find patterns and nuances, then surfacing what actually works (by stage conversion %) then.

e.g. when a deal stalls at security review, Olli can say: "9 similar deals got stuck here, and ones that closed had a forwardable email from your CIO → CIO."

(And then Olli will *go write the message*)

Solving two things: 

(1) Reps follow the process but it's not what works in *that* scenario
(2) You setup trackers to get insights, but nobody does anything after

So if reps don't know what to do next, because the playbook doesn't cover their specific situation, that deal just stalls out and dies. 

But Olli knows: 

By "tracing" the little decisions that play out across thousands of cycles, by piecing together all emails / calls / slacks and how it's always changing.

It's also why an internal dev just spinning up a quick Claude Code project is fine if you're trying to get reps the same outcomes you already get, just faster and with less effort. (Not bad)

But if you want to fundamentally change the choices reps make in deals to focus on the outcome, it's a pretty wicked (and expensive) thing to build.

So that's why we're building Olli for you.

content:
If you’re presenting at SKO/RKO, for the love of AE's everywhere, here's a shortlist of 6 things you can do to keep people dialed in, vs. checked out. 

I use them in every keynote/workshop I do too (15 of them in Q1).

AE’s: you can use these for group meetings too.


1/ I build slides for toddlers.

Big shapes, lots of colors, a handful of simple words that are easy to track with. A lot of text = people reading and not listening.


2/ I switch slides, a lot.

I typically have 60+ slides for a 30-minute slot. Which sounds like a crazy amount. But each slide is like a mini-reset for the brain.

Keep it moving, you keep them watching.


3/ Start with something nostalgic / relatable / funny.

Moments of spectacular failure, my celebrity lookalike, old movie quotes the audience has to finish. If people laugh / shout / think, they’re with you vs. on their phones.


4/ Drop in little verbal cues.

Phrases like, “You won’t want to miss this,” or, “Now here’s my point,” are like conversational glue and keep people stuck in the present with you.


5/ Switch up your speed/tone.

Some slides are *really fast* but.... some.... are... s l o w. 

SOME ARE LOUD, some are soft. 

Variety keeps attention.


6/ Land 1 big idea, that’s it.

Everything should be focused on a single, sticky soundbite. 

The # 1 most important thing, that months later, people need to remember. Because we all go back to "normal" life after and forget 95% of info.


Anyone else got # 7 to add?

4/ Belief is the thing.

"If you don't believe, if I can't *really* feel that, then why would I believe? And if I don't believe, why would I buy? I want to meet the sellers who are fanatical about what they've got."

content:
This is the best analogy for complex selling I've ever come across: 

Selling in “vectors” → ↘︎ ↓ ↑ ↖︎ ←

Which comes from this quote by Elon Musk (love him or hate him): "Every person in your company is a vector. Your progress is determined by the sum of all vectors."

Little physics refresher: a vector = magnitude + direction.

Vector *addition* says when they're added together, where and how far they move depends on:

1/ Are they moving in the same direction?
2/ Which direction are the strongest vectors pointing?

Say you have 1 vector that’s a "3" and another that's a "5."

→→→
→→→→→

If they’re aligned, together, they can move 8 units:

(→→→)(→→→→→)

But if those two vectors aren't aligned, they cancel each other out:

←←←
→→→(→→)

Here's all that's left:

→→

Now, bring back the idea of complex deals: 

Every *contact* is a vector.

And if we define selling as simply moving a buying team from where they are today (a problem), to where they want to go tomorrow (a payoff).

Then baked right inside all deals are the two elements to a vector:


1/ Direction. 

Everyone has a (conflicting) opinion about the right path. Exec priorities set the destination, but project teams have to figure out the way there. 

2/ Magnitude. 

Measured by influence. Some contacts can take a project the distance and make fast progress. Others struggle to create any progress at all.


So, some questions to ask in your deal reviews are: 
 

1/ Direction: 

- Who's working against our deal? What do they know that we don't?

- What projects are pulling our contacts in a different direction?

- Where, exactly, are people falling out of alignment? Is everyone even thinking about the problem in the same way?

- What's the sequence of events we need everyone to stay aligned with?


2/ Magnitude:

- Which direction are the highest-influence vectors pointing? 

- Towards us? A competitor? Or a different approach all together?

- Who has a level of "social capital" incongruent with their title? Managers we overlooked? VP's we're wasting time on?

- What's the narrative our highest-influence contacts are sharing? Are we enabling them with the right message? 


The other point here is how big of a change you're creating.

If it's a big change or large investment, that's moving the team very far from where they are. Which may mean you need vectors to move "15" units:

Now →→→→→→→→→→→→→→→ Rollout

Vs. a small change, or low investment, with just a couple vectors:

From this: → ↘︎ ↑ ↖︎ ←
↓
To this: →→→→→

AE's, something you're free to do when you don't have the answer, and need to get deeper in discovery: just write down the wrong answer. Then:

You could put a list of 3 on a slide: 

_____

A. Each month, _[ 5 ]_ campaigns are cancelled without the channel analytics needed to launch.

B. In the past 6 months, each campaign drove [ $2.5M ] (B) in pipeline.

A x B = [ $12.5M ] in lost pipeline, which means ~$XM revenue.

______

Then, you'd ask: 

"Does a typical campaign drive more or less than $2.5M in new pipe?"

And you can edit or tag the buyer you're talking to with a comment in the doc, highlighting that piece.

content:
Here’s a simple exercise I gave our AE’s yesterday. It’ll take you 10 mins, and tell you if your emails to exec-level buyers are actually landing… or not.

(1) Draft an email to one of your top account’s execs.

Pick something early stage, just after some initial disco. When an exec getting engaged means new momentum for you. 

(2) Send it to your partner / spouse (or roommate).

Right when you see they’re busy with something. Cooking dinner, wrangling a toddler, both perfect times.

(3) Interrupt them and tell them to read it.

After, ask them to tell you what the point of the message is. Whatever they say back to you is going to tell you a LOT.

Now, you may say:

“But they’re not a [ job role ], so they won’t get my product’s value!”

Yes, true. But that’s also the point of why this works as a good test.

Just like your target exec, your partner:

- Has zero context coming into the message
- Can tell if it sounds genuine or not (they know you)
- Gets easily confused if it’s too complex to follow
- Will default to skimming it because they’re busy

So is it a perfect 1:1 test? No, definitely not. 

But one thing’s for sure:

If your partner who's not your ICP (well I guess technically they are your ICP, in a different sense, but I digress... ) can replay the point of your message, then someone who IS your target definitely can too.

Plus it's a "safe" way to practice.

content:
When I ran a P&L for the first time, I'd have a weekly 1:1 with our CEO, and he’d always do this thing, that, at first, annoyed the heck out of me.

But I realized why he did it, and I started doing the same:

He’d effectively stop the meeting before I could deliver my full update, because he'd already picked out 1 thing that mattered, and started *doing* it.

He'd hear something he could change, open his laptop, and execute.

So we never got to everything on my list, but I always left with 1 thing off my list. 

Which created momentum, and I realized that was a gift. 

Over time, I started to frontload where I needed: 

- A blocker cleared
- An intro made
- A decision
etc. 

For example, when we started the enterprise segment, I had to "borrow" CS resources from another P&L owner, to help service our first large customers. Before we hired on our own. 

So while we chatted, he emailed Finance to change how we'd book those costs. Which cleared up a bunch of internal tension.

And I've come to believe (and practice) the same over time: 

The best execs you'll ever work with create "momentum."

- A decision today vs. a "I'll circle back"
- They cut scope vs. adding requirements

Sales leaders: it's the exact same idea with your reps. 

Pick 1 thing in your next 1:1, and do it with them: 

- Ghostwrite an exec-to-exec email for a stalled deal
- Edit the POV your sales engineer will use for a demo

Whatever it is. Don't just add to the list. Subtract from it while you meet.

Your team will *feel* the difference, and I promise they'll start to look forward to meeting with you more and more.

content:
My brain when an AE says they're going to "break into" a target account: 

"You mean like George Clooney in the 2001 classic, Ocean's 11' right??"

But as it turns out, it's kind of the perfect analogy.

So I went with it for yesterday's 25-min crash course on account planning (that doesn't suck). 

We set a record for signups: 1,305. 

Slides, recording, frameworks here: https://lnkd.in/gdm-vuQz

Here's my Ocean's 11 parallel, which I thought was a fun one.

1. Picking a Target

Danny Ocean decides they're targeting Terry Benedict's casinos, because of the sheer scale of the upside, and a very specific reason (a "point of view"). 

He's got to win back Tess (his ex-wife).


2. Mapping the Opportunity

There's this scene where Rusty (Brad Pitt) and Danny map out the vault schematics, laying out the plan step by step. Including how to navigate around the "security" (blockers).

They're wildly detailed about thinking steps ahead (land + expand).


3. Anchoring to a Compelling Event

They choose a *specific* night when the vault is full (fight night). 

Timing's everything, b/c if you've got a true "compelling event" (merger, product launch, etc...) you can tap that momentum to get big deals done, fast. 


4. Build the Deal Team 

Danny needs a crew of specialists—Basher for explosives, Yen the acrobat, etc.—just like a good account plans setups how you'll direct your full deal team. 

Everyone's got a specific role. Big deals don't get done alone.


5. A "Living," Flexible Plan

Account plans can't be static scripts. They've gotta adapt as things change in the account, and you discover new blockers. 

Like where Basher's explosive fails, and they have to pivot. Or when Yen gets injured, and they have to rethink how they’ll get him into the vault. 

So, yeah... it's a pretty good parallel.

content:
Well-meaning but pretty weak tea advice you'll see around LinkedIn: "Sellers, don't talk to executives about features, focus on outcomes!"

I mean, sure. 

Of course you've got to connect your message to a topline metric. 

But what ends up happening when an AE hears this is they *avoid* talking about  product altogether, so the exec ends up thinking...

"...umm so what exactly do you do?"

Then the AE's message falls flat, because it sounds like everyone:

"We'll increase your revenue, and decrease your expenses."

(Thank you, McKinsey.)

So here's a different flow you can test this week. 

____

(1) What's changing?

Start with a shift in the exec's environment (internal or external). Something that already has mindshare to create an, "Oh they get it," moment.


(2) What's the right approach? 

A *specific* recommendation on how to respond to the change, that only you can say, because of what your product enables. To create a, "That's interesting, say more" feeling. 


(3) What's the good / bad? 

NOW this is when you talk positive/negative outcomes. It'll land, because there's credibility and context wrapped around it. 

____

Here's an example:

(1) Shift: 

"You're rolling out small format stores: 1/3 the space, a fraction of the SKUs. So associates can't rely on customers wandering into a purchase anymore."

(2) Approach: 

"That means every conversation has to be intentional: the play is a specific product suggestion built into each associate's tablet, based on a blend of what's in *that* store's inventory + *that* specific customer's history."

(3) The good/bad: 

"Retailers doing this see basket size hold, even with 70% less floor space. The ones who don't see store revenue shrink along with square footage."

____

content:
If you're moving into mid-market or enterprise in 2026: here's a shortlist of 10 things I strongly believe you can (and should) build your sales process around:
 
1/ Effective deal reviews happen in < 60 seconds.
 
If you can't compress a deal into short, specific bullet points on numbers, names and dates, do you really know what it's about? 

1 page is all you need to spot gaps.

 
2/ Building a business case *is* the sales process. 
 
Not just one activity inside it. All other activities roll up into and are strengthened by it.

 
3/ Deals get done during the convo's about you, without you.
 
So write it out. Content can be part of your champions' conversations, even when you can't be. Plus, content keeps your own team (AE's, SE's, CSM's, etc.) on the same page.

 
4/ Writing is about discovery, not documentation.
 
It's the process of learning what you *don't* know (and then figuring it out). Making it the most-important, least-developed skill for sellers.


5/ Efficiency is about less activity, not more.
 
More "finesse" than force: sellers who build more influence in the buying process win more revenue, with less activity over time.

 
6/ Buyers don't trust your ROI.
 
Numbers without a narrative are meaningless. But numbers *do* validate a decision the buying team's already made, based on the story.

 
7/ There are two types of problems: math and drama.
 
"Drama" is why the math problems go unsolved.

 
8/ Selling priorities > solving problems. 
 
Reps solving genuinely-costly problems lose deals all the time. A process has to frame the problem around an exec-level priority first.

 
9/ You don't "find" deal champions. You build them.
 
Like IKEA furniture. Over time, your process should transfer ownership in the deal from you, to them, by co-creating their solution.

 
10/ Multithreading isn't about adding more contacts. 
 
More contacts = more dysfunction. Create the minimally-viable committee, to build a "social safety net" around your core champions.


Which of these 10's most interesting? 

And, what would you add that I missed?

content:
Ever peeked inside an exec's inbox?

Most AE’s haven't, so today on Black Friday, walk into any Walmart with your laptop and try to get some work done. 

You'll get the idea:

People throwing elbows, pushing up to the front of the line to grab something: "a few minutes," meetings, approvals, decisions, signoff, etc.

So, some things to keep in mind while communicating with an exec:


1/ Execs typically read your emails during other meetings. Or during early mornings / late nights. 

- If you have something longer (e.g. a 1-page exec summary), try sending in the off hours. The chance it's read goes up. Schedule for 5:30am or 8pm.

(And if you're sending a 30-slide deck that's covered in vendor branding? Might as well just go ahead and delete that. It's not getting read.)

- If you’re sending something mid-day, keep it to ~4 sentences. Again, they’ll read it while multitasking.


2/ It’s basic… but asking for time triggers the “I’m so busy” reflex. More likely outcomes are an internal referral, from a forwarded email with a short opinion. 

Craft your CTA's accordingly, example:

You: "Would you want to weigh in first, or ask the team?"
↓
Exec: *FWD* 

interesting, plz look at this.

-Sent from my iPad


3/ Even better, write your champions a forwardable email and have them send it, CC'ing you. Execs prioritize internal senders over external senders.


Any other tips you'd add? 

Either because you're an exec, or, you found a practice that works?

My call Tuesday with a VP of International Sales was dead in the water when we hopped on.

Sellers know the feeling.

VP hops on, he's looking at his phone, clicking on his computer, responding with super short answers.

The truth is -- it's not you. It's not your product. It's them.

They have a lot going on and you're something they would rather push off (in this case for the 4th time this quarter).

But now they are here. What should you do?

First, here's what not to do:
-Don't catch him up on what's new with your company
-Don't pull up a branded slide that scream's "here's that pitch from 2 months ago, remember?"
-Don't break the ice and see if they caught the ball game last night

You need to show something.

Not just anything.

The One Thing.

In this case, I pulled up the half-page business case and said "read this."

160 words of reading later + "what concerns do you have?"

The response. 
"I don't have any concerns. I think, actually, if anything, the last couple of weeks I spent having all of the strategic reps present to me on their account plans, and it sort of doubles down on the.. we're not able to consistently [exact thing we are solving for in the "problem" section of the biz case]."

17 minutes total we went from dead on arrival to sponsored meetings with two new stakeholders, POC planning session scheduled after that and a properly qualified deal.

The message? 

Earn your prospect's attention with One Thing that commands their attention (if they are on a call with you, the One Problem they are looking to solve).

content:
There’s this “breakup” email a lot of sellers use that says:

“Have you given up solving for [ problem ]?”

Which is counterproductive IMO, because it suggests that either:


1/ There’s no real problem worth solving for.

When something’s a genuine problem, your prospects don’t just say, “Eh, you know what? This is hard. I give up.”


2/ It’s not you they might have given up on.

It’s a very real possibility they gave up on you, not the problem. They went their own way, or decided to kickoff their project with another partner.


3/ De-prioitizing something isn’t giving up.

It’s actually an executive skillset. Choosing to “let fires burn” so you can shift your team’s time and attention to other projects.


Something like this always worked for me instead:

Subject: Checkout Project Kickoff

Hey Erica,

Seems like eComm shifted focus, or kicked off the checkout project already.

Either way’s cool. But our services team’s holding time for you just in case.

(We'd need to kickoff by January 5th, to be ready for your Feb deadline.)

What can I let them know?

___

Any other "breakup" emails you all like, that *actually* get replies?

Which is true — you do need to get above the line. 

But that line isn't a cut and dry thing that's easy to spot.

Enterprises are more like social networks than hierarchies. 

Influence doesn't sit neatly above or below a certain set of titles.

Instead, influence = building a track record and the "social capital" to shape conversations, move deals forward, and create change.

Some things I like to look / listen for here are contacts who:

(1) Previously worked for a direct competitor
(2) Worked with the buying exec at a prior company
(3) Everyone waits to hear their answer first before speaking

Which means the lines will fall differently inside your accounts.

What are some other things you look for to "trace" the power line?

If you just drafted a follow-up email with a stack of links / attachments / ideas inside it, try this. (You're 3X more likely to get it read & replied.)

1/ Send out the 1st, most important point. 
"With the CFO convo coming up..."

2/ Schedule a reply email with the 2nd point. 
"By the way, here's 1 more..."

3/ Schedule a last nudge if you don't get a response.
"Just had one last idea for you..."

(Which is why I say "3X" more likely. 3 parts.)

It's the same amount of "thinking" for you as a rep.

You already wrote out the long email, with 3 different points in it. But this way, you'll get more mileage from it, since:

- Each point is short / snackable, so your buyer can digest and use it. 

- You're top of mind while moving the deal forward (vs. "just checking in").

Example from one of our AE's, Kora Hodge: 

She's wildly creative, which means 1 message can easily have 3 ideas inside it. 

While she was setting up her champ for a CFO convo, she had:

• Customer testimonial on using Olli (the sales agent) as interim manager, while backfilling an open role to save headcount $

• Soundbites on seat vs. usage-based pricing models

• Biz case visual

All killer stuff. That are actually 3 killer emails. 

"Hey, example your CFO... holding a month on backfill hires Olli for the team.."

"By the way..."

"One last idea..."

Surely some of y'all are doing this, right?

content:
What's 1 simple but strangely helpful sales practice you've picked up?

I'll update this post as we go, with some of the interesting ones here. (So we all get a nice 'lil menu of ideas to share with our teams.)

To start us off: 

→ When you send out a group calendar invite, send a 2nd and separate invite for 10 minutes, that starts right after, with just your champion. 

"So, what was your crew DM'ing you about during the convo?"

_____

Updates: 

1. Leave-behind as a "living" doc — Present from 2-3 slides, add on specifics as you go (requirements, current vs. future state, etc.) Grows with the deal and travels without you.

2. Give prospects 1 specific "value add" homework — gets the truth about whether they'll actually change and do the work: progress comes from their work between meetings, not yours.

3. Video intro new stakeholders — When someone gets added to the invite, send 30 seconds introducing yourself. Humanizes you before opinions form.

4. Assign your team to specific buyers in demos — Each person owns 1-2 stakeholders. Watch their body language, DM them on Zoom, or sit next to them on-site. No spectators.

5. Pre-demo survey — 60-second form to get the surface-level stuff answered before, so you can dig deeper live.

6. BLUF your emails — Put the ask first so it shows in the phone preview. Context goes below signature or nowhere.

7. Same prep, every deal — Use it with internal teams, keep it in CRM. Consistency lets you improve it over time vs. reinventing each time.
