So often (me very much included), we skip the hard work of writing out a strong problem statement, because it's wayy easier to leave it at what the deck says about our "personas." You know, like: 

"Margaret the Manager struggles with inefficient processes, and broken workflows that can't dynamically... yada yada..."

(You've seen those decks, right?)

But if you can’t frame a high-cost, high-priority problem, that deal's gonna stall.

It’s just a matter of time.

But if you can frame up a strong problem statement with your buyers, you’ll win.

It’s just a matter of time.

So here’s an example of "what good looks like."

It's from one of my 30 Minutes to President's Club episode this year. 

(And heyo! one of the year's top tactics form yesterday's holiday episode: go search 30MPC on Spotify / iTunes, skip to minute :20 )

- Target Account: IKEA

- Situation: IKEA's shifting to a smaller footprint stores, as part of their push into more digital orders, not just in-store sales.

- Problem Statement: See the image example here.

In short, our job as sellers is all about:

1/ Framing up the use case we're uniquely positioned to enable
2/ Showing multiple layers of impact (with customer data)
3/ Benchmarking/creating context on the size of the gap
4/ While showing it’s only growing worse over time
5/ All aligned to a company-wide priority
6/ Using the customer's language 

Notice some key phrases here you can use too:

- "Which means... [ next level of impact ]..."
- "If not addressed by [ timing ], it gets worse..."
- "Despite trying... [ failed attempts ]..."

What's another phrase that works when talking problems?

content:
I write emails to an account I made my daughter, so that for her birthday one year, I'll gift her an inbox filled with years of memories stored up. Here's a list of 15 ideas for living I sent her recently, and thought it might be fun to share.

What's 1 "rule for a good life" you'd add?

__

1/ "Pre-bus" your table at restaurants. Stack your dishes, silverware, cups, and wipe up all the crumbs. Waitstaff will notice, and they'll smile.

2/ If you wouldn't take advice from them, you don't have to take criticism from them either. 

3/ Leave one thing 80% done at the end of the day, and let yourself finish it first thing tomorrow. It's an easy way to build momentum into a new day.

4/ The smartest people can explain hard things to a 3rd grader.

5/ Related: you'll beat out people much smarter than you if you're the easier one to work with. (But you're very smart little lady, so this won't come up much.)

6/ Also related: if someone asks you to do "A," think about what's likely next: "B and C." Then you can give them A, B, and C all at once.

7/ Just go to sleep and send that email in the morning if you still want to.

8/ Buy the cheap seats, then talk to the people around you.

9/ The thing you're avoiding saying in a conversation is usually the main thing that's worth saying.

10/ Bring snacks.

11/ You can't make good coffee without good beans. Get the fundamentals right, don't worry about all the other stuff around it.

12/ When people repeat themselves, listen twice. They didn’t forget, they just don't feel understood and it's important to them.

13/ The decision is usually right there in your body—a tightness in your chest, or lightness in your step. Listen to it, because otherwise you can rationalize almost anything if you talk with yourself long enough.

14/ Never come back from one trip without your next trip on the calendar. It always gives you something to look forward to. 

15/ Every once in a while, drive the long way home. You'll have a new idea or thought you otherwise wouldn't.

____

What else would you add?

content:
I haven’t read 95% of the top sales books. I’ve never gone through a formal sales training. Instead, I learned how to sell “by analogy.” 

Which isn't a new idea:
‍
- Arnold Schwarzenneger took ballet to improve his poses on stage. (Kyle Asay pictured here, but I couldn't find a good photo of Arnold)

‍- Kobe Bryant tap danced to strengthen his ankles/coordination on the court.

I didn't know it at the time, but this idea started for me when I hit a point where I wasn't sure what I wanted to do with my career. 

I figured consulting would help me learn a lot and find out 🤷🏻‍♂️

So I got a job building financial valuation models, and to help me get that job, my roommate Greg spent *hours* drilling me with mock “cases.”

In a 90-minute sprint while sitting on our bunkbeds, we’d cover M&A, expanding market share, calculating fair market value, etc… 

Which was like doing 9 or 10 high-level discovery calls / business case writing sessions, every day.

Then, once I got that consulting job, I started building 100+ tab Excel models for massive enterprises. it forced me to structure and clarify my thinking.

Which was easily the best sales training I "never" had, because it laid the foundation I continue to use while writing up business cases years later.

So, what exactly is a “case?”

Cases are structured ways of building up a POV to guide executives. 

They work by:

1/ Giving you a small set of facts to start.
2/ If you ask the right questions, you get more data.
3/ Then you match the right framework to the situation.
4/ Next, you develop a concise set of recommendations.
5/ Finally, you lay it all out in a concise narrative.

Which is the process of crafting a "POV" in sales.

If you want the best "training" on this, here a few options: 

1/ Check out the frameworks at the post below my name above 
2/ Go to the "practice case" section on Bain, BCG, and McKinsey's sites
3/ Type this prompt into your favorite AI of choice:

______

"I'm interviewing at Bain & Company to become a management consultant—and I need you to help me with a strategic case interview, as a mock practice session.

You're a senior-level consulting executive, presenting a real-life case with a high-level, strategic problem to test how well I build a structured point of view on the problem, conduct discovery to get even deeper insights, and over time, you'll give me more data to help put together a sharp presentation where I reflect back a tight and cohesive narrative.

Start off with a real-world problem and interact with me as the interviewer, providing a graph of data or visuals or the next step to go even deeper. 

IMPORTANT: Don't over-share upfront, make sure I'm digging in with my discovery.

At the end, you'll evaluate my performance, highlighting where I was sharp, and what was still underdeveloped and needs work next time around."

content:
Here are my top 10 soundbites from Peter Sheehan on leading enterprise sellers — plus 1 insane stat: 226 people joined our live convo, 98% (221) were still logged on when I closed Zoom. 

Ask anybody who runs webinars and they'll tell you: 

98% of people staying locked in for a full webinar is wild. 

It just doesn't happen. (Especially because we did this at EOQ last week.)

So here's my summary below, but watching the entire replay will easily be *the best 25 minutes* you spend all quarter. Guaranteed:

→ https://lnkd.in/g474bWsM


1/ The "Middle 1/3" Approach

Focus your energy as a leader on the middle 33% of deals—because you'll win a third no matter what, and you'll lose a third no matter what. 

That middle third is where 80% becomes 120% of quota.


2/ The AE's Job Description = Value

AE's are the keepers of the business case—if they don't own "why do anything," and link it to a very specific customer metric, nobody will.


3/ Writing vs. Pitching 

Buyers don't need your pitch. They need you to enable them.

"Do the job your customer doesn't know they have to do—think and communicate in their language, not yours."

With clear, written messaging they can "shop around" to cover themselves and cut reputation risk. 


4/ Documents travel where you can't. 

Decks don't get forwarded; 1-pagers do. 

Here's what Peter's team uses: 
→ https://lnkd.in/gay4AEZA


5/ The Business Case IS the Sales Process 

Build it from discovery through closed-won + upsell, as a single ongoing artifact that lives and evolves. That doc becomes the deal—not a summary of it. 

It literally IS the deal.


6/ Start Deal Reviews 5 Minutes Late 

Create a written deal review framework, and build prep time directly into your meeting culture: use the first :05 to review silently. 

It makes these convo's way more productive and tactical for reps.

Here's the framework: 
→ https://lnkd.in/gGc6b2Ab


7/ Create a "Writers Room"

Peer-driven feedback sessions where reps workshop their business cases together. Direct correlation between attendance & revenue. 


8/ Interview Your Own Procurement Team 

Want to convince reps? Have your internal buyers explain what they actually use (and ignore) in vendor sales processes.

If you missed it: the CISO / CIO at Treasure Data ($170M CDP, serving 4B users) is dropping behind-the-scenes soundbites on how she makes buying decisions.

_____

(1) Your Champion Fights Without You
→ Internal meetings decide your fate. Every deck, email, and demo must arm your advocate to win arguments you’ll never hear.

(2) We Map Cultural Alignment
→ We watch how your team shows up, with humility, ownership, and precision. Culture leaks in every email, every meeting. If we sense chaos here, we expect it in support, billing, and delivery too.

(3)  Responsiveness Is One Signal
→ Speed matters. Relevance matters more. We’re watching how well you understand our context, not how fast you hit “send.” Clear, contextual answers build trust. Generic ones cost you.

(4) Be clear, not clever.
→ Messaging that tries to be everything to everyone resonates with no one. We don't need grand visions. We need to know exactly how you solve our specific problem. 

(5) Show real ROI, not fantasy math.
→ "15 minutes saved / day = $1M in value." Really? That's not a business case. That's wishful thinking. Show us measurable outcomes, or don't show up at all.

(6) Win My Team Before Winning Me
→ When an engineer says, “This actually made my job easier,” I take notice. Adoption is the loudest endorsement you’ll ever earn.

_____

You can have a right-fit product that solves a genuinely-costly problem, and still lose with execs. 

Unless you shape the convo's happening about, you without you. 

Which you'll do in 2 ways:

(1) Craft a highly-specific message that links the exec’s focus to an approach they believe.

(2) Script how their own, trusted team delivers that message internally — when you’re not in the room.

AE's, got a group meeting on the calendar this week? Here's an underrated tip I use in my deals to avoid the whole "let us sync up internally" dead end.

→ Send a 2nd invite to just you + your main contact, for the :10 mins after. 

Like this:

- Group invite: 10:00 - 10:30am
- You + 1 contact: 10:30-10:40am

Set it up with your main contact (ideally a champion) like this:

"No doubt you'll want to sync up with your team after [ meeting ]. So I've found it helpful to hold 10 mins right after the call, for just you and me to debrief. 

We'll let the group jump, nail down next steps, and I'll send you a forwardable summary with it all after. You up for it?"

Now, once you're in that 1:1 after, ask:

"I'm guessing you were getting some Slacks / Teams messages during that — what'd the group think?"

9 / 10 times, they'll give you the insider's take. 

Assuming the call went well, you'll get intel you'd typically never hear.

(Which you can put right into your exec summary and follow-up 📄)

content:
Here are 5 *slightly-awkward* discovery questions I like, that signal you're different than the typical AE who's never thinking post-sales. That you're up to dig into what happens after the contract's inked.

(Especially key if you're selling complex / enterprise deals.)


1. Unexpected Outcomes

"Obviously, [ your main product benefit ] is the goal. But if your biggest win came in a totally different area we didn't initially expect, where would a win like that show up?"

→ Start it off with a win scenario, and get them thinking past the first use case into (potential) expansion areas.


2. Past Failures 

"Could you walk me through a time your team invested in something that technically worked, but didn't deliver the outcome? What happened?"

→ Finds their real definition of success, internal change management / political dynamics, and what metrics actually matter.


3. Resource Check

"If this gets approved, what's one resource your team will have to 'borrow' from another team to make it successful—and how comfortable are you having that conversation?"

→ Cross-department dependencies are very real. Best to call out delivery roadblocks now, they haven't planned for later.


4. Executive Sponsorship

"When you show this to [ exec sponsor ], what's 1 question they might ask, that you're hoping they don't... and what would your honest answer be?"

→ Often, what someone's telling you and what they know internally about an exec's concerns / skepticism are different things.


5. Six Months Later:

"Let's say it's 6 months from now and you're in a QBR. Someone asks, 'Was this worth it?' What do you pull up on your screen to prove it was? And what would make you nervous about showing that?"

→ Helps you define real success metrics, and how they'll be tracked.


Okay okay, I said 5 questions... but here's one more:


6. Plan B

"What's your Plan B if this doesn't get approved?"

→ What's funny is I've found that my deals tend to be less "real" if there's no Plan B. Not the other way around. If something's truly important, there's always another option they're looking at.


Could you see yourself testing one of these?


PS, Olli the AI Agent we built is crazy good at crafting disco questions. If you'd want to put him to work on some of your toughest deals, drop a note & I can get you access.

content:
Most of us think discovery is asking questions, in a conversation.

But here’s a different approach to find all the stuff you’re missing out on.

The “3rd level” type feedback that’ll end up changing your deal:

(1) Write down the wrong answer
(2) Show it visually
(3) Wait to be corrected

Here’s how: 

(1) Write down what you heard last time, with placeholders.

Let’s say you’re selling Figma to Spotify. You might write 3 bullets:

_____

- We sunset the GLUE design system while expanding beyond music.

- But with a [ 12:1 ] engineer:design ratio, that’s [ 225 ] points of rework now:

- Instead of “aligned autonomy”, we hit [ 5,000 ] different components that need to be rebuilt, at a cost of [ $X / dev squad ].

_____

KEY: bracket or highlight text you’re not sure of, and want feedback on — especially surfacey-level pains, but no real impact / data to it.

→ Hit the *View Blog* option at the top of this if you need a starting point.


(2) Next, pull up that problem statement on the screen.

Either in a doc or slide but DON’T put this is presenter mode.

Ideally with minimal design: black font, customer logo, that’s it.

Make it feels like theirs, not yours, with THEIR language/phrases. “Aligned autonomy,” and “GLUE” are examples.

Then have a small handful of comments pre-staged, e.g. “What’s the ratio of designers to devs in a typical Spotify squad?”


(3) Wait to be corrected.

You can start simple, “Hey, here’s what I heard…”

Then drag over the text in a certain bullet and pause, let them read. As they start to see the question + wrong placeholder, they’ll jump in.

“...it’s actually a 7:1 ratio, so we’ve got 300 not 225 designers.”

^increasing the value/need for Figma as a result.

Then, as they share that, EDIT THE DOC LIVE.

^there’s something satisfying here, where you’ll keep getting deeper and deeper feedback, with people feeling like, “Oh, they’re listening and we’re getting somewhere.” So they'll keep going.


Now, you've got something for them to forward in follow-up. 

Anyone already doing this? 

What are you finding if so?

content:
There are 3 different levels of selling:

Most people learn how to make the jump from 1 → 2.

Only the rare seller makes the shift from level 2 → 3.

If you look at the last few deals you ran, did you get to level 3?

Level 1 is features. "Here's what it is."
↓
Level 2 is benefits. "Here's what it does for you."
↓
Level 3 is identity. "Here's who you'll become."

You only get to Level 3 by building something *with* your buyers. 

Never by taking your thing, and selling the benefits of it *to* them. 

It's why I talk so much about building business cases in writing:

A biz case = the plan your champion built to, (1) unblock a specific priority (2) with a unique approach (3) that gets an outcome. 

And by building that plan, they become someone who's thinking differently, deeply, and more intentionally about a project they'll back internally.

Here's a classic example from LEGO (shoutout @justcopytips for the image).

So, what level are you selling on?

content:
I strongly believe we should pay SPIFFs to AE's who get actual "no's" in deals. (Which, yes, means paying some amount > $0 for a $0 revenue outcome.)

Here's my thinking:

In the context of a complex deal, the # 1 job of an AE is to guide a decision. 

To run a process *with* your champion, that simplifies the path to either:

- A confident “yes.” Closed won.
- A clear “no.” Closed lost. 

But in my opinion, it's that second one, a strong "no," that's hardest. Because getting a "no" means you just got 12+ people aligned on:

(1) The fact they need to make any decision in the first place
(2) Some type of "decision criteria" to guide it
(3) The path they chose
(4) Willingness to tell you why (instead of just "forgetting" to follow up)

Which is hard. And it's also the job.

Just getting past # 1 in the list means you got the buying exec to an, "Oh, we should do something here…" moment.

THEN guided their team to something other than "vibes" to decide.

So, here's a framework to help you do this:
→ https://lnkd.in/gSUMDhKY

Plus a step-by-step on using it. 

(Which first came from one of our customers while running our renewal, and then I started to share it with new logos.)

→ Step 1: Build the Wishlist

Get your champion a forwardable to collect the buying team's top 3 items on their wishlist. What needs to be true of a solution? Collect and add here:

https://lnkd.in/gSUMDhKY


→ Step 2: Spend "$100"

Give everyone "$100" to spend across all criteria. They'll realize they can't just make everything "high priority" now. And because they can spend $80 on one and $0 on others, you'll see just *how* important each is.


→ Step 3: Ask Questions

Don't let the convo just fizzle when it gets hard. Ask stuff like:

- "What are we optimizing for that your customers don't actually care about?"

- "If your biggest competitor was in this room, what would make them 'happy,' thinking we way overweighted one criteria?"


→ Step 4: List Approaches, Not Vendors

See Monday's post on this. An example of IKEA debating:

- Internal AR/VR Build
- Buying a 3D Platform
- Buying a "Pay Later" Platform


→ Step 5: Stack-Rank Each Approach

Rank each from 1 (worst) to 3 (best). Then multiply by the total $ devoted to each, so the ranking acts as a multiplier.

The sheet here uses a 'SUMPRODUCT' function so it's weighted:

https://lnkd.in/gSUMDhKY


PS: RFP's count here. Because unless you wrote the criteria, you were just handed how the customer's making a decision. You didn't guide it.

PPS: 2 new AE's start today, and yes, they're getting this SPIFF.

If your prospect was awake for 30 hours straight, right before your next meeting / demo / call, etc. starts today:

How would you change your approach?

- Shorten your sentences, keep it snappy
- Ask more questions, less monologues
- Focus on 1 point, not 10

My point is: 

→ It's a pretty fair analogy for what selling right now is.

I don't know about you, but H2 in 2025 is just... different. Seems like we're all feeling a little more chaos and overwhelm than a year ago. And our prospects are thinking about 1,007+ things that don't have anything to do with us. 

So effectively, we're selling with people at 20% brain battery 🪫🧠

Which means it's our job to make things SIMPLE.

Example: what if...

...instead of throwing a stack of product decks and case studies at someone, basically saying, "Here, your figure out the message for your CXO..."

...we sent them a 1-page exec summary, in an email with 3 bullets?

You know what's a total bummer?

When your champion’s excited. Exec sponsor's on board. And then…

Your deal slips, momentum dips, and your closed-won column wobbles.

content:
Little update on how I'm interviewing Mid-Market AE's right now — with the test I run you could take and run with too @ sales leaders:

1/ Pick an actual customer and why they bought.

2/ Send your candidate a couple call clips to watch before your call. Actual prospects, actual objections, real messaging live. 

3/ Have them run a 5-7 minute discovery, paired with a bite-sized demo (think 60 seconds). And you're interacting as the customer you picked.

4/ Hit pause. Then I break down feedback for them. Nuance they missed, what they need to switch up and change.

>> Now this is where the process comes to life:

A top hire is testing YOU at the same time. 

So you want them walking away feeling like, "Dang! This was WAY more helpful than anything I'm getting right now..." And you're giving them something they can use, regardless of whether they're hired. 

5/ Have them the exercise again while you play a new customer. 

>> This is the second key: 

You're looking for the change between the 1st and the 2nd run. 

Can they adapt quickly? Are they coming alive with the critique / feedback? Did they shut down and stay same-same in the 2nd? 

It's a signal of quickly they'll ramp. It's more about their rate, than just their baseline. 

6/ Finally, have them apply that discovery to follow-up in writing. 

Can they craft sharp, tailored messaging that'll get forwarded around by your buyers internally?

Do # 1 - 6, you'll find your person. 

Any other hiring pro tips from all the leaders out there I could be using right now? How do you run "tests" in your hiring process?

content:
Executives see your deal as just 1 of 10+ options they *could* be focused on. 

So your deal's likely going stall out if it's just framed around "competitors," not "categories" of spend (as Jen Allen-Knuth would say).

Take "revenue" as an example.

It's an outcome metric, with a LOT of different inputs. 

So unless you're in an RFP, your "competition" isn't in a G2 or Gartner grid. It's all the different levers they could be prioritizing to "drive revenue."

Here's the practice to use:

→ Recommending an "Approach"

Which is the top pattern I''m seeing our agent, Olli, correcting for AE's in deals when running a "stuck pipeline" play. Get this wrong, stuck deal. Get this right, pipeline velocity.

Recommending an approach is all about:

- Picking the right driver path
- Through a series of connected metrics 
- Compared to all other alternatives
- Built in a narrative like this: https://lnkd.in/gay4AEZA

Here's an example:

→ Let's say IKEA is trying to figure out how to boost online sales. And let's say our platform builds 3D visuals with AR/VR tech.

- We think there's an opportunity to drive up Average Order Value
- Tapping the "large items" category: Kitchens, closet organizers etc... 
- They're high-priced, and hard to visualize in your own space.

So customers aren't confidently hitting "buy now" online. 

First thing: 

There could be other driver paths in IKEA’s focus. Like product bundles to increase # of products purchased. So we have to address that first.

→ You do this in a written exec summary: https://lnkd.in/gay4AEZA

Which builds a narrative around the fact large category sales is declining the *fastest,* as IKEA moves to "small format" stores in urban areas. They can't stock full size items anymore, like they could in massive stores. 

So you're leading with:

1. Priority: Small format stores to capture urban markets
2. Problem: The "imagination gap" when customers can't see large items

If we’re aligned there that’s progress. NOW, we're ready to talk about our approach to that problem/priority compared to: 

- A buying team contact saying the main blocker to large item sales is the upfront cost. *Which means a "Buy Now, Pay Later" option.*

- Someone agreeing it’s the “Imagination Gap”, but says, "We can vibecode anything! Let's build AR/VR internally!

So now, there are 3 approaches to drive large category online sales: 

1. Internal AR/VR Build
2. Buying Your 3D Platform
3. Buying a "Pay Later" Platform

See? It's not just about other 3D platforms. It's a wider frame. 

Give it a shot with this framework. It's how you'll develop your thinking, and guide how your champion messages you to their exec: https://lnkd.in/gay4AEZA

More on this coming in a part 2 tomorrow too.

content:
Average sellers ask questions to get information. Standout sellers ask questions to create emotion.

Here are 3 examples to help you make this shift ⤵


1/ Confidence:

This feels like, "Oh wow, they really know their stuff."

→ For prospects feeling in over their head / don't know where to start.

Q: “Most people overlook X, which always turns out to be key. So let's start there — to what extent have you already explored X?”


2/ Empathy:

This feels like, "Finally, someone who gets me.”

→ For prospects who are standoffish, or misunderstood.

Q: “Is there something about this issue that others you’ve explained it to just don’t seem to understand?”


3/ Calm:

This feels like, “Ah, I can finally catch my breath.”

→ For prospects feeling anxious, like they’re always falling behind.

Q: “Oh wow, you’re further ahead than what I’m used to seeing. What have you already tried, that seems to be working?”


We could go on, but the idea is to always ask:

1/ What’s happening in my prospect’s life?
(e.g. layoffs inside their team)

2/ What negative emotion is this causing?
(e.g. anxiety, fear, uncertainty)

3/ What’s the opposite, positive emotion?
(e.g. hope, indispensability)

Then, ask accordingly. Release & replace.

Hope you can give it a shot this week,

content:
↔️ Horizontal vs ↕️ Vertical is emerging again in AI just like it did in SaaS with a bunch of landmines in the middle. Vertical is more interesting, IMO.  Here is why...

↔️ Horizontal Products = Incremental Gains * Lots of Tasks ↔️ 
This is the obvious category.  Chat GPT, Microsoft Copilot, etc.  These horizontal products get traction because users get incremental gains across a large variety of tasks and uses.  

But they have the same hurdles as horizontal SaaS products.  They can be used for so many different things which is a pro and a con.  The cons manifest in hard-to-activate users and build a habit.  

I think this area is over-explored at the moment. 

↕️ Vertical AI Products = 10X Gain * A Specific Task ↕️ 
Two of my favorites in this category are Fluint and EvenUp.  Fluint helps enterprise sales reps generate business cases.  EvenUp helps personal injury lawyers generate demand letters.   

Both of these provide 10X experiences on a very specific task. 

There are some common themes between these products:

1. Moderate Frequency - An injury lawyer, for instance, has to prepare a demand package for every injury case, while an enterprise sales rep must create a business case for most buying processes.

2. Tangible Connection To $$$ - In the case of Evenup, it's the settlement amount of the case, whereas for Fluint, it's the value of the enterprise deal.

3. High-Value Asset - The value associated with both companies’ outputs are typically high, often reaching five to six figures.

4. High Friction To Creation - The pre-AI manual creation process for both involves high levels of friction and is time-consuming to execute effectively.

5. Data Set To Draw From - Both EvenUp and Fluint have access (or building) to  data sets that they can draw from to do something that wasn't possible before. EvenUp leverages millions of public records on medical documents and case files, enabling them to tap into an entire knowledge base that would be challenging or impossible for a human to replicate. On the other hand, Fluint utilizes various data sources, including internal business cases and information gathered from sales calls, to customize their approach for each customer.

I imagine these are going to be great wedges into the broader workflow of their customers.  I believe these narrow use cases are under-explored at the moment. 

☠️The Middle Ground = Death Zone ☠️
Anything in the middle is trouble. 

That typically looks like a product providing incremental gains across a low volume of tasks.  

There are many products like new note-taking and presentation tools that fit this category.  They make the creation slightly better, but I have to replace a deeply engrained workflow to get those incremental gains.

content:
Here are my top 10 notes from the frontlines of founding / building / selling an AI-native product from 0 to 7 figures ARR — and what's new since 2022.


1/ Budget coming from payroll vs. tech.

Not everything is sliding into a "tech” or “software” line. 

I'm more often seeing teams delay backfills, or repurposing headcount, to create net-new budget for us. That didn't happen in pure SaaS days.


2/ POC ≠ pilot.

POC = “Will it work?” (Tech risk)
Pilot = “Will it get the outcome?" (Outcome risk)

Most people confuse this. Any AI product worth its salt should get you a POC with low resourcing, FAST. A pilot = fully resourced deployment, just in a limited scope to prove the outcome. 


3/ High NRR should be the norm. 

Our NRR's hovered between 150% and 160% over the last year — 

It's pretty common we'll land with 1 segment, then expand in the first 90 - 100 days after showing early evidence. 

Going enterprise-wide, upfront, does happen. But land and expand is hot right now, and more the norm. 


4/ "Decision criteria" is often just… vibes.

Things seem formal, like, "Oh yes, we've formed an AI committee.."  

But there's rarely a well-defined problem statement / specifics on how they'll run the evaluation. 

That's a big opportunity: 

When you find a champ who'll commit to running a process with you, get them clarity on how to guide the internal decision.


5/ Execs staying involved later stage.

I've been a little surprised (but also stoked) at how often a CRO/SVP Sales will say, "No, keep me on the invite" when I ask if they want us to run things direct with their team instead.

AI initiatives have their own board slides right now. So they're staying in the details for longer.


6/ There’s a speed mismatch.

Teams want to move fast. But security does not (understandably). So you'll end up having to threading the tension between two timelines:

(1) urgency from the business
(2) caution from risk / compliance

Expect both, and plan the sequence ahead of time.


7/ Services = high-value.

Used to be seen as lower-margin, lower-multiple. Now they’re often what makes the move to an agentic approach stick.

(And gives buyers confidence you won’t be another AI science fair.)


8/ Buyers are building again.

Everyone thinks they can spin up an MVP in a sprint with internal teams.

They forget all the "papercuts" that add up: debugging, building out tools for agents to properly use, fighting for resources.

Respect the “build” motion. But map out what scale will actually take them.

There's also a very real debate on when to buy horizontal vs. buy vertical (that's its own post)


9/ You can’t be vague.

Every deck says “increase revenue, decrease cost.” Lol.

People just want to know: what’s different here, really? And how does this actually work? 

The more specific you are, the more trust you earn.


I said 10 things in the post... but I'm about to be late for a meeting. 

So would love hear your # 10 for the list: 

Whatcha seeing in your deals?

content:
Here's a short story from my next book, coming at the end of the year.

I can't wait to share the rest with you soon.

_____

Friday afternoons are sacred during ski season in Colorado. 

I keep my calendar blocked so we can head to the mountains early, before traffic sets in, then I catch up on work at night.

One week, halfway through the drive on I-70, my phone rang. Josh, my champion at one of the top three credit card brands at the time, had been working with me on this deal for months and was calling.

"Hey, I gotta take this," I told my wife.

"About to meet with our SVP," Josh said, slightly out of breath. 

"Text me a few bullet points so I don't miss anything."

I pulled over, swapped seats with my wife, and while she merged back into traffic, I forwarded our working doc to Josh. Then thumbed out a couple quick bullets from it inside a text.

"BOOM! This is good. We'll get it done," he texted back.

Saturday came: 

"Hey, SVP's on board, bullets were perfect. Thanks for the help."

With a 3-year deal signed right after. (Well, after lots of redlines and procurement. But you get the point.)

The ancient Greeks had two words for time that capture this idea: months of work often come down to a few brief but brilliant bullet points.

(1) "Chronos" is linear time: days, weeks, and months you track in a CRM.

(2) "Kairos" time is different. It's a specific moment, when an opportunity is closing and about to disappear. It's about significance, not duration.

The parallel is complex deals don't happen in 6 or 12 month cycles. 

They happen in brief "kairos" moments: 2-minute syncs, texts between execs, Slacks between meetings. When your message, messenger, and timing align.

But those Kairos moments can also be scripted and planned. 

After this deal, I was watching a TED Talk from Bill Gates about fighting malaria. He'd written an 18-minute presentation, with a bunch of slides and statistics.

But the whole talk came down to one moment. Less than 10 seconds.

He calmly opened a jar, releasing mosquitoes into the crowd, saying, "There's no reason only poor people should experience this."

That one moment generated more malaria funding than all the research and data and slides in history. With *billions* in funding committed afterward.

We applied the idea by building "innovation briefs" for Fortune 500's, who were looking to buy emerging tech through our platform. Targeted briefs, with exactly the companies they needed, pulled out right when a prospect was leaning in.

"Wait, how'd you build this? This would have taken our analysts months."

We'd pull that moment forward, right upfront in the cycle.

You can, and should, curate the same types of brief-yet-brilliant experiences where your audience leans in, your message sticks, and they can't help but commit. This book will show you how.

After all, complex deals don't close over months.

They close in moments.

_____

content:
This is one of my all-time favorite discovery questions. But you'll have to try it to really "get it."  

You ready for it?

→ "What's an example of that?"

Kinda underwhelming at first.

But the reason it'll make a big difference is you'll get a story from inside the buying team, which you can then attach to your message. To help make sure it sticks with the buying team exec.

Which is what so many reps miss:

Data, ROI, value reports are all good... 

But small anecdotes get big deals done.

Just watch how the exec grabs onto a short, 15 - 20 second story, then repeats it over over again during the cycle, and all around their company.

e.g. from a cybersecurity platform:

You start the exec meeting by dropping an anecdote you picked up after calling on their security team:

"Last Friday at 6pm, Tom got a text from his daughter's principal saying they were holding her spot in the school play. He never made it—he was still at the office manually reviewing 10,000 login attempts after a security alert."

Then, you'd follow that up by saying:

"In fact, your team spent 60+ hours last week on manual security reviews, and 89% of those alerts turned out to be false positives."

That anecdote of Tom missing his daughter's play puts the numbers in context.

It makes them feel more urgent, because we focus on more emotionally striking statements — even if another statement is objectively more significant.

Plus, it's easier to remember.

TL;DR find a small but striking story, and your message gets way "stickier."

content:
This is a weird parallel... but AE's, hang with me here: the # 1 and ONLY thing guaranteed to stick with your buyers is how they feel, not what you say. 

But most of us couldn't label: 

(1) what our prospect's feeling walking into a meeting 
(2) our plan to leave them with a specific emotion after

Well, meet the "feelings wheel."

(Thanks, therapy.)

It starts with the 7 major emotions in the center, then gets more specific as you move towards the outside. 

Here's an example: 

____

(1) What's the main thing they're already feeling?

Let's say a team doing an internal build is blocking your deal. 

Well, are they feeling....

...Sad → Lonely → Abandoned?
(like everyone's willing to throw away 6 months of their work)

...Angry → Critical → Skeptical? 
(like a vendor couldn't possibly get all their internal nuances)

...Surprised → Confused → Disillusioned? 
(like what's even the point of what we're solving for here?)

Those are wildly different places to start from. Which should change your approach to running that deal: 

____

(2) What's the plan to leave them with a specific emotion after?

Someone who's:

Abandoned needs collaboration 
Skeptical needs confidence
Disillusioned needs hope

So for each of these, you'd switch up your approach: 

- Collaboration = outline why you need their tag team in a go-live 
- Confidence = matching a peer reference with similar complexity
- Disillusioned = revisiting the  problem statement and priority

Which should make its way into... everything.

How your prep your internal team, how you write a forwardable email, how you frame up the exec summary, how you guide your champion's next step. 

____

"After this meeting, we need them to feel [ X ]" is a dedicated line at the top on my key account prep sheet for context. 

And no, after a few of these, you don't need to pull out the wheel any more.

I know it's not exactly hard "dollars and cents" ROI... 

But anyone else listing "emotion" as part of account prep? Or am I out in left field with this one?!

content:
When the internal buying convo's happening about you, without you, go off script and your champion can't adapt... well, $50k - $100k+ of quota just evaporated into thin air.

AND YET, most sales teams spend 80% of their time, tech spend, and training focused on live sales calls. (Which = ~10% of the buying process)

That's whack. 

So here's an in-depth breakdown to fix that: 

→ How to build champions, by building business cases together. 

In a way they've internalized the storyline (go read Michael Shields' latest post on what happens when they don't).


1/ Start light with a few sentences on 1 page + placeholders.

Know the questions and gaps you need to fill in. 

→ “Hey, if I plan to build out a recap before our call with [ next stakeholder ], Are you down to add a comment or two on waht I've missed before?”

Gain agreement live, then drop your recap into a shared space. 

(Go look below my name on this for frameworks to start with)


2/ Co-sell the problem first.

- At the start of the next call, pull up what you wrote. 

- Include your (potential) champion’s comments to showcase the collab.

- The key is that THEIR name shows up in your doc. Not yours. Which is how you "rent" their track record to back the words on the screen.

Then pull in the next contact’s point of view:

→ “Here’s where we left off after our last convo. What stands out, and what are we missing from your point of view?”


3/ Assign actions and track down customer data.

Add some placeholder data inside and say:

→ “No doubt I’m off base here, this is based on our typical customer benchmark. So wondering who we could work with to update this?”

People can’t help but correct what’s inaccurate.

It’s a great way to test if you’re actually building a champion too. Do they follow through? Do they make time in a busy calendar?

And, very important: can they get things done internally?


4/ Continue to update and develop async.

Talk *specifically* about what you’ll both do between meetings. 

(People tend to follow through on verbal commitments.)

It keeps momentum high, and it’s like this quote from Jeff Bezos:

→ "The great memos are written and re-written, shared with colleagues who are asked to improve the work, set aside for a couple days, then edited again with a fresh mind. They simply can't be done in a day or two."


5/ Show your work-in-progress to the exec sponsor.

Ask them to weigh in early. They should see it long before they sign off. 

The big faux pas here is making the “big presentation” the first time they see it.

(I like sharing in edit mode, with everyone’s comments in view. It changes the posture to a working session & listening. Not presentation & pitching.)


The process works, and it’s way more fun to sell this way. 

Selling with buyers > selling to.

What tips would you add in?

content:
At the risk of over-simplifying things, every complex deal (that you'll win) has this 1 point in common. Hands-down, it's the most consistent point I’ve picked up over the last decade+ of doing this job:

→ A VP-level contact, with a bold personality, who got there quickly or nontraditionally.

Complex deals are less about the size of the contract ($), more about the number of contacts (#).  

Which means you've got a whole lot of differing opinions and conflicting incentives, all trying to agree on a path forward. 

And sure, you need champion(s), plural. 

But really, you need 1 anchor, who's going to be the center of everyone else.  And this type of VP profile generally means: 

(1) The right blend of influence and interest. 

Where they both *can* and *want* to make something new happen. And they're just weird/bold/outspoken/interesting enough to break the norm.

(2) They’re close enough to the day job.

So they can still "feel" why your specific approach and product is valuable, vs. an executive who has to stay higher level.  

(3) But they also know the overall company priority. 

They can link the day job and what you do back to top-line initiatives, in a way somebody who’s lost on the ground floor can't. 

1 + 2 + 3 = you have a shot at getting the deal done

If you add # 4 (you turn them from a contact into a champion) and # 5 (you enable them to go sell internally with a clear message). 

Then, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = Closed Won. 

By selling with champions.

So in our deal reviews, I’m always asking: 

→ Can you pull up our "main" champion's profile? 

Then I'm looking at what their last 3 - 4 years looked like:

- Where did they come from? 
- Did they get pulled over by an exec who left/recruited them? 
- Did they run through multiple levels / titles in fast succession? 

And then I'm writing 1 prompt of all our transcripts / emails / deal data:

"Show me 3 soundbites from [ Contact ] where they've got a strong opinion and will speak out." 

Those soundbites will tell you A LOT.

Because if they don't share a strong opinion with you, how confident are you they'll do that for you, when you're not in the room?

content:
Here's one more of my favorite discovery questions.

It's all about finding "The Thing Behind The Thing." Try asking: 

"Being able to [ summarize your main benefit/outcome ] is obviously helpful. But beyond the obvious, what would a successful project like this enable you to do, that you can’t today?" 

Most times when you ask about outcomes, you'll get the same, persona-level answers everyone's after. 

But to really build out a strong business case, it's about getting to the second- and third-order consequences of what you're enabling. 

(It's how you'll build interest at an exec level, and across the whole company.)

So the keys here: 

(1) You're taking the most likely answer off the table in the first part.
(2) Listen to exactly how they describe what comes next. 

Some examples: 

- Faster page loads → increased conversion % → higher revenue / visitor
- Better quality control → fewer defects → reduced warranty costs
- Better reviews → higher patient scores → increased reimbursement

And the key is, what specific words and phrases do they use for the 2nd / 3rd order answers?

content:
Last night, we’re all sitting around a big L-shaped couch around 9:30pm on a Saturday night. 

I’m spent, so I decide to go to bed, say “goodnight” to everyone in the L, they say “night” back, except my dad. Who’s totally locked into his iPad. 

“Dad… goodnight.” And nothing. Just focused.

(My parents are in Colorado this weekend, hiking on vacation.)

So I ask my mom, who’s next to him, “What movie is dad watching?”

Saturday night, in the zone. Must be a good one.

“Oh it’s not a movie. Case lectures,” she says.

Translation: he’s watching other radiologists present images from nuanced and obscure patient cases, talking about the latest diagnostic techniques. 

So, even in the twilight years, chair of the department, on vacation, he’s watching cases. 

And loving it. 

He’s like his own dad in a lot of ways: even when “Pop” couldn’t operate anymore, he’d still scrub into the operating room as an advisor. 

I didn’t go into medicine, but I hope this is a “generational” thing:

Finding work that feels like play. 

Which is a huge gift.

A lot of my next book (coming this fall) was written at 9pm some nights, or 6am other mornings, because I had a lot of fun, and wouldn’t have been able to sleep because I was thinking about it.

And maybe one day, I’ll catch my daughter, late at night on a family vacation, locked in on her iPad learning and loving it. 

(Here’s her at 6 months old, with Papi reading to her from the journal of American medicine 😂) 

Now of course, everyone has to do lots of stuff they’ll hate. Admin, bureaucratic work, soul sucking stuff. But on the whole:

I’m writing this for two reasons:

(1) Have you found “work” that feels like play? If so, how could you spend more time doing it? 

(2) Who’s someone that’s almost weirdly passionate about what they do? Could you spend more time with them?

Even if it’s not your field, there’s something energizing about that.

content:
Most enterprise deals will come down to 2 things:

1/ Discovering an internal priority execs are already sold on.
2/ Credibly showing how you’ll impact a specific, related metric.

Applied to your deals, the idea here is always work to:

1/ Build a narrative linking your champions’ biggest problem to a company-wide priority. Connect the dots in writing for them.

Because way too often, they’ll go heads down and focus on their own issues, without explicity calling out the strategic link.

2/ Create a logical bridge between a top-line metric and its drivers your project can directly impact.

e.g. maybe an ecomm prospect's focused on driving up Average Order Value as a key revenue driver — but it's been on the decline lately.

Does your platform help there?

Great. Show the impact on current → future order value, when your platform recommends bundled orders and dynamically adjusts discounts based on shopper / loyalty history. 

To get the right mix of new products + discount strategy.

An exercise in here for you:

If you went deal-by-deal in your pipeline, could you label the exec-level metric you impact? And why it matters to the exec?

What would happen if every QBR/deal review started with just those 2 questions? 

And you looked for customer-specific answers vs. persona-level fluff?

content:
The minimum viable “score x stage” is a concept only a few sales leaders anchor exit criteria to — but every team should. 

There are two big reasons why:
 
(1) Frameworks make deals "visible," and let you test them against a standard: what don’t we know, but should? Do we have enough to keep going?
 
(2) It's equally about guiding a prospect’s decision as your own team, and ensuring you’re both not racking up too much “deal debt.” (Investing time in deals that won’t yield results.)
 
To show you what I mean, we teamed up with Ebsta on a data report that studies 665,000+ deals. 

Since it’s fairly universal, we used MEDDPICC, and normalized stages to breakout the average score x stage:
 
– Stage 1 = 2.9 / 5
– Stage 2 = 3.3 / 5
– Stage 3 = 3.6 / 5
– Stage 4 = 3.7 / 5
– Closed Won = 4.2 / 5

It’s interesting data, because it’s also the guiding idea behind the "Sales Process 2.0" we've been working with customers on:

→ Define 1 clear exit criteria x stage based on buying behavior
→ Capture “evidence” in a written business case, scored x stage
→ Ensure the score (and deal) grows stronger at every stage
 
You can think of a 1-page business case as the customer-facing version of your internal MEDDPICC scorecard — created with them, building over time to guide a decision.
 
Got a lot more data I'm breaking down with Guy Rubin live on Thursday:

https://lnkd.in/ga_p7rui
 
We'll talk how to map this data onto your current pipeline too, so you know exactly which deals to advance — and which to walk away from.

Hope to see y'all there.

content:
@ sales leaders: let’s say a founder comes to you and says, “Hey, we’re churning like 35% of our customers — they say the post-sales experience with us is brutal. What should we do?”

You likely wouldn’t say: 

“First things first, increase new logos acquired to make up the gap.”

That would be a wildly expensive and difficult way to grow.

Instead, you’d likely say priority # 1 is to keep the customers they already have. Why are customers leaving? Can we fix that?

Now, you also wouldn’t say *stop* acquiring new logos. It’s always “and-and,” just lower on the list: 

1. Fix post-sales.
2. Acquire more.

And yet…

WE DO THIS ALL THE TIME in our sales process.

Most sales teams *think* they have a top of funnel problem. When it should actually be 2nd or 3rd on the list.

Because so often, the fix for 19% close rates (aka “churning” deals we already have) in practice is... just more prospecting. (19% close rate = 5.2X coverage)

So here's a gut-check I'll often ask on our demos to consider: 

“If we pull up a few of your Stage 2 - 3 deals *right now,* how many have a written problem statement? One that:

- Includes the buying team’s data
- References a strategic priority
- In that specific customer's words?

Often, it just doesn’t exist.

The discovery's stuck at a persona-level, the "problem" is "they need [ X ] feature," and the sales experience is all product-centric.

Even in deals where we already spent $2k - $10k+ to source that deal.

If you're with me, here are my top 3 steps to start focusing on the mid-funnel:

- Grab this framework: https://lnkd.in/gay4AEZA
- Compare it to this scorecard: https://lnkd.in/gnpe66fT 
- Test for it in deal reviews like this: https://lnkd.in/gdnk5EKV

content:
If enterprise sales was a movie, here's the cast: 

1/ Mister Rogers (h/t Jen Allen-Knuth)
- Never gives an opinion, just asks "What's everyone think?"
- Schedules follow-up meetings to discuss the previous meeting
- Brings 8 people to a 15-minute check-in

2/ Stealth Researcher
- Knows pricing, competitors, customer references before call 1
- Asks oddly specific questions about things you never mentioned
- Has screenshots of your LinkedIn profile from 2019

3/ The Process Pro
- Insists on following their 47-step vendor eval forms
- Reschedules meetings if no agenda 48 hours in advance

4/ The Accountant
- Negotiates shipping costs on million-dollar (software) deals
- Asks for discounts before seeing the price

5/ Title Collector
- Name-drops execs they've "worked with" at every major company
- Wants to grab coffee to "explore synergies" 

6/ Technical Skeptic
- Assumes your software will break their entire infrastructure

Here's one of my favorite early-stage discovery questions: 
 
"I’m guessing [ paraphrase the topic / problem ] isn’t your full-time focus right now, so what projects would you say are listed before this on your team’s next meeting agenda?" 

I use this one, because most reps ask questions that tie back to their product, which is an issue: it just creates the illusion of buying interest. 

Kind of like shining a flashlight in a dark room, while keeping the light focused on a small corner — you can't see what else is there.

Better to move the light around the room. (It’s how you’ll spot the ghosts.)

That's what the phrasing of the question helps you do, because it assumes there are *higher* priorities:

-  Prospects are more likely to give you the real story
-  Meeting agendas are practical / easy to visualize
-  Which leads to a more specific answer 

And hey, if they confirm it's the # 1 thing, it usually comes with a little more context as to why.

You tried a version of this before? What'd you find if so?

content:
AE's, getting ghosted in the mid-funnel? Here's my email rewrite for one AE with a 3-question framework, that cuts out the classic problem you might be making too (without realizing it):

The problem: most of our mid-funnel emails are "repelling." 

Meaning, we push deals *further* away instead.

The opposite of that is a "magnetic" email: 

Messaging that draws us in.  Here's the before & after + framework: 


→  The "Before" Email (Repelling)
________

Subject: Almost June 

Hi Katy,

I'm thinking we need to get our kickoff scheduled this month, to make sure your team's ready for the August design sprints we discussed. 

I'm concerned we're falling behind on our timeline, and if we're not able to confirm in the next week, we'll probably have to delay to later this fall. How is that going to affect your overall project goals?

Let me know how I can help, I'd love to setup that kickoff for us all soon.

______


^this AE sells a design platform, and it's not a "bad" email.

I asked her what 1 word her contact is likely feeling in her day to day. 

Her answer was "overwhelmed." (Her champion is talented, and every exec wants her leading their projects.) 

So, what happens when an overwhelmed person they’re falling behind? (They ignore you, and go into survival mode.)

So we flipped that emotion into its opposite, in our re-write: 


→ The "After" Email (Magnetic)
_________

Subject: Design Sprint

Katy, talked with our team to make we're set for your design sprint.

We built a shortlist of steps for kickoff, to make sure we're on track. Turns out, you're ahead of the game with the component library you built for [ project X ]: ~45% of the way there, just need [ items X and Y ] next.

Anything changed with timing on your side? 

(I know the fall launch is key, so we're up to adjust if so.)

_______


See the difference? 

Now, here's the framework to try if you're getting ghosted:

(1) What negative emotion is killing momentum? 
e.g. overwhelmed

(2) What’s the opposite, positive emotion? 
e.g. calm, on top of it

(3) What words flip that negative into the positive?
e.g. "ahead of the game"

💌

Contrary to what you'll read around here... you can't spot the "rockstar" rep every sales leader wants to hire by quota attainment:

Lines like "180% to quota" and "210% of plan" are good. 

Of course.

But what most reps forget to share while they're interviewing is how *team* attainment changed, because they joined.

Good reps are solo acts, legendary reps are multipliers.

They not only beat their number, they raise the bar. Everyone else around them starts to elevate their game, too. 

And that's the job of every sales leader: 

To beat a *team* target. Because the number your leader carries is always, always bigger than what any 1 rep (even a "rockstar") can deliver.

(Caveat: I have hired and work with reps who very literally represent 30% of new ARR booked. Even at 9-figure run rates. I'm setting them aside.)

Here's a quick example of this: 

→ 2 teams of 6 reps each + $800K quota/rep.

→ Team A: The "Rockstar"
Rep 1: $2M
(+) Reps 2 - 6 @ avg. of $600K/rep
(=) $5M 

→ Team B: The "Multiplier"
Rep 1: $1.4M
(+) Reps 2 - 6 @ avg. of $750K/rep
(=) $5.15M

Most every sales leader wants to lead Team B.

Now, you might be thinking, "A $150K difference isn't *that* big."

That's true. 

But for the leader on Team B, they're (1) less reliant on a single contributor, (2) they have a happier team overall, and (3) they'll have better rep retention. 

Less turnover = less ramp time + more upside next year with tenured AE's.

So the next time you're interviewing for a role you'd love to land: 

Don't just talk about your attainment. Show how you helped drive up team performance:

- Putting together an SKO session.
- Documenting frameworks that are working for you.
- Using your commute time to call a peer and trade ideas.

That's the rep every leader wants on their side.

AE's are taught to ask about the "decision process." Which is okay. But what buyers *don't* say, then go do internally (and we never see), is where deals are actually won and lost.

So, sales leaders: 

Here's how to learn how the “internal sale” really goes down in your deals.

1/ Pick a deal that closed recently with each AE.
Ideally one with an open/transparent champion.

2/ Have them write up the decision process they know. Based on what they heard / helped with during the purchase.

3/ Ask them to send a version of this email. To setup a short call, for more context/follow-up questions.

_______

Subject: Process Feedback

[ Buyer ], thrilled we get to work together now, thanks to all the time you spent on [ project ]. There was for sure room for me to be a stronger partner, too. 

So I’m wondering:

Would you be up to share what happened behind the scenes? 

It'd be interesting to compare how I *think* you evaluated us, vs. how your team actually did. (e.g. emails, convo's, docs, I never saw, but you worked hard on.)

Lunch on me if you’re up for it?

_______

4/ Together, ask your champion (now customer) to point out gaps. What'd they do, that you didn’t see?

5/ Look for a couple patterns in what you hear. Guide that step in your next deals.


We give feedback to our reps all the time.

But how often do our AE's hear it directly from our buyers?

What you hear together will be fascinating. Promise you that.

content:
Lawyers and Artists: my two ways for thinking about enterprise sales in the next 10 years. Because each get paid to do what you won't let AI do by itself.

(But they're both enabled by AI.)


→ Lawyers:

The "technical" path. They're paid to not be wrong.

Sure, you could have AI draft your investment agreements, but the downside of being wrong here is big and expensive. 

So we'll pay $1,000/hour for technical expertise. They know the nuances and you don't. (And in part, we're buying confidence.) 


→ Artists: 

It's about "taste." An opinion on how things should be.

Sometimes, you'll look at art and say, "I could do that." And at times, we could — but we didn't. 

When there's no objective right or wrong, we have to choose what to keep and what to delete. Leaving behind something that's curated, and satisfying.


*Both are ways to group the core skills behind enterprise sales.*


→ "Lawyers" have technical skill: 

We're paid to guide enterprise-wide decisions when the stakes are high, the downside's expensive, and execs crave confidence.

→ "Artists" have taste: 

We're paid to create something new, to motivate a stalled group to follow, with a message that leaves them feeling, "Wow, so well said. Better than I'd say." 


It's not perfect, but here's the skills matrix I've been sharing with leaders we work with. A blend of both technical skills and taste. 

Nobody's born an artist. Or a lawyer, unless you're Louis Litt. You work at it.

content:
Get this: the framework that all of history’s greatest stories are built on. From Steve Jobs intro’ing the iPhone, to MLK’s “I have a dream.”

The story is always shaped with this alternating pattern:

- What is (current state, sad / negative)
- What could be (future state, happy / positive)

The graphic shows the "sparkline" from Nancy Duarte’s research.

It's the kind of story arc that sucks you in, and keeps you locked in.

Every AE can use this basic outline, too.

_____

1/ Beginning:

Describe your buyers’ current reality in a way that feels scary accurate.

Lead with a truth they’ll agree on. One that shows that you "get it." 

You deeply understand their context. 


2/ Turning Point # 1

Start contrasting "what is" vs. "what could be."

Make sure the difference between these is as wide as possible.

Your job is to create desire, then show how your ideas fill that desire.


3/ Middle:

Your storyline has to raise the stakes here. What’s it all for?

Then continue to alternate: what is / could be / is / could be, etc.

Create and resolve tension in the story, demo, wherever you tell it.


4/ Turning Point # 2:

Make a clear call to action. What should people do?

Clarify the rewards that’s waiting for them if they do.


5/ Ending:

Recap the big idea, and create a sense of calm confidence.

_____

A note I’ll add too: good stories aren’t all “plot.” 

They’re all people. They're about who we’re becoming.

Less, "send your employees surveys to measure happiness." 

More, "become a caring leader, focused on the human experience."

What hooks us is always a matter of identity. So contrast:

- Who someone is when they first meet you.
- Who they could become after (+ adopt your ideas).

Give it a try this week: 

In business cases, demo prep, or short convo's prepping your champions.

“Hey, sounds like there could be a good fit to help with X, based on Y, so I can plan to draft up a summary for us, based on what I heard.”

Now here’s the key setup:

“If I get you that first draft, I’ll have a couple questions no doubt, and probably miss a few things. So if I share it with you, you open to giving quick feedback?”

Their response is a good signal here ^

→ Step 2: Schedule it.

“You’ve probably going a stack of Slacks / emails after this, so, what if I send you a 15-min calendar invite to review it?”

“You don’t have to join a Zoom or anything, just to carve out the brainspace for you.” (They’ll smile.)

“When should I sent the invite for?”

^this tells you a LOT about priority level. 

→ Step 3: Send it.

Write the summary, then drop a link to it in the body of the calendar invite.

And, since it’s on your calendar too, you can drop a quick comment in the doc during the invite. 

(If they keep the invite / share feedback, that's a VERY strong sign.)

content:
Learning to work on both the "right and left of the decimal" is some of the best advice I ever got, and a must-hear for AE's learning to sell strategic/enterprise. When I first had to own a P&L, it's what my old VP of FP&A would say:

"Nate, you're only thinking on the right of the decimal right now."

Or when I'd make a big ask: 

"You're way out on the left side... what's the right saying?"

Take a number like $10,100,000.27 

→ The "right side" is the day-to-day details: what happens in any one deal/store/site on a day swing small numbers, down to $ and cents. 

← The "left side" is high-level strategy: decisions that show up with 7 / 8 figure outcomes months/quarters/years later.

Neither is "better." It's always "both-and." 

Because...

- Strategy without operating detail
- Operating detail without strategic context

...will both fail.

So when you're selling enterprise, your job is simply to:

(←) Help people on the right message up to people on the left. 

- Sounds like: "Oh wow, you said that way better than I could have." 

- Skillset: Enabling a manager who loves the technical ability you give reframe why it's important to them, around what's important to an exec. 

- Frameworks: Written inside a crispy exec summary, shared with a forwardable email that makes it easy to just hit "send" internally.


(→) Help people on the left understand people on the right.

- Sounds like: "Oh really? That's surprising... how'd you find that?"

- Skillset: Discovery + deep research that creates 'nonobvious' insight, and leads to an exec seeing old topics in new ways. While feeling "in the know."

- Frameworks: A sharp problem statement packaged up inside a short POV. 

^if you'd want to test these frameworks out, you can either hit the 'view my blog' option, or drop a comment and I can DM them to you.

content:
Ever had a "champion" go dark, then pop up weeks later, saying: "Hey, we're all set to sign now. $X for Y scope. I'll start the process..." ?

If you've seen that scenario (they ghost, then come around with a practically-done deal), it's often a sign:

→ They decided it was easier / less risky / better for them to fly solo.

We often talk about "testing" champions in a deal, for example:

- "Will you introduce me to your CXO?"
- "Can you share this data with me?"
- etc... 

Which is all well and good — you do need "evidence" someone's not just talking. They're actually moving things forward. 

But what about when they "test" us, the sellers, and decide they don't need or want us to run the deal with us?

And that's the thing: 

The strongest influencers in an org (who you want to champion you) are going to run you through their own tests:

- Teamwork: "Do they bring me something I need and don't have?"
- Transparency: "Am I okay with them hearing closed-door convo's?"
- Trust: "Am I 100% in? Do I really trust this is the right path?"

If you've got the 3 T's squared away, THEN you're running a valid test. 

So when you setup a convo like: 

"Hey, seems like we both see a fit, but if we're not able to put some numbers to this, the project's likely going to stall. So how can we get..."  

And you ask for access/data/etc... it's a more clear yay/nay. You do or don't have a partner on the customer side. 

Otherwise, if you hear "no," could it be we failed their test first?

content:
Here's a legendary case study from Expedia, that's all about solving $100M+, enterprise-scale projects by framing up a sharp problem statement (and attaching it to an exec priority).

Their former Head of CX, Ryan O'Neill, was looking at call center data:

- For every 100 customers, 58 contacted support
- So support was fielding 20M customer calls/year
- They cost $5 each, creating a $100M/year issue
- And growing, with more customers booking online

So, support leaders were asking: 

"How do we cut time-to-resolution from 10 to 2 minutes?"

To cut cost-per-call from $5, to $1, and create a more efficient call center.

→ But what if that wasn’t the problem? 

The actual question to solve for was:

**Why was Expedia getting so many calls in the first place?**

The challenge is nobody actually owned that problem. (O'Neill gives the full breakdown on this in 'Upstream' by Dan Heath, very good read.)

So he took his data to their CEO, Dara, who attached *preventing* customer calls in the first place to his top priority. 

With a new project team, he looked at what drove call volume:

People needing their itinerary. It wasn’t getting through to their email.

Which reframed things entirely:

(Problem 1)   Slow resolution means high cost-per-call
(Approach 1) Faster call resolution reduces costs

Versus:

(Problem 2)   High call volume from itinerary requests
(Approach 2) Cut call volume by making itineraries accessible

After reframing the issue and making it visible on the dashboard and in emails, call volume dropped from 58%, to 15%. 

This is EXACTLY what enterprise sellers do: 

→ Find and frame high-cost, high-priority problems. 

So, here are two points on this:

(1) How to write a sharp problem statement:

"Every [ frequency ], at least [ reach ] are experiencing [ pain ], costing [ loss ]. If it’s not addressed by [ timeline ], that means [ consequence ]."

Applied to Expedia, this reads like: 

"Every month, at least 1.67M customers can’t find their itinerary and have to call support, costing $8.35M to resolve these requests. 

If it’s not addressed by end of year, we’ll see another $500M in lost, repeat purchase revenue from frustrated customers opting out of our loyalty program."

(2) "Layering" problems:

- 1st Level: “We’re paying $100M per year in support costs.”

- 2nd Level: “Angry customers aren’t enrolling in our loyalty program."

- 3rd Level: “Customer lifetime value (CLTV) increases with loyalty members making repeat purchases, so now, we’re missing $500M in future revenue.”

You could even say sales/marketing spend inflates CAC, spent for more first-time customers to offset lost loyalty revenue. 

(Which is really throwing off their unit economics.)

So Expedia dropping call volumes to 15% of bookings: 

- Saves almost $75M per year in support costs 
- Saves an estimated $500M in future revenue

That's huge. 

So a question for you: 

What % of your deals have a written problem statement? With edits or data from the buying team?

content:
If you're selling complex B2B deals: here's a shortlist of 10 things I strongly believe you can (and should) build your GTM process around:
 
1/ Effective deal reviews happen in < 60 seconds.
 
If you can't compress a deal into short, specific bullet points on numbers, names and dates, do you really know what it's about? 

1 page is all you need to spot gaps.

 
2/ Building a business case *is* the sales process. 
 
Not just one activity inside it. All other activities roll up into and are strengthened by it.

 
3/ Deals get done during the conversations about you, without you.
 
So write it out. Content can be part of your champions' conversations, even when you can't be. 

Plus, content keeps your own team (AE's, SE's, CSM's, etc.) on the same page.

 
4/ Writing isn't documentation. It's discovery.
 
It's the process of learning what you don't yet know (and then figuring it out). Making it the most-important, least-developed skill for sellers.
 
And the core reality we've built Fluint around.


5/ Efficiency is about less activity, not more.
 
More "finesse" than force: sellers who build more influence in the buying process win more revenue, with less activity over time.

 
6/ Buyers don't trust your ROI.
 
Numbers without a narrative are meaningless. But numbers *do* validate a decision the buying team's already made, based on the story.

 
7/ There are two types of problems: math and drama.
 
"Drama" is why the math problems go unsolved.

 
8/ Selling priorities > solving problems. 
 
Reps solving genuinely-costly problems lose deals all the time. A process has to frame the problem around an exec-level priority first.

 
9/ You don't "find" deal champions. You build them.
 
Like IKEA furniture. Over time, your process should transfer ownership in the deal from you, to them, by co-creating their solution.

 
10/ Multithreading isn't about adding more contacts. 
 
More contacts = more dysfunction. Create the minimally-viable committee, to build a "social safety net" around your core champions.


Which of these 10's most interesting? 

And, what would you add that I missed?

content:
7 reasons you shouldn’t sign that offer — even if the OTE looks good:


1/ Leadership doesn’t know the details.

If you ask, “What, exactly, are your top 20% reps doing differently?” 

And you hear… “They work really hard at mastering the product." That's probably not wrong, but it's likely far from what's actually happening. 

Compared to an answer like:

“They directly engage with exec buyers before Stage 3, by...  so they win 45% vs. 20% of deals, at an ACV of $89K vs. $46K...”


2/ Year 3+ isn’t exciting.

Most learnings and earnings come in Year 3+. The OTE may look good in year 1… but what comes next?

Let’s say you’re promised a growth path into enterprise.

I’d ask, “What’s the win rate in midmarket vs. enterprise?”

Because what if enterprise’s close rate is half of MM? If there’s no solid PMF upmarket, is that still exciting?


3/ A history of big swings in comp plans.

The comp plan you’re signing onto will change, no doubt.

So ask, “How does this compare to last year’s plan?” And, “How would you expect this to change next year?”

It’ll help you understand if you’re in a good long-term spot. (See above.)


4/ Territory rules are wonky.

Ask, “Which accounts will I work on?” (strategic work)
Or, “How are new leads distributed?” (higher velocity)

You should hear sound reasoning that’s good for the customer, too.

If you hear something like, “Everyone gets 10 zip codes”... run.


5/ The interview’s totally unstructured.

How dialed in is their process? Are the exercises specific and engaging?

If you’re bored or confused, that won’t change later.

Chances are reps feel like they lack clarity, and their internal process and enablement is just as messy.


6/ You can’t help but go overboard.

If we’re truly fired up about something, we overdo it.

They ask you for a sample account plan you already built, but you decide to go build 3 new ones, “So get this, Jenny said she was researching Nike yesterday, so I took a swing at…”

You’re just genuinely excited to start learning about their customer.


7/ Attainment’s on the decline.

I’d be more optimistic about a team with 50% rep attainment today, *IF* they were at 20% last year, and made serious changes.

Compared to another team at 50% attainment today, that was at 80% last year.

That’s a big red flag.


What'd I miss?

"I'm 75% to goal, X and Y slipped. I missed getting IT involved early. So I'm spending today getting July deals threaded with IT."

That's how you'll stick the landing today (as Paul Stansik would say).

Even if you're not ending at a 10/10.

content:
We've been building something, quietly. More like building *someone.*

His name is Olli.

Official launch is next week... but I couldn't wait. 

Late night, off the cuff video (sorry marketing). TL;DR here: www.fluint.io/olli

Olli's *the* AI agent specifically designed for complex deals. 

Over the last few months, I've been selling with him, ramping and teaching him, like my little shadow. (He's also got 120k+ deals under his belt already.) And I've grown increasingly convinced of a few things. So before Olli meets the world, a preview on our thinking + early look:


(1) Most AI lacks an "opinion."

And I think most of *want* someone who works with a point a view: something that "just works" from day 1. (Like Linear vs. Jira, for example.)

A built-in set of practices. Not, "Here, figure out how you want this setup."


(2) Hire *someone,* don't configure 50+ *somethings*.

Agentic selling should feel like onboarding a new hire—someone who brings experience, history, learning, then gets better over time.

Not a workflow sequence diagram you have to map out, with 30-100 "micro-agents" you have to stitch together. (Who's got that kinda time?) There's a niche market for the AI scientists here. Just not the ICP we build for.


(3) GTM = multiple roles all rowing together.

The job-to-be-done map in complex deals spans:

- RevOps (what's changing in our data?)
- Enablement (what do we do about it?)
- Training (here's how to do it...)
- Management (is it happening?)

An agent (that's effective), has to connect all that into one whole. Building anything less as a point solution is just going to struggle to get an outcome.


(4) High-value work, not admin tasks.

The broader narrative everyone loves is, "Free your sellers! Eliminate CRM data entry! No more admin tasks!"

And, I mean, yeah... but is the hard, strategic work actually getting done, even with that? The complex and sticky stuff—like a meaningul POV baked into an exec summary with a forwardable targeting the skeptics?

That's the stuff to build for. Not the admin.

It's hard and that's why it's worth it.


(5) Integration is good... but Agents need net-new tools to work with.

It's why so much that's coming out is just another chatbot.

Or a way to talk to Google from Slack. Fine. But it's why, before Olli, we built stuff like living documents, guided flows, playbook UI for Olli to show up in.
You can't put a new paradigm into old world SaaS. UX is very much alive and well, but it's actually got to be "AI native."


(6) Upstream execution drives everything.

What Olli does in Stage 1 will directly change what types of plays need to be run in Stage 3, 4, etc... downstream. First outreach to upsell, it has to flow.

(Plus Stage 1 + 2 actions = context nested inside Stage 3 + 4, etc.)

Full cycle or bust baby.


Thanks for nerding out with me. Meet Olli a little early: www.fluint.io/olli

Holy moly. Starting Friday feeling a weird combo of exhausted and excited: been running FAST on a'lotta things (launching Olli, finishing book # 2, new hires, closing on new capital, landing some fun new logos, etc.)

It’s felt like my trainer’s gone insane, holding their finger down on the “faster” button on the treadmill. While I’m already SPRINTING. (The trainer is me.)

But because of that, it’s put me back to the basics while selling.

Zeroing me in on the core, must-do stuff.

So here’s a shortlist I keep coming back to:

(1) Find the customer’s language. “How are you hearing your [ CXO ] talk about this? At your last all hands / offsite, what was their ‘catchphrase’ for this?” To lead with that in my follow-up: subject line, exec summaries, etc.

(2) Cover less topics, more deeply. “Hang on, can you help me understand that a little more?” “Layering” my discovery instead of “spreading” it out wider.

(3) Using next steps to gauge intent. “To match your timing, is this a ‘let’s talk tomorrow’ kinda thing, or more for later in the quarter?” Helps me “rank” my pipeline based on urgency.

(4) Engaging blockers early. “Seems like you want this more than [ revops ], unless I’m off there, what’s missing for them?” Why wait until too late to engage?

(5) Cut, cut, cut. 3 bullets > 1 page.

There’s more. But next meeting starting 🫡 

So to keep building out this shortlist together:

What’s your # 1, go-to skill you always make sure to do?

(Even when weeks get a little wild, what do you always come back to?)
