content:
I recently “stole” a late-stage deal out of another sales platform’s pipeline (even after the CRO’s revops advisor had been recommending it for months.) 

Here’s the skill that made it happen: 

→ Problem “framing.” 

And it’s hard to think of a skill that's more important than this for AE’s right now. Because the options/alternatives your customers have is only going up.

Here’s a copy/paste/trimmed convo with their CRO:

_____

CRO: “[ Peer CRO ] mentioned you in one a community chat. So before we’re all in on [ sales platform ], I thought I’d meet you quick.”

Me: “Nice. Well to start, can you walk me through what you’re solving for, and I can shortcut you to details from there?”

CRO: “We grew insanely fast, and our last CRO never had a second to breathe and tighten how we forecast. So slipped deals are just taken for granted. 

Part of it is we bundle physical and digital products, so it's complex. Lots to align on, so our revops consultant is rolling out [ platform ] for action plans. 

Making sure we’re sharp on project management, outlining steps to evaluate and close. Keeping prospects on track with the tasks we both need done.”

Me: “So deals slip if prospects don’t follow through on tasks. When’s that happening typically? Like, ‘Stage 3’ or later, things go sideways?”

CRO: “Right, exactly.” 

Me: “Have you had deals where a prospect is pulling you along? Like, really trying to accelerate things?”

CRO: “Yeah, [ customer ] was that way.” 

Me: “What happened there?”

CRO: “We worked at the national level, to help launch their new service line. Letting them handle custom designs for short-run orders. 

It was great, because typically we just sell on cost reduction. So this was a new way of framing the value: a pathway into new markets.” 

Me: “Solid. And back of napkin: 

What percent of deals have a tailored story like that written down? Some type of strategy to get you away from a same cost savings message?”

CRO: “Oh, maybe 10%.” 

Me: “Gotcha. So for the 90%, to what extent do they slip because buyers don’t think the ‘why buy’ is worth it? Even though the ‘how to buy’ is clear? 

Kind of like you gave them homework… but they’re not even sure they want to take the class.”

CRO: **Slacking ops team** “Hey can you join this.”

______

At that point, we reframed the convo: 

- Project management for late-stage deals
- Vs. tailored exec summaries/account plans for early-stage deals

So we went from...

Problem # 1: Tasks to close fall behind
Solution # 1: Project management

To...

Problem # 2: Prospect de-prioritizes us
Solution # 2: Executive messaging

We never lose on content quality at Fluint. 

(Head-to-head’s / POC's are my absolute favorite.)

But the trick is selling the problem, before the product.

So the net for you:

- What's an entirely different problem you can solve?
- A problem that makes another offering’s “features” irrelevant?
- What are 2 - 3 disco questions you'll use to shift the problem frame?

content:
Here are 5 phrases I use in my discovery calls. Every. Single. Day.

They'll help you go deeper and build influence, without the cringe.

Anyone can use them, and if you use all 5 in a convo, that's powerful.


(1) "Could you tell me more about when…"

Encourage stories that release emotions, not short statements.

Catharsis is powerful.


(2) "To spend just another second on that…"

It's rarely about 10X covering more topics.

It's about going 10X deeper on the topics that are most important.


(3) "Ah, so, the reason I’m asking this is…"

Share your intention. You'll encourage transparency, and get the full story.


(4) "How does this relate to when you said…"

Create a bridge back to earlier answers, or from others on the buying team.

It builds a pattern in the buying team, and shows you're listening.


(5) "Got it, so in my experience…"

Share your point of view to break up the interview.

Which helps you earn the right to go deeper.

content:
Big deals happen offstage. So your # 1 job is to script the backroom drama: a simple narrative to drop in Slack threads, exec convo's, etc... but you've gotta avoid these 5 mistakes.

I broke them down in a tag team with 30MPC: https://lnkd.in/g5NeFPCM

(Back at it with the legends Nick and Armand!)

Top 5 mistakes to avoid: 


→ 1. Making it yours, not theirs.

How many edits and redlines came *directly* from the buying team? 

Fluint data (73k+ deals) shows win rates jump 3X with 3+ edits from buyers. The "rule of 3." Because they’re taking ownership. It's theirs now.


→ 2. All numbers, no narrative.

An ROI model isn’t a business case. It’s a future maybe, without context. 

Narratives bring meaning to the numbers, then the numbers validate the decision your buyers already made based on the story.


→ 3. Your branding, not theirs.

Buyers don’t share branded decks with their execs. It's just a fact of life. 

Wrapping your message in pretty polish just signals “bias.” (Better off sticking with a white page and black font, or the buying team’s brand.)


→ 4. Long and vague.

Think in paragraphs, not pages. The headlines & highlights. 

Make it scannable with the BLUF (bottom line up front) to link back to an internal project/priority. Numbers, dates, unique catch phrases.


→ 5. Way too late. 

You're starting it late-stage to "get a deal closed." But the point isn't documenting what you know. It's discovering what you don't — early. 

So share it early, with gaps.

content:
I left a CEO meeting a few years back feeling insanely frustrated. But after I stopped pouting and finished my juice box, I had an "aha" moment that completely changed how I think about selling to the C-Suite. 

With a few must-do's I still use every week. 

Some context:

We sold to enterprise innovation teams, so the VP Innovation intro'd me to their CEO for a 20-min convo, to run through the project we wanted to get funded. I thought it went pretty well, we got a greenlight for the next meeting.

Which was with their broader team, and a few different business unit heads.

CEO kicked off the call: 

"Nate, nice to meet you. Since I didn't get a chance to talk with you yet, to hear what you and Erica are thinking, let's start there with the group." 

And here's the thing: 

We HAD met before. 

We spent 20 minutes running through the plan with him and Erica. 

He just had zero memory of it. 

He asked almost identical questions as last time, as if that first convo had been completely wiped from his brain. So at first, I was like: 

"How rude is this guy? Seriously??" 

But after that meeting, it hit me: that was 100% on me. 

Apparently, everything I said in the first convo was so uninteresting that the CEO wasn't going to waste any brainspace on my words.

It was the opposite of sticky. 

It was totally forgettable.

So I started doing 3 things before these convo's.

(I'll break them down live next week: https://lnkd.in/gdZTxAwB )

1/ I write out a 1-page business, then compress it down to a 2-sentence soundbite, with 4 parts: what's changed, an insight, good/bad outcomes. A wildly simple way of packing the full convo into 30 seconds.

2/ Then I come with 1 question that I think will lead to a, "Huh, I hadn't thought about it like that" moment. Which helps that soundbite sink in. 

3/ I pick 1 word I want the exec to feel after (which is the only thing guaranteed to stick: that feeling). It usually the opposite emotion of what their day feels like.

Written docs are the “container” your process lives in, because:

e.g. POV drives a problem statement, that sits in the full biz case, which is context for a go-live plan, etc.

It’s how we see where, exactly, a customer is in the buying journey. While making it visible to everyone.

content:
Most sales books are full of fluff or painfully outdated. But I’ve got one “must-read” recommendation - and here are 3 takeaways you need to know now:

1) The steps you take to sell your product are not the steps your prospects take to buy it

If you have a 3 month sales process, you probably meet with the customer 6-12 times over that period, and exchange a decent number of emails. 

But most of the work to evaluate your solution is happening without you. It’s happening in 1:1s between your champion and their boss. 

It’s happening in internal slack threads. It’s happening in team meetings where people debate pros/cons of different solutions. 

While you are sitting by your laptop hoping for a response to your “can I get an update on progress” emails, your buyers are evaluating without you. 


2) You communicate with both facts and feelings in the sales process - and feelings matter more

Feelings are sticky - you’ve probably heard the phrase “people don’t remember what you tell them but they remember how you make them feel.” 

And all feelings aren’t equal - the most important emotion to drive in sales is confidence. When buyers are confident, close rates are 2.6x times higher!! 


3) Match your buyer’s language, format, design as much as possible 

Nearly every company gets this wrong. Everything sales and marketing sends to the customer is 100% branded for their own company. Their logos, their quotes, their stories, their product. 

Great books lead to great takeaways. If you haven’t yet read “Selling With” by Nate Nasralla you are rapidly falling behind the modern buying experience. 

For a deeper breakdown, take a few minutes to watch the video!

content:
AE's: look at how this ad swaps vague for "visual" language. 

"Pretty people" → "supermodels"
"Big cities" → "London" 

Harry Dry broke this ad down in a great episode of "How I Write" with David Perell, and I sent it over to one of our customers last night.

It's a favorite of mine, even though it's B2C vs. B2B.  

Because it's a fast and easy practice for AE's to sharpen their writing: 

Just get way, way more specific:

Vague <—————X-> Specific
"Pretty" <——————> "Supermodel"

There's usually a gap between what we see in our minds, and what reality actually is. So to start a new project in B2B, you have to believe:

1/ It’s known
2/ It won’t hurt too much

If you can't picture exactly how something will happen, your mind adds more time and cost and energy and pain, etc... 

It paints a grim picture to keep us away from the unknown.

So, don’t say:

“Setup's a snap with white-glove support and a dedicated customer advocate.”

Instead, say:

“You’ll spend 3 hours over 2 weeks with Juan during data migration. Then, Lucy's your go-to. Email or text her anytime.”

With a picture of Juan and Lucy:

Vague <————————X-> Specific
"White-glove"<————X-> "Juan and Lucy"

When you write something down, picture someone asking:

“Can you be more specific?”

If you can, then say that.

You’d be surprised how often deals are lost because of wild imaginations.

content:
This was the most memorable period of my career, and it forever shaped the way I sell: roadtripping through small towns of middle America, meeting dozens of customers in a few short months.

This was over a decade ago, while building my first startup. We figured the best thing to do as an unknown brand was hit the road.

We built a platform that organized a nonprofits’ donor data, then video-conferenced a fundraising coach to guide them on strategy. 

To create some context here: 

This was before Zoom was “a thing,” and our ICP was the type who did all their bookkeeping / fundraising on paper. Or a spreadsheet, at most.

So the best way I can describe bringing that product to market was like telling someone who loved MapQuest printouts about Google Maps. With a built-in tour guide, who’d had looked at all their life’s travels.

Lots of raised eyebrows.

So we’d setup email campaigns (paying an intern like $0.02/email to research them, because a Zoominfo subscription felt like a luxury). Inviting people to a community center, school, or even a park—wherever we’d set up shop.

Then we'd repeat in another town.

There was this one stop we did, about an hour outside Des Moines, Iowa.

One guy who showed up ran a nonprofit for families who couldn’t afford a true memorial service. They'd provide a proper burial and service, for $0.

He was wearing overalls, stained, with dirt all up in his fingernails. Because he had just been digging a grave. Very literally.

And I remember seeing his expression while I showed off this pretty, colorful dashboard to a group of people with a little projector, talking about how we’d match them with a personal fundraising coach who understood them. 

Like “Match . com for nonprofits.”

The look on his face right then, and the core of our conversation after everyone else filtered out of the room, was, in short: 

“How could someone *possibly* understand my job without rolling up their sleeves, and grabbing a shovel?”

And I know this example is a little intense.

But I think about that look a few times a year, when I'm too wrapped up in my product, and need to remember the core question every prospect is looking at me with, thinking:

“You’re an outsider. How could you possibly understand me?”

So my points in sharing this with you:

(1) The little stuff goes a long way. If you’re showing up to a construction site, for example, rent a pickup, not a Prius.

(2) Figure out a way to get on-site with your ICP early in your ramp. Even if you’re in SMB, walk down the street.

(3) Your discovery questions aren’t for you to get the information you need. They're to create the emotion your buyers need. (And the most powerful emotion is to feel understood.)

And here's a 2012 iPhone photo from that season. Of one of our first sales hire back in the day, and a good, good friend to this day, Travis.

What’s the most memorable customer visit you’ve done?

content:
Here’s a $0, 5-minute exercise you can run with your AE's, to show them just how much of their messaging gets through to executives (or not). 

Executives out there, is this not spot on? 

I ran this for Workday’s enterprise team as part of a program Andrew Barry designed for them, it was a total hit.

Step 1:
Have each AE pick a topic they absolutely love. Their thing. 

Step 2: 
Have them present on it for 5 minutes to a group of 3 - 4 AE's. 

Step 3: 
Meanwhile, other AE's in the "audience" try to get some emails sent during it. 

Step 4: 
At the end of the 5 mins, ask the AE's in the audience: what stuck? What do they remember?

The point is to replicate what it's like to work with someone who has so much going on, so much flying at them, their meetings are an exercise in mindshare.

So you're always starting off with "continuous partial attention." 

And your job is to insert small phrases: 

- "The reason I'm telling you this is..."
- "Given your focus on X..."
- "You might think... but actually..."

Try it out. 

You'll notice each AE gets better and better at reeling a distracted group back in. 

Finding short phrases that keep them stuck in the present. Like honey for the brain 🍯

content:
I relate far too much, far too often with Andrew Wilkinson's take: "Most successful people are just a walking anxiety disorder harnessed for productivity."

(This isn't me labeling myself a "successful" person to be clear.)

There's been a pretty consistent pattern in my career, where a major milestone (record quarter, an exit, biggest career deal, building a new biz unit from $0 to 30% arr, etc...) were all followed by a "crash."

Lots of work, exhaustion, then wondering:

"How the heck am I going to top that?" 

Combined with a total inability to shut down my work brain for more than 60 seconds, scrambling to figure out how to stay high on the win.

So I built a little checklist I've shared on LinkedIn here before.

My bar is usually ~5-6 of these. Above that: 

I let my toddler brick my iphone, then go do something that has nothing to do with B2B SaaS. Time to touch grass, go make that bowl of pasta topped with extra pasta, or whatever your thing is.

So whether you're hitting end of month/quarter on a high, or a low:

How many of these sound familiar today?

_____

1/ Always on

You have no new email, but you refresh anyway, just in case someone needs a reply. You’re worried a deal will fall through if you reply late.

2/ Sleepless

You’re tired, but wired. In bed with your mind racing, thinking about what didn’t get done. So you wake up spent with a foggy head.

3/ Error prone

You see yourself as thoughtful, but lately, the quality and detail of your work nosedives because it takes too long.

4/ Irritable

Your mood constantly changes. A simple question like, “Hey, could you upload that doc to SFDC?” can set you off.

5/ Numb

It’s like life is on volume level 1. Everything seems muted. You lost the ability to feel what others feel. You feel isolated, misunderstood.

6/ Drained

A full to-do list used to be energizing. So much opportunity! Now, it’s suffocating. You can’t get started for fear of not being doing it all.

7/ Escapism

You’re too tired to do things that feed your soul. So you just doom-scroll, binge-watch, etc. feeling no better after.

8/ Mis-prioritizing

You believe health is important. But cooking a meal, going to the gym (or even a short walk) seem like luxuries you don’t have time for.

9/ Multi-tasking

You switch lanes to the short one at the stoplight, while replying on Slack, then quickly jump into your calendar before the light turns.

_____

- Sending out marketing templates

*Your value’s only going up over time.*

Those are the "20%" skills like: 

- Offline research to build a POV with hard-to-find intel
- Tag-teaming with execs & partners to secure warm intro's
- Asking thoughtful, unexpected questions that trigger emotion
- Uncovering / resolved deal risk with trust & transparency
- Rolling this into sharp soundbites buyers share internally
- Converting skeptics in a group of 20+ to greenlight high-stakes deals

Which means the GTM teams who… 

1. Teach their humans how to do the "20% work"

Creating more and more value with and for their customers.

The rise of agents isn't the death of humans, it's the rebirth of creative, thoughtful selling.

content:
I think we've lost the plot on the whole "digital sales room" thing.

The way most sales teams use these just creates the illusion of helping champions sell internally, but it's not actually moving the needle.

Maybe it's just the echo chamber I'm in, but here's my (hot) take:

There’s nothing inherently strategic about a branded page with a bunch of template content stuffed into it. 

The value prop...

“Don’t send links and attachments in an email! Put them on a beautiful page!”

...is fine. 

It's okay for a certain subset of buyers. 

But I think we need to ask an altogether different question:

“Do we know what we're trying to say to this account?”

And its 2nd cousin: 

“Can our buyer message us to their exec, in < 60 seconds?"

From my view, answering those questions are more about the fundamental design behind HOW you go to market. The way you structure a sales process, to build your message *with* each buyer. Something specific to them.

Because the fact is: 

The message *is* the sales process.

Getting to a set of unique, "account-based" soundbites that'll play on repeat in an exec team's internal meeting. THAT is when you've led with a point of view,  you framed deals around a priority that matters to the customer, you found and filled your discovery gaps, etc.

So, sales leaders, the next time you're in a deal review, and someone's talking about all the people viewing their sales room.

Just ask:

"Can you tell me why this exec will buy from us, now?"

Is the answer clear? (not vague)
Is it "account-based"? (not generic, and persona-based)
Is it fast? (not "let me look back at our last couple calls...")

Because if your AE—the one who studies how to do this, and the one getting paid on this deal—can't answer clearly, you confident your buyers can? 

Will sending them 4 case studies, 3 demo videos, and 35 slides (all on a single page with buying steps and deadlines, of course) change that?

content:
AE’s: when sales leaders tell you to “build a POV” (point of view), here’s what they mean — and how to do it.

To start, you’re looking at a “driver graph” here.

(I broke this down in a short video a couple weeks ago — testing out some text vs. video here, to see which y'all like more/I'll make more of.)

Driver graphs comes from the FP&A world, which models out all the cause-and-effect relationships behind a company’s core metrics.

To build a POV, look at the left side and ask:

1/ What’s the highest-level metric your end buyer (the “EB”) owns?

2/ When they stand up at their next board meeting, which path down the driver graph are they focused on?

e.g. if revenue’s down inside an e-commerce business, is that because:

- customer base shrank year-over-year?
- same base, but they’re spending less?

3/ If they're spending less, and the exec talks with their SVP and VP about why net-sales-per-customer is down, let's say they find declining order values (AOV).

What’s been trending there?

4/ Let’s say it's a drop in cart volume (# items / order). Well, the question is, how are they gonna fix it?

That’s where your POV comes in (see the last visual, Venn Diagram).

Let’s say you sell a code snippet that looks at website/purchase behaviors, and recommends product bundles, to drive more cross-sell at check out.

Then, your POV = the intersection of what’s changing + what you do differently/uniquely to fix it.

It's a “think big, act small” approach, as my friend Brandon Fluharty says:

- Big impact at a high level
- Grounded in specific actions

To help you build a credible storyline between:

- Left side: what metric you’ll influence
- Right side: how you plan to impact it

Do this, and you’ve built a point of view that's credible across the entire buying team. Plus, you've got the foundation for:

1/ A full biz case that resonates at an exec level
2/ Framed around a high-priority problem
3/ With a believable approach to fix it
4/ And a clear way to measure it

Fluint's AI writes tailored, account-based docs like these — POV’s, 1-page business cases, account plans — at scale (it can help you build a driver graph too).

document.title: How to Craft a Point of View

content:
Lots of CRO’s are merging their AE and AM roles, with AE’s keeping accounts for 6 - 12+ months, since expansion win rates are ~2.3X* higher. Here's a framework to help build expansion pipeline, if you're in this role.

*45% expansion vs. 19% new logo (Ebsta/Pavilion 2025 data)

The point here: 

Best not to just copy and paste your outreach to prospects, to customers. A blended portfolio means it's time to test a new approach.

______

Subject: Idea, [ Customer Priority ]

Been a minute since [ last event / touchpoint ], [ First Name ].

I was just thinking about [ their original exec priority/project ] —

Talking with the team on your progress, we’ve got an idea for you on [ related use case you haven’t tapped into yet ].

How’s [ day of week ] work to run it by you?

- [ Your name ] 

PS, check out [ document / image / peer example ] before we catch up.

______

Couple tips: 

1/ Talk with your delivery/CS team. How's actual progress to goal, vs. the original timeline you setup during the first sale?

2/ What's a related product/approach that, if bundled in, would get the customer to their outcome faster? Or, something you cut scope on upfront?

Next: 

You're welcome to comment "EMAIL" or "PIPELINE" if you'd like, but the whole thing is in the post already. 

The proof right upfront. 

And this is the key to the framework: 

3/ What's a related "artifact" you can share as "evidence" your idea is worth digging into? 

^this is the key, and why when it's used well, you'll book a call pretty dang near every time

repost.content:
The $1M Google doc that started a company. 

Nate Nasralla, co-founder of Fluint. 

Most sellers think they close deals.

Nope. Buyers do. 

And that single insight led him to build Fluint — a platform changing how B2B sales are won.

Foundation
Nate’s journey started after the acquisition of his first startup, DonorPath. Post-acquisition, he stumbled into selling large nonprofit contracts — seven-figure deals at a time — even when the market said it couldn’t be done.

These are long enterprise sales cycles, but one snuck through very quickly.

Confused, he went back to his first buyer, Charles, and asked: “What did you do internally to get this signed?”

Charles shared a simple, two-page internal memo he’d written — using none of Nate’s sales decks, none of the branding, just simple, direct language for the board.

That’s when it clicked.

Sales reps don't close deals. 

Champions do.

Obstacles
The idea was clear. But building Fluint wasn’t easy.

No big checks.

No easy sales.

No shortcuts.

Every feature had to be scrappily tested — from Figma sketches to Google Docs — validating what could one day be scaled by software.

But, Nate faced the deeper challenge of keeping conviction alive.

“It’s not any one big low moment,” Nate told me. 

“It’s the constant weight and accumulation of hard, long work over years that tests your commitment.”

“That’s what’s most important for founder conviction.”

Climb
Nate’s strategy was different.

Instead of building quietly, he built publicly.

He shared frameworks before he had a product.

He proved “message-market fit” before building “product-market fit.”

He used it carefully, always in service of the principle “enable champions to sell internally.”

By the start of 2023, Nate had only 1,500 LinkedIn connections.

Today, he’s one of the most trusted voices in enterprise sales — by everyone from first-time AEs to Fortune 500 CROs.

Not because he chased virality.

But because he had something worth saying.

Achievements
Fluint raised a small venture round, “Venture-strapping.”

Launched the first “living document” that learns and adapts.

Built a fast-growing community of 30,000+ sellers.

And most importantly, helped individual AEs change not just their pipelines, but their entire companies’ go-to-market motion.

Nate’s proudest moment?

Seeing one AE turn Fluint’s frameworks into a new operating system for their entire enterprise team — proof that belief spreads from the ground up.

Lessons
I asked Nate how he would advise founders who build publicly. 

Own a specific moment in time.
• Snickers owns hunger, “you’re not you when you’re hungry”
• Fluint “What are they saying about you, when you’re not in the room?”

Say an old truth in a new way.
• “You don’t close deals. Buyers do.”

Make your message travel.
• “Create frameworks people want to forward, copy, and share.” This is how you build in public.

Principles come first.

Product follows.

A little bit ago a prospect stopped me on a call and said, “No BAMFAM?”

I stared back... then said, “Umm, I have no idea what that is.”

He laughed, and explained:

“Book a meeting from a meeting. It’s the mantra we live by.”

Which was the moment I realized I’d been letting the # 1 easy-to-do-but-high-impact step in my process slide. 

So I got back to it:

1/ I set calendar invites to end at 25 vs. 30 mins, or 50 vs. 60 mins. As a reminder to save 5 - 10 mins (at least) to talk next steps.

2/ If it’s a group convo with lots of roles, I’ll send a 2nd invite to my champion / main contact for 5 - 10 mins right after, to catch up just us on feedback.

3/ And it's nothing crazy, I’ll typically just ask: 

“Seems like there’s a fit, and I have a recommendation on next steps, but what do you think? Was this interesting and important enough to talk next steps?”

So it’s the new “metric” I have for myself:

→ What % of right-fit prospects do I book a next step with?

If I keep that high enough, eventually, it'll show up in my win rate.

What else are y'all doing to keep next steps rolling?

content:
AE's making the jump to Enterprise: "Price's Law" is often the difference between getting $1M+ signed faster than a mid-market deal, or, not at all — so here's what it is, and how to use it.

Price's Law says: 

"The square root of people perform 50% of the total work." 
(image credit: Devon Nall)

Which means:

- In a 1,000 person company, 32 do 50% of the work
- In a 10,000 person company, 100 do 50% of the work

You catch that? 

→ Headcount jumps 9,000 people. 

→ But, the people who really make a difference only goes up by 68. Leaving with 8,932 more people to filter through and get distracted by.

Then, if you take those 100 people who "matter," and spread them across 15-20 business units, really, this means ~5-6 people out of every 500-600+ can truly get something done — and that's who you want to sell with.

They're hard to find, in short.

So here are a few things I do, to figure out who to build into a champion: 

1/ Look for VP's/Directors an executive's consistently brought with them across multiple different companies

2/ Throw out a general question to nobody in particular in a group meeting, then watch to see who everyone waits to hear from first, before voicing their opinion

3/ They know their numbers. I show them a problem statement, they can put specifics on it, without having to "call a few meetings to run some reports."

4/ Or, they'll challenge you on it with simple, direct language, "No, that's not right. It's actually X, because Y. Update that." 

5/ Other small tells, like, they edit an exec meeting agenda directly as you talk, or they'll put a meeting directly on an exec's calendar, for tomorrow. 

(^others will get in line, writing a request to an EA, or a "suggestion")

6/ Just ask: "If you actually want this project to move forward without stalling out, who's the # 1 person you'd trust to make it happen?"


What other "signals" show you someone's got the juice?

content:
I’ve read a lot of sales books. Most are full of fluff or painfully outdated. But I’ve got one “must-read” recommendation - and here are 3 takeaways you need to know now:

1) The steps you take to sell your product are not the steps your prospects take to buy it

If you have a 3 month sales process, you probably meet with the customer 6-12 times over that period, and exchange a decent number of emails. 

But most of the work to evaluate your solution is happening without you. It’s happening in 1:1s between your champion and their boss. 

It’s happening in internal slack threads. It’s happening in team meetings where people debate pros/cons of different solutions. 

While you are sitting by your laptop hoping for a response to your “can I get an update on progress” emails, your buyers are evaluating without you. 


2) You communicate with both facts and feelings in the sales process - and feelings matter more

Feelings are sticky - you’ve probably heard the phrase “people don’t remember what you tell them but they remember how you make them feel.” 

And all feelings aren’t equal - the most important emotion to drive in sales is confidence. When buyers are confident, close rates are 2.6x times higher!! 


3) Match your buyer’s language, format, design as much as possible 

Nearly every company gets this wrong. Everything sales and marketing sends to the customer is 100% branded for their own company. Their logos, their quotes, their stories, their product. 

A killer quote from the book exposes this problem: 

“If a company’s brand is all over the materials they send me, the chances that I forward it to my team are next to none. Because it’ll look like a massive billboard.” 

Companies don’t make large purchases because you emailed over a billboard version of a PDF.

Companies make large purchases because they see how you fit with them and solve their problems. 


Great books lead to great takeaways. If you haven’t yet read “Selling With” by Nate Nasralla you are rapidly falling behind the modern buying experience. 

So go fix that :)

Our champion screenshotted a Slack thread with his CFO: "This was great. I copy/pasted, he messaged, and we just talked live. We're set, send it."

- Opened with a company-wide shift

- Added their data on problem
- Linked back to their inside joke "so.. surprise!"

- Referenced a memorable anecdote from their reps
- Did the leg work + highlighted alternatives

(3) Overly designed, pretty slides are counterproductive. 

Ain't nobody sharing your billboards internally.


TL;DR: 

Short soundbites get deals done. 

Make your messaging snackable, and it'll get shared.

content:
New logo win rates falling to 19% (across $48B of pipeline and 655k deals in this study) is why I'm convinced mid-funnel is the next frontier of GTM:

1/ A 19% logo win rate means you need ~5.3X pipe coverage on your ACV. (A wildly expensive and difficult way to grow.)

2/ You can't expand accounts at that much healthier 45% win rate. (Far more efficient growth pattern, IF you land the account in the first place.)

And from Morgan Stanley's X-Ray data: 

3/ Future customers = 44% - 80% of a company's enterprise value (which depends on logo acquisition)

Top-funnel's had it's day, and it increased from '24 to '25

And it's not going away, to be clear. 

I'm just saying it's just been the main focus for so many teams, for so long, which drove high, high amounts of innovation, process, tech, etc... 

But mid-funnel "innovation" has largely been: 

"So, we made you a pretty landing page with your logo, and a bunch of decks and case studies and stuff you can hunt through :)"

We need more focus on the mid-funnel now. 

For example; you probably saw a leaked memo from Shopify CEO, Tobi, making the rounds last week. About company mandates for how to deploy AI. 

I've already seen 2 customer examples of this. 

Where CRO's are writing their own versions internally, too.

Because most GTM teams were just kinda dabbling with AI on "Level 1" over the last year, without operationalizing it in a truly meaningful way:

→ Level 1: “How do we cram AI into our *existing* process?”
→ Level 2: “How do we use AI to build the *right* process?”


→ Level 1 is forcing AI into the same ol' process — no fundamental change in strategy, same activities, just a little more efficient.

e.g. “Hey AI, fill in these CRM fields so I don’t have to.”

It’s a fine starting point. 


→ But Level 2 is what I find way more interesting:

“How are we using AI to do what we needed, but *couldn’t* a year ago?”

e.g. "Could our mid-market reps run cycles with the same level of strategy and thoughtfulness our key account reps do? "

and, "Could they do that while increasing the # of opps they manage at once, so rev growth doesn't always hang on headcount growth?"

⤴ that's what our team's focused on building for

Odd at first. But also, it makes sense: win rates dropped -10% from '24 → '25, to 19% overall, while deal values JUMPED by +54%. 

(One more great nugget from the Ebsta & Pavilion 2025 benchmarking study I shared yesterday)

If you've ever heard an exec say, “Sorry, we can’t afford that small of a budget,” that's what we're seeing in the data (my read of it, anyway).

What they mean is most AE's think scoping out a bigger contract means working "low and slow." Low win rates, slow approvals. 

But the reality is often the opposite: 

Scoping larger deals often *increases* win rate.

Because execs know underinvesting in a project that matters is a bigger risk than increasing their investment upfront. So they're saying, “We can’t afford that small of a budget,” in a different way. 

More like: 

“This is too important, and this feels too cheap to risk it.”

So companies are still spending, just in a more focused, intentional way.

They’d rather spend $500K than $50K (or $5M vs. $500K in some cases) to make sure a project is resourced, gets done correctly, and the change sticks.

The trick is knowing what type of situation you’re in:

→ (Strategic) Selling to a company-wide priority.
→ (Functional) Solving a specific business unit's problem.

If you’ve tapped a priority, it likely means the exec won't risk a project going off the rails. So you can lose to someone with a scope/price 10X yours.

In other words, top reps are the ones who make the shift:

→ From selling "products" (small contracts)
→ To selling "projects" (big scope of work)

Signs you've made this shift:

1/ People refer to an internal project with a "codename"
2/ Which is referenced in an all-staff meeting agenda
3/ Or a board meeting or ELT meeting agenda
4/ With 3+ business unit leaders involved
5/ Because it impacts a specific P&L item

It'll show up in your deal content, too: 

- Projects: account-specific memo crafted with the buying team
- Products: same ol' template deck you just slapped a new logo on

Sam, Guy, glad you kept the benchmarking studying rolling for the year-over-year look. It's a gift for the GTM community.

“Thanks, we’ll talk internally and let you know.”

Classic. Here's a graceful way I've been avoiding that dead-end to my calls.

Towards the end with ~5 mins left, I've been asking:

“To suggest some next steps, no doubt you'll want to sync up with [ revops, enablement — insert your personas here ] internally on feedback. 

But I'm wondering, if we said for just a second this choice was just yours, would you feel confident enough to move forward?”

And then just listen. 

Which will tell you if your prospect's either:

(1) All in, and they need to sell their team.
(2) Skeptical, and using the “team” as an escape route.

The hypothetical lets you find out, so you can dig in:


(1) Yep. They’re all in.

Why do they see a fit? What do they want to make sure others understand? 

This shifts you to an opportunity to shape internal buying conversations.

(e.g. writing a short memo with key points you can’t let them miss)


(2) It’s not an immediate yes.

Why the hedging? If you hear this, you can share:

“If you’re not certain this is the right fit for you, it probably doesn’t make sense to bring the rest of your team into this…”

So you’re able to address the issue together.

The fastest moving deals I'm working on right now (including a 2-year deal that just closed on Friday), all have these 3 things. 

If you've got all 3 in your deals too, I'm ~80% certain you'll get it done:

→ Names
→ Numbers 
→ Dates

(1) Names

What's the internal "codename" for the project you're aligned with? 

Don't have a specific, named initiative you're rolled up into? That deal's probably going to stall inside a big org without it. 

But if you do, next question:

Can you pull up the names of who's backing that project as contacts in your phone? Do their names show up in recent text threads?

Nice.


(2) Numbers 

From inside the buying team, detailing the *problem.* 

(Not a "guess" at the ROI.)

For example:

"Customer LTV fell below $1,000/shopper, down from $1,350 last year. That's because only 40% of loyalty members make more than 2 purchases..."

Which turns something vague like "churn" into something more vivid.


(3) Dates

No exec sets a priority without a target date/deadline. 

If it's meaningful, trust me, it's time-bound. 

So what's the date coming from inside the buying team? Did we break it out into a series of milestones? How are we pacing toward each?


Try focusing the first ~60 seconds of your next deal review here. 

Even better, pull up the exec summary you wrote (a 1-page brief with the names, numbers, dates — in the customer's language).

You don't need much more than that to find the gaps.

And if none such exec summary yet exists...

content:
Reps building 3-4X coverage AND missing quota happens more frequently than Taylor Swift's concerts selling out. Yet, so many sales leaders are stilling use pipe coverage as the feel-good measure of, "We're set, we'll hit targets."

For some teams this'll feel a little too "101," but it's also my point — 

It's known, but so rarely done well.

So at the risk of oversimplifying this topic, there are 2 types of teams:
‍
- Type 1: Wins by “volume.”

Close rates hover ~20%. Leadership’s hammering prospecting to make sure reps "get after it." Always feeling like pipe coverage is too light.
‍
- Type 2: Wins by “rate.”

Process broken down by stage, measured weekly/monthly, targeted programming rolled out based on leaks to win more — with less pipe.
‍
→ The 1st type of team wins by "force, the 2nd wins with "finesse."
‍
Here's an example from an HR tech company we work with. 

The typical AE on their team:

- Built roughly $1M in pipeline/quarter, vs. a target of $250K.
- Which is typically seen as a "good" 4:1 ratio.
- But really, they leaked revenue between Stages 3 & 4.
- The ~40% Stage 3 → 4 rate cut their overall win rate to 21%.

Sound familiar..?

As a quick aside, here’s how you’ll know which type of team you're on. Mid-quarter, you’ll either hear:
‍
Type 1:

“Can you pull a few of those deals forward?”
“Why aren’t we sourcing X new opps, minimum?”
“What if we go back to them with a bigger offer?”

And my personal favorite…
“Setup the meeting, I’ll handle this one.”

(lol)

Type 2:

“What’s happening in the buying team at S3?”
“Can we navigate it with them upstream, at S2?”
“What process / skill gap will that mean closing?”

Okay, back to our example:

Deals stalled when the HR team got excited, their demos went flawlessly, they were multithreaded, quantified “pain,” etc…

But then? Nada. Silence.

Deals got de-prioritized by Finance + Ops mid-funnnel.

Which meant reps needed to engage the COO/CFO — not just the CHRO.

So how'd they approach it?

- Enabled reps to build a sharp point-of-view.
- Writing out that POV in an executive summary.
- Sales leaders coaching to that write-up in 1:1's.
- Scorecard created to measure strength / deal gaps.
- RevOps tied exit criteria to Ops & Finance validating it.

Which meant their approach in S1 → S3 completely changed. 

*They didn't solve the S3 → S4 gap in S3 or S4.*

They went upstream. Enabled reps with a new approach, leaders switched up how they ran deal reviews, and win rates jumped. (28% overall vs. 21%)

So, some questions for you:

1/ Which sounds more like your team? Type 1, or 2?
2/ If you're a "Type 2" team, where's the process breakdown?
3/ What, specifically, are you planning to address that this week?

content:
Here's what'll happen on pretty much every Zoom / Teams call this week:

- We all talk at ~150 words per minute
- But we understand / process at ~750 WPM
- Which means 80% of our brainspace is free to wander
- So we all end up 100% distracted by other thoughts

And that's not even taking into consideration everything in our heads we *want* to communicate, but can't fit inside those ~150 WPM. (PS, I recreated this graphic based on one I saw a while back: let me know who made the original?)

So these phrases are like conversational "glue," to keep someone stuck in the present with you.

_______


1/ "This matters, because ______."

- Link back to what's important from their point of view.


2/ "Earlier you mentioned ______. Which tells me...."

- Show you're listening, others want to listen more too.


3/ "Most people think _______, but actually..."

- Surprise is a strong emotion, and emotion grabs attention.


4/ "Are you open to a different take on that?"

- We all lean in when we're curious about what's next.


5/ "What are you seeing, that I'm missing?"

- We tune out when we feel misunderstood, so create space to talk about why.

_______

Thought to share this after an exec stopped me mid-call on Friday and goes: 

"Hang on. I have to reply to this," while an email came in. 

And you know what? I Ioved it. 

Because 2 minutes later when he said: "Okay, I'm back with you," I had his attention. And I used the pause to think about what I actually wanted to say. (Hitting pause is WAY better than trying to have 2 conversations at once.)

But what he did is pretty rare. Most of just go into multi-task mode. 

So give some of these a shot this week.

I know, I know. Sell the next step. Book a meeting from a meeting. But it just doesn't go that way sometimes — even though the prospect is a solid fit, and right inside your ICP, they're lukewarm and won't commit to a time. 

Some would say "cut 'em loose" right then. Maybe so.

1/ Just call it out. 

"Sounds like this is interesting, but not a 'this week' kinda thing."

2/ Offer a 3rd option. 

"If you're like me, stuff only happens if it's on your calendar. How about this?"

3/ Send a follow-up invite. 

"I'll send you an invite, with an exec summary in the body. Use the time for an 'async' meeting. Then, use the calendar link to book a new time after. If I don't hear back, I'll assume it's not a focus for you.

You up for it?" 

- If no: well, that's your answer. Bless and release.

- If yes: duplicate the invite while asking, "what date should I set it for?"

^that date tells you just how (not) urgent something is, and when's best to drop them a line on next steps after.

content:
This is a story so ridiculous I couldn’t not write it up.

So please don't put it on LinkedIn Lunatics. Or maybe do?

I run a lot, and it's common for runners to get some aches and pains. It's just part of it, and I generally have a high pain tolerance.

So last week, I'm sitting next to the bathtub, barefoot, while my daughter's playing in the water. And I'm whining to my wife that my foot's been hurting way more than usual.

My wife: "Well did you look at it?"

Me: "I mean, yeah, it just hurts a lot."

My wife: "Okay... well would you let me look at it?"

Me: "No I'm fine."

My wife: "You sure you want to do weekend runs on it?"

Weekend runs are when I run for a long time, and enjoy some trail time. It's always a priority and we often build Saturday's around that time.

So I balance on one leg, lift the other, and she turns on her iphone flashlight. 

She shines it on my foot and goes: 

"Nate you have a big shard of glass in your heel."

Turns out I'd be running around for 3 days with glass in my foot. (I'd shattered a coffee carafe that week, and didn't realize I stepped on a leftover piece.)

Now here's where I'll let my "influencer" hang out: 

Customers live with problems (glass) in their business (foot) all the time. Until you (my wife) shine a light on it and ask: 

"You sure you want to live like that? Because you don't have to."

It's kind of wild how we often just go numb to our problems, and block it out. Until eventually someone points out it's standing in the way of matters.

But most times, we under-index on problem discovery, we over-index on product, and don't spend nearly enough time shining a light on what's really happening / what it means for a priority in the prospect's world. 

We just kind of accept a vague, persona-level problem statement that never really highlights the issue. 

So, here's something to try: 

→ Write a sharp (as glass) problem statement for 3 different deals: 

→ "Despite trying [ failed approach / project ], our team still can’t enable [ high-priority initiative ], because [ frame the problem's root cause ]. It's already cost [ loss ], and if we don't make a change by [ critical event ], that means [ next-level impact ]."

^ how unique / different does it come out for each deal?

document.title: How to Find & Fill Deal Gaps: Crash Course

content:
"Reps would be terrified if they knew how many of their deals died in a 30-second convo at the end of a 1:1 with their contact's boss." Like:

"Hey, so I’m looking at this…"

"Not a priority; let's circle back in six months."

"Oh okay."

This was Kyle Asay's point when we were talking about this idea of selling to priorities, not just problems, a while ago.

And it's why I love how Reid Hoffman defines exec leadership: 

"Deciding which fires to let burn." 

It's all about priorities, in short. 

When an exec funds a new project or creates an internal initiative, that 1 "yes" is also 100 other "no's." So they ignore most everything that's not the # 1 thing.

It's why deals slip and stall: 

We found a problem, but not a *high-priority* problem.

To find out if you've tapped an exec priority, look for meeting agendas. 

Because your deal will either be:

(1) The meeting
(2) In the meeting
(3) After the meeting


(1) If your deal's *the* meeting, you’re the priority.

So if you ask: 

"If we look at your exec team's calendar this week, which meeting will this come up in? ...what agenda items are listed ahead of this?"

And your contact corrects you: 

"Oh no, this *is* the meeting. It's the whole agenda."

You're in good shape. But, if other stuff is ahead on the agenda:

(2) You're *in* the meeting.

You’re aligned with one topic, which can be okay too. 

Most deals fall here, after you scoop out strategic deals. 

But... 

(3) Beware the "deal" where you keep hearing: 

“Oh sorry, we ran out of time last meeting, hoping we’ll get to it next week.” 

This means you're a thought raised in passing *after* the meeting.


Check out the visual: 

If you draw an "X" on the curve with where you think a few of your Q1 deals are, where do they fall?

content:
Sales leaders, here’s a simple, 2x2 framework for 2025. 

Rep productivity largely boils down to 2 questions:

(1) What % of deals in our pipeline match our playbook? 
(2) When deals do match, does sales velocity $ increase?

In short: 

(1) Adoption: “are we doing it?”
(2) Impact: “does it work when we do it?”

So there are 4 possible ways to answer (the grid).

Two notes on each question: 

(1) Adoption: 

If you see a low % of deals matching your playbook, it’s probably suffering from complexity, and lack of focus. 

So try this: 

1/ Throw out your old playbook.

2/ Add back 1 core framework to start.
Which impacts revenue the most? (See topic below.)

3/ After 80% of deals have that framework executed, you earned the right to “add” something more. What’s next most important?

(e.g. deals stalling at Stage 3 b/c no exec engaged? Well, what % of your deals *actually* have a tailored exec summary written out?)


(2) Impact: 

There should be a WIDE gap in velocity (win rate %, cycle time, contract $) between deals that do vs. don’t match your playbook.

If you see:

- A big velocity jump: spotlight that to drive more adoption. This is the “opportunity” zone.

- No big change in velocity: there’s a gap in the playbook. You’re in the “optimize” zone. 

If you’re in this optimize group, here's a breakdown on what a modern, sales-led GTM playbook looks like: https://lnkd.in/g5Jtcdt5

content:
Here's how to write a "magnetic" mid-funnel email. Because the emails most reps send to slipped and stalled deals are "repelling."

(They push buyers further away, instead of drawing them back in.)

Here's why:

Sales leaders and trainers always coach reps on finding the "negative impact," the cost of the problem, critical events, etc… 

Which are absolutely important, no doubt.

But then? 

How they apply the messaging works like that classic saying from middle school science class: “opposites attract.”

Remember playing with magnets in science class?

- Positive ends of a magnets stick to the negative ones.
- Two negative ends of a magnet repel each other.

Same idea with stalled deals. Except we’re talking emotionally-charged emails.

Here's an example from a strat rep at a major design software:

She reached out while working a deal with real momentum — a “compelling event,” a respected champion, the works.

But then, silence. Her champion went dark.

(Yes, you can have a "true" champion who goes dark. That's another post.)

Her manager helped with an email, coaching her to use "we" language, to ask about impact, etc. Well intended, but can you spot the issue here?

It’s “repelling" because the main emotion is “you’re falling behind.”

And when I asked her what her contact, Katy, was likely already feeling?

Overwhelmed.

She's a rising star, respected, in-demand at her org. Project requests are always pressing in: it's straight up overwhelming.

So, what happens when you tell an overwhelmed person they’re behind?

They ignore you.

I mean, heck. I’d do the same. Wouldn’t you? 

So... what’s the opposite of overwhelmed? 

Calm. Ahead. On top of it.

Which is exactly the emotion we went for in our re-write. Check out the example, then grab the full framework here: bit.ly/magnetic-emails

content:
AE's are taught to ask about the "decision process." Which is fine... 

But what buyers *don't* say, then go do internally (and we never see), is where deals are actually won and lost.

So, sales leaders: 

Here's how to learn how the “internal sale” really goes down in your deals.

1/ Pick a deal that closed recently with each AE.
Ideally one with an open/transparent champion.

2/ Have them write up the decision process they know.
Based on what they heard / helped with during the purchase.

3/ Ask them to send out a version of this email.
To setup a short call, for more context/follow-up questions.

_______

Subject: Process Feedback

[ Buyer ], thrilled we get to work together now, thanks to all the time you spent on [ project ]. There was for sure room for me to be a stronger partner, too. 

So I’m wondering:

Would you be up to share what happened behind the scenes? 

It'd be interesting to compare how I *think* you evaluated us, vs. how your team actually did. (e.g. emails, convo's, docs, I never saw, but you worked hard on.)

Lunch on me if you’re up for it?

_______

4/ Together, ask your champion (now customer) to point out gaps.
What'd they do, that you all didn’t see?

5/ Look for a couple patterns in what you hear.
Guide that step in your next deals.


We give feedback to our reps all the time.

But how often do our AE's hear it directly from our buyers?

What you hear together will be fascinating. Promise you that.

content:
Here's a nontraditional (but in my experience, wildly accurate) type of interview question to filter for high-potential strategic / enterprise AE talent. 

(Territory and timing impact quota % to a higher degree in strategic roles, and the old "tell me about a time when..." just aren't very good filters.)

Let’s say you have two vehicles. 

Each driven 10K miles (or kilometers) / year:

- A car that gets 20 miles per gallon (MPG)
- A truck that gets 10 miles per gallon (MPG)

If you need to cut costs, which is a better upgrade?

- Replacing the 10 MPG truck with a 20 MPG truck
- Replacing the 20 MPG car with a 50 MPG car

^think about that for a second

How would you break it down?

What's your answer?

Most people choose the car: 

- The cars saves 30 MPG vs. 10 MPG with the truck 
- On a % basis, it's a 150% savings vs. a 100% savings too

But, counterintuitively, *replacing the truck* is the better value. 

That’s because:

- The truck goes from 1,000 to 500 gallons.
- While the car goes from 500 to 200 gallons.

So you end up saving 500 gallons (truck) vs. 300 (car). 

(Example from the 'Art of clear thinking.')

What's my point with this? 

- Strategic reps develop an uncanny ability to save customers from bad decisions that, at first, seem right — but don’t ultimately get them an outcome.
 
- Which they do by slowing down long enough to think more deeply about the customer's problem than even the customer does. 

- Then, they use that insight to reshape the customer's thinking, by highlighting a hidden and counterintuitive reality. 

When you can do that, your prospects will thank you. 

(And typically, buy from you.)

So it's less about a candidate getting the answer "right." 

It's more about seeing they break down problems and the questions they ask. If they can do that with a quick scenario like this, then moving to deeper exercises with your own customers, to see how quickly they learn, makes sense.

Sales leaders: 

What's one of your go-to interview approaches?

content:
"Show buyers current vs. future state” is classic sales advice, and it's good stuff — but *how* I used to apply it created way too buying friction.

Maybe you're causing deals to stall for the same reason?

Just in case, here's what I was doing wrong, and the shift I learned:

- Instead of contrasting current vs. future *outcomes*
- I was contrasting current vs. future *process*

Here's why that nuance is so important:

- Contrasting outcomes = measure of *value*
- Contrasting process = measure of *change*

These are very, very different things:

Nobody likes change, 'cause it's risky and hard. 

(Which means highlighting lots of process change isn’t helpful.)

So here's how I learned to approach the advice instead, with examples:

1. Find the gap between current vs. future outcomes
2. Confirm that making a change is wanted / a priority
3. Find a small, specific scenario in their process
4. Show current → future process for that scenario only

Now you've got a clear vision + a bite-sized example. 

Let's do an example from an FP&A / finance platform.


→ Instead of saying:

"Excel spreadsheets means lots of errors and manual data entry. We'll replace all those spreadsheets to automate all of your EOQ forecasts."


→ You'd say:

"Since you rolled out usage-based pricing to a segment of customers, you're probably noticing the most forecast variance there, right? 

Okay, so, let's start by comparing a machine-generated forecast to your Excel version, over the last quarters, for that segment only."


→ Plus, you can setup a "hyperlinked" decision this way:

When a new buying decision references a previously-executed decision, made by the same person, with a positive outcome. 

Like this: 

"You already setup a process for CSM's to gutcheck usage-based numbers, based on what they know about those accounts, right?

Nice. Well, we'd keep that process in place, because our ML reads frontline account notes & call transcripts, to factor all that data into the #'s." 

Same... 
but different... 
but still same.

Here's a shortlist of questions CFO's are asking your champions, when you’re not in the room. They're from my 1:1 convo with OnlyCFO —

How many of these are you bringing up first in your discovery?

1/ Why do we need [X] now? We were fine before.

- Increases revenue

My adds on a few other questions to prep your champ for:

1/ What’s the biggest assumption you’re making when showing this outcome?

content:
Here's a shortlist of 10 "facts" I strongly believe you can (and should) build a sales process around:

 
1/ Effective deal reviews happen in < 60 seconds.
 
If you can't compress a deal into short, specific bullet points, do you really know what it's about? 1 page is all you need to spot gaps.

 
2/ Building a business case *is* the sales process. 
 
Not just one activity inside it. All other activities roll up into and are strengthened by it.

 
3/ Deals get done during conversations happening about you, without you.
 
Written content is how you guide the customer journey, while keeping the full buying team + your own AE's, SE's, CSM's, leaders, etc… on the same page.

 
4/ Efficiency is about less activity, not more.
 
More "finesse" than force: sellers who build more influence in the buying process win more revenue, with less activity over time.

 
5/ Writing isn't documentation. It's discovery.
 
It's the process of learning what you don't yet know (and then figuring it out). Making it the most-important, least-developed skill for sellers.
 
And a core use case we've built Fluint around.

 
6/ Buyers don't trust your ROI.
 
Your numbers without a narrative are meaningless. But numbers *do* validate a decision the buying team's already made, based on the story.

 
7/ There are two types of problems: math and drama.
 
"Drama" is why the math problems go unsolved.

 
8/ Selling priorities > solving problems. 
 
Reps solving genuinely-costly problems lose deals all the time. A process has to frame the problem around an exec-level priority first.

 
9/ You don't "find" deal champions. You build them.
 
Like IKEA furniture. Over time, your process should transfer ownership in the deal from you, to them, by co-creating their solution.

 
10/ Multithreading isn't about adding more contacts. 
 
More contacts = more dysfunction. Create a minimally-viable committee, to build a "social safety net" around your core champions.


Which of these 10's most interesting? (Lmk, and I'll drop you a framework / write-up to help.)

And what would you add, that I missed in the shortlist?

This is pretty fascinating. If you look at how execs make big, strategic, expensive (and potentially risky) decisions, you’ll see a pattern:

- The case for that investment is written down.
- A written narrative is built with similar points.
- It’s stripped of the “shiny” sales decks have.

Here’s a “prime” example of this:

→Amazon acquiring Ring (the doorbell company) for $1 Billion in 2018.

The entire memo came out during some litigation, dug up by techemails . com (one of my fav reads), and it’s ~5 pages long.

If you’re not a nerd, you’ll probably miss the lessons for sellers hidden inside.

Lucky for you, I am that nerd 🤓

So I wrote up a shortlist of 7 lessons you should know:

https://lnkd.in/gzT2cDW8

Here's the first: 

→ The core elements to every business case. Which is also the rough structure behind the acquisition memo (full copy of it in the write up):

1/ Situation:

- What’s happening in the home protection market right now.
- How this market connects back to Amazon’s strategic priorities.

2/ Problem:

- The fact they’re behind, and late to the market.
- Amazon’s competitive positioning is weak, and getting weaker.

3/ Approach:

- Either: (1) build internally, (2) create partnerships, (3) buy/acquire tech.
- Their M&A recommendation, and why it’s the highest probability of success.

4/ Options:

- The differentiators & “capabilities” of each “vendor” in the evaluation.
- Blink: company & tech overview, valuation, acquisition thesis.
- Ring: company & tech overview, valuation, acquisition thesis.

5/ Recommendation:

- Why buying Ring is likely the best path forward.
- Next steps, resources, and timeline for final diligence.

The next 6 lessons I added include:

- What language execs respond to.
- Why “big doors swing on small hinges.” (Thanks Krysten/Jason)
- How to get quick signoff on big contracts.
- How to write with "density" to pack a punch.
- Starting your case simple, and evolving it over time.
- What reps miss when differentiating from competitors.

Use them, and you'll start to get responses like in this email from Jeff:

"I'd buy it right now."

content:
Here’s how to format an executive-level message in sales, with a quick 30-second exercise. (So your message actually gets read, not ignored.)

The ideal formatting: 

- white page
- black font
- lots of redlines from the buying team 

That's it. 

Make it look and feel “internal,” by cutting out your company's branding. (Which just triggers the feeling, "Eh, another vendor selling me.")

And I know, I know. 

Enablement / marketing teams spend literal weeks wrapping all your content in nice colors and pretty images etc... but hang with me.

Here's the 30-second exercise to show you why simple works:

(Step 1) Read this:

"This morning, Jamie walked into her kitchen. But then, she dropped a bowl of yogurt that splattered all over the ground, and she stepped in it."

Now go back and read it once more ⤴

(Step 2) Now, picture that kitchen: 

- What color are the cabinets?
- The bowl, what does it look like?
- What about the type of floors Jamie's on?
- The type of yogurt Jamie was planning to eat?

Chances are, it *looks a lot like your own kitchen.*

And the yogurt brand / type *you* prefer to eat.

Because we fill in the blanks with what's familiar to us. 

So when you cut out all the branding you wrap your slides, docs, and messaging in — which again, just signals to a customer, "You're in my world, not yours" — you'll make it easier for them to fit your message inside *their* world. 

Then they can walk around with it, try it on, picture their future with it.

That's good for you, and them.

content:
Here's how I think about what most every CRO/VP Sales is being asked right now: "What's our to plan add revenue, without more people and pipeline?"

(Sales "efficiency," in short.)

Sometimes, it’s easier to tackle a hard goal by flipping it upside down. To first ask, “Well, what does an *inefficient* sales process look like?”

Answer:

One that has to win by force, not finesse. By constantly throwing more spend  at people and pipe creation (two biggest cost drivers).

So if you model out a process, it’s just a set of rate/volume equations:

- Volume: how many reps do you have selling?
- Rate: how much does each rep sell?

That’s the simplest version, and it gives you total Sales Capacity:

- RRE (ramped rep equivalents) 
- RRR (revenue per ramped rep)

And as your "RRR" increases, you’re way more efficient.

Because:

(1) Driving up RRR retains talent and creates upside.

- As % of reps attaining quote grows, attrition drops
- When a role does open, it's easier to fill with talent
- More tenured vs. new reps increases the % likely to exceed quota

(2) A smaller number of highly-productive sellers minimizes cost.

Requiring more "RRE’s" to hit your annual plan means:

- More first line managers to manage them ($$)
- More benefits, payroll, and recruiting cost ($$)
- More spend on pipegen to support them ($$)
- More enablement & revops complexity ($$)

So, while you could constantly add more opps to the pipeline — then hire a larger number of lower-attaining reps to manage them — that’s not an option if efficiency is also a requirement.

So the next question is, how do you drive up revenue/rep (RRR)?

→ Short answer: 

- Map process + exit criteria to high-value buying behaviors
- Build written frameworks that test for "evidence" it's met
- While enabling the buyer's internal sale (where deals die)
- Invest in (tech, training) the skills that drive adoption here ⤴

→ The answer we're building to stop deals from dying mid-funnel: fluint.io

This story from the early days at Amazon completely changed how I've been running my demos, and it might do the same for you. It's worth the read.

(From Jeff Bezos' interview on the Lex Friedman podcast.)

____

"I have a saying that when the data and the anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are usually right. 

An example of this was metrics that showed our customers waited less than 60 seconds when they called the 1-800 number to get customer service.

But we had a lot of complaints that it was longer, and it seemed longer than that when I would call customer service myself. 

So one day we're in a weekly business review, and we get to this metric and the guy who leads customer service is defending his metrics.

So I said, okay, let's call. And I picked up the phone and dialed the 1-800 number, and we just waited in silence, for what did turn out to be a really long time — more than 10 minutes.

[ ^can you imagine how uncomfortable everyone in that room was ]

Which *dramatically* made the point we weren't measuring the right thing, and that set off a whole chain of events. So you have to get people's attention, and they have to really buy into what you’re saying to get energized if you’re going to fix things.”

____

I had listened to this right before a follow-up call, when my champions showed up to tell me their CRO had shot our deal down: 

"We upgraded spend with Gemini, she says we don't need other AI tools now."

So I asked: 

"Can we open up a few deals in Stage 3, right now, and show me what your reps sent to the buying team exec?"

They were solving for mid-funnel deal stall, where their pipeline went to die. So the goal was scaling up a tailored, 1-page exec message before S3:

- Quality problem statement
- Framed around an internal priority
- To highlight deal gaps during reviews
- And enable champions to engage buying execs

In the past, I would have talked about all the ways we're better/different/etc... than Gemini.

Instead, we poked around Google Drive, Salesforce, Gong, etc... 

And we found a single, half-baked summary (that was largely generic and hadn't been updated after the latest calls). So then I just asked: 

"What percent of your sellers have used Gemini?" 

"Almost 100% of them."

"And what % of deals have what you need?"

"Maybe 10%, and that's generous."

So we just sat quietly for a bit, and it sank in. (I looked at the recording, it was only 20 seconds of silence, but it felt like 10 mins, hah.) 

They shared the same with her. 

Contract signed 3 days later.

______

That's an example from my world. 

The takeaway for you, in your world: 

If you're asking prospects to deadlift facts and stats and differentiators, try to find a small anecdote. Something they experience. It goes a long way.

What's one way prospects "experience" your demo?

content:
Should you sell ROI or COI (cost of inaction)?

In short, it's both, but here’s what most reps miss:

If I hand you a quarter, am I handing you either "heads" or "tails?”

Well, it's both. You can’t separate the two from each other.

ROI and COI are two sides of the exact same coin too.


When you…

1/ Quantify and layer problem metrics to find COI, for example:

High support costs [ # tickets (x) time / ticket (x) hourly pay ]
↓
Low NPS Scores from unhappy customers.
↓
Expansion pipeline decreasing
↓
Future customer LTV lost

(You'd use specific customer data here.)


Then you…

2/ Flip the *exact same* metrics upside down to find ROI:

Support costs drop as ticket volume drops
↓
NPS Scores go up with happy customers
↓
Generate expansion pipeline

(And again, you'd use specific customer data here.)


→ Value = the contrast between COI and ROI.

If COI grows costlier, and ROI increases, there’s more value.

The big difference, though, is that:

- ROI = a *maybe* measure far off in future.
- COI = a *certain* amount customers lose now.

So buyers discount ROI for its level of “believability.”


Missing a COI focused message is 1 big reason deals slip and stall.

content:
If you're an AE, here are 10 ways to punch up any executive summary. 

To make sure it's one your buyers will actually read, love and share:

1/ Lead with internal language referencing an exec priority.

2/ Use a two-sentence TL;DR at the top with the ask + timeline.

3/ Add a short anecdote, to create a visual that supports the data.

4/ Make sure your data points come from inside the customer's org.

5/ Whenever you add data, it's a chance to cut word count.

6/ Count the # of rewrites to your problem statement. If < 3, you've got work.

7/ Include alternative approaches that were ruled out. Always think, "Could this customer solve this problem with another category entirely?"

8/ People read headers, bold, tables, bullets and underlines. Usually in that order. If they like all that, then they'll read again from the top. 

9/ Execs think in "ranges" of possibility. Use scenarios and sensitivities, not a single ROI number.

10/ Show how that range depends on what you need from them. Time, people resources, change management. Not just $ in a contract.

content:
If you sell a highly technical product, keep this in mind.

You don’t know need to know more than others — you just need to help buyers communicate more clearly.

Even if you make up a few words along the way... 

Like in this example, from a convo while writing my first book.

It's a pretty interesting excerpt, from a Sr. Director Data Science at a Fortune 200 finance firm ⤵

____

Nate: “Reps who work with technical buyers can feel intimidated, like they should know more than a buyer. What’s your take on that?”

Her: “I can see it. But for me, I like working with people who have different knowledge. If they’re a data science expert, what’s the point? I don’t need that. I have that.

What I need is help communicating the value to my business.”

Nate: “What’s an example of a seller who did that well?”

Her: “Well here’s one. Culturally, we’re a ‘build’ organization. I mean, we even built our own CRM. And data science is hard to tie to revenue, so it’s hard to make a case to buy something when the default is build.”

Nate: “Sounds frustrating.”

Her: “It is. We have this chicken and egg problem. We need to spend to prove our impact on revenue. But we don’t have the proof, so we don’t get the spend. So then we just start building to solve the issue."

Nate: “And what was the issue in this case?”

Her: “Grunt work. Spending months of time on basic data work in Python, instead of actually looking at and sharing results from our models."

Nate: “Okay got it, and that wasn’t easy to communicate?”

Her: “Well that’s the irony, and the message we developed with this sales rep. We’d been spending 6 months of people time at minimum on these types of tasks. And the thing is, people aren’t free. So by building, we were spending quite a lot.

But we weren’t showing the cost of our time to achieve an input. All the value we create is in a model's output. So the more we cut the cost of an input, the greater our value. You follow?”

Nate: “Yep, I’m with you.”

Her: “Okay, so when I first proposed new spend, our finance team saw a vendor as new. Something extra. Telling them about how we'd improve our data processing didn't matter.

But our people’s time? They took that for granted. It was already budgeted. So we re-approached it as a cost-reduction argument.

Re-allocating the spend for a basic data task to software from a person meant the cost of that job decreased. Plus our team was freed to develop new models.

So our cost-per-insight went way down. Which was a completely made up metric. Nobody tracks that. But I liked that it was so much simpler. The two things. More insights, at less cost to produce them.”

Nate: “And that’s what this rep helped you come up with? Lowering your cost-per-insight?”

Her: “Yes, and it worked.”

_______

TL;DR:

1/ You don’t have to be smarter than others. Just think differently.

2/ Simplicity sells. Even if it’s a made-up term, give your buyers the language they need to communicate more clearly.

Lol @ the product decks some reps try to pass as a “business case.”

Even with a personal “why us, why now” slide... that’s not a business case.

Here's a rundown on how to craft a true business case.
 
→ Language:

As you build out each "Lego Block" 🧱 in this — sections you'll stack up over time — make sure each piece has your champion's words. 

You're building this together, and their name goes on it. (You're not the author.) So it has to sound like them.

(Go here for a deeper dive on this: https://lnkd.in/g_VK_D5e )


🧱 Exec Priority:

Your goal here is to align with a project's internal "codenames" and catchphrase to signal you're aligned with a priority the C-Suite is *already sold on.*

That creates context and raises the stakes, setting the stage for a good problem statement. 


🧱 Problem Statement:

Visual language that paints a clear picture. If you’re going deep in discovery, you’ll have the inputs to quantify this with ruthless specificity.

Then, link a workflow issue to a strategic framing, using the phrase "which means" to get to the problem’s costs + consequences.


🧱 Recommended Approach:

Create a logical connection between their problem and your product, while sharing a “non-obvious” insight and the "beliefs" that walk buyers up to your solution.

Then, set up a decision: which path will the buying team take, by what timeline?


🧱 Outcome Scenarios:

This should tie into 1 & 2 above, and align with how execs think: in terms of tradeoffs and scenarios. Not a single "ROI" number. 


🧱 Investment:

Finally, setup the convo on change management. Your buyers are investing a whole lot more than just their budget. 

Show you know this, and have a plan to ensure it goes smoothly.


There you go. 

A business case buyers will actually read, love, and share 🤌🏼

content:
90% of sales teams set themselves up for slipped deals. 

Because they've built their entire sales process (and therefore, forecast) around their seller's activities — not internal buying activities. 

(Example: it really doesn't matter if a rep "sent a proposal," what matters is evidence of the buying team reading it / editing it / sharing it.)

So, what's the fix?

Mapping each stage to buying behavior. With exit criteria tied to specific pieces of "evidence."

Here are 7 specific steps + exit criteria:


→ Stage 1: Frame a high-cost, high-priority problem in writing.

- Exit Criteria: Your buyer shares a written problem statement with their team, framed in a way that aligns with your solution.

- Target Skill: discovery.


→ Stage 2: Multithreaded validation, from different points of view.

- Exit Criteria: No less than 3 buyers read your problem statement, agree, confirm it aligns with an exec-level metric.

- Target Skill: multithreading.


→ Stage 3: A relevant executive sponsors a project.

- Exit Criteria: The executive tasks their team with evaluating & recommending a new course of action.

- Note: this can also happen earlier, in 1 / 2 above, but the deal can't progress to a later stage without this.

- Target Skill: executive access.


→ Stage 4: The entire buying committee agrees on an approach.

- Exit Criteria: The committee decides on an external solution, with a specific set of requirements that align with yours.


→ Stage 5: You’re confirmed the "provider of choice."

- Exit Criteria: The committee stops other discussions and everyone’s input is locked into the scope.

- Target Skill: differentiation.


→ Stage 6: A compelling event continues to drive the close date.

- Exit Criteria: The committee sticks to a target kickoff date based on a desired outcome, and agrees to a backdated set of tasks to get them there. 

- Note: this will be started earlier; are dates actually running on schedule?

- Target Skill: mutual action planning.


→ Stage 7: Pricing, procurement and commercial terms finalized.

- Exit Criteria: Dried ink accepting all terms of your deal.

- Target Skill: negotiation.

_____

1/ Map process stages to buying vs. selling behavior

2/ Create specific exit criteria that gate / test for this

3/ Look for the longest stage-to-stage time and ask: 

 - "What’s happening inside the buying org here?" 
 - "Why haven’t they moved forward already?"

4/ Pin point the fear / doubt / uncertainty / confusion

5/ Intentionally address that during the prior stage

6/ Repeat 3 - 5 from longest → shortest stage time

______

The two big ideas here: 

- You can’t troubleshoot what you can’t isolate
- Slowdowns = what’s happening in the buying org

But most sales processes aren't built to enable good buying behaviors. Which are the two big mistakes in most sales process design:

- Stages are clumped up, without clear exit criteria.
- Exit criteria = seller activity, not buying behavior

Just my $0.02. 

Thanks team Lightspeed for making this data public 🙌🏼
