Here's a major reframe for B2B sales teams moving upmarket: 

→ Big deals get done in a series of small moments that matter.

Working from left to right in this graphic:


1/ We tend to think about sales cycle as calendar months. 

Call it 5 months, from May to October. 

"How long's this opp going to take to turn into revenue?"


2/ But our buyers think about it differently: 

Hours away from their day job. So 5 months for us may = 7 hours for them. 

Those hours CAN be compressed into a matter of a weeks vs. months, if you're anchored to an internal date, messaged with the right soundbite, that taps into an authentic urgency. 


3/ But really, inside those 7 hours, there's just a small handful of moments with the power to close or kill a deal. 

So you can/ should take a dozen meetings, then boil them down into a set of short sentences that shape thinking (and the outcome of your deals).


So the question is, how do you "pick" the *right* sentence?! 

Start by filling in this framework. 

It's 2 - 3 sentences that compress an entire deal into its core elements, to fit inside the moments that matter.

______

"Because of [ a significant change / shift in the customer's world ], now's the time to [ respond with a specific action your differentiator enables ]. 

When we do, we'll find [ positive outcomes aligned to a customer priority ]. If we don't, [ negative outcomes continue, and get worse ]."

content:
Here are 5 phrases to try sharing when you're losing someone's attention.

Which is basically every few minutes on a Zoom / Teams call, because: 

- Most of us talk at ~150 words per minute
- But all of us understand / process info at ~750 WPM
- Which means 80% of our brainspace is free to wander
- So we end up 100% distracted by other thoughts

And that's not even taking into consideration everything in our heads we *want* to communicate, but can't fit inside those ~150 WPM.

(Saw this graphic a while ago and rebuilt it; not sure who did the original?)

So these phrases are like conversational "glue," to keep someone stuck in the present with you.

_______


1/ "This matters, because ______."

- Link back to what's important from their point of view.


2/ "Earlier you mentioned ______. Which tells me...."

- Show you're listening, others want to listen more too.


3/ "Most people think _______, but actually..."

- Surprise is a strong emotion, and emotion grabs attention.


4/ "Are you open to a different take on that?"

- We all lean in when we're curious about what's next.


5/ "What are you seeing, that I'm missing?"

- We tune out when we feel misunderstood, so create space to talk about why.

_______

What else do y'all find helpful when you see someone's emailing / slacking / texting / zoning out on a call?

content:
John D. Rockefeller was the first billionaire in the US.

He was once asked, “How much money is enough?” 

He was the richest man on earth at the time, and immediately replied: 

“Just a little more.”

If I'm honest, it's been the same for me lately. Which kind of sucks, it's not actually a fun feeling.

It's the same for a lot of people in sales too, even if it’s unspoken. Because we "acclimate" to whatever standard of earning / spending / living we’re at today. 

Then, we want just a little more. 

And guess what? Sales makes it happen. 

Commissions jump from $1K, to $10K, and for some, to $100K over time. Which is great, and I'm all about the transparency and education and posts on financial freedom and earning power on LinkedIn.

That's the bright side, and I've written some of them.

But what I RARELY read here is the shadow side:

When we start to confuse, (1) what we earn, with (2) who we are. Which is when we start to fear what slowing our pace on the commission treadmill actually costs us — 

Our identity.

Like we become less of a person when we earn less. The only real antidote for that way of thinking (that I’ve experienced, at least) is to give. To intentionally move in the *opposite* direction, by writing a check that feels a little like...

"We sure about this...?" 

My wife and I sat on making a big donation for a few weeks, wondering, "Is this TOO much to give?" And when we finally did, I can't tell you the amount of joy and gratitude that came after.

And just to be clear: my point in sharing this isn't a "virtue signal."

It's just to write on a topic we don't really read about around here: giving money away. Something that's pretty dang effective in fighting off the “more monster,” exactly because we've all got legit financial stuff to worry about:

- Mortgages
- college funds
- daycare (sidenote: at first I'm like, "how is this is so expensive?" and then I'm like, "teachers only make how much for watching my child?!?")
- random car repairs
- pipes that break 
- big healthcare bills. 

It's all been a part of our past year. 

But when you give, regardless of amount, even with all that's going on, it’s a statement about what you value above other things. 

(And we eventually become what we value.)

One shoutout on this topic, too: 

Jen Allen-Knuth's the one consistent example of this I've seen around here. For the past ~30+ Saturday's, she's shared about giving and adopting to support rescue animals.

And I can confirm, who she's become in the last years of getting to know her is wayyy more impressive than anything her W2 may say. (Well, 1099 actually, because you should def contract with her for training work.)

content:
Here are 5 phrases I use in my discovery calls. Every. Single. Day.

They'll help you go deeper and build influence, without the cringe.

Anyone can use them, and if you use all 5 in a convo, that's powerful.


(1) "Could you tell me more about when…"

Encourage stories that release emotions, not short statements.

Catharsis is powerful.


(2) "To spend just another second on that…"

It's rarely about 10X covering more topics.

It's about going 10X deeper on the topics that are most important.


(3) "Ah, so, the reason I’m asking this is…"

Share your intention. You'll encourage transparency, and get the full story.


(4) "How does this relate to when you said…"

Create a bridge back to earlier answers, or from others on the buying team.

It builds a pattern in the buying team, and shows you're listening.


(5) "Got it, so in my experience…"

Share your point of view to break up the interview.

Which helps you earn the right to go deeper.

content:
If you're trying to land your first $100K+ deal, here's are 9 things you'll need to know about the "inner life of enterprises."

So you have more empathy for your deal champions...

...and avoid getting ghosted in a 6+ month cycle.


1/ The Law of Large Numbers

It’s hard to have a meaningful impact on revenue.

Adding $10M in revenue is just 0.0001% of sales for someone like Apple.

Don’t over-index on this in your messaging.


2/ Meetings = Forcing Mechanisms

Large companies have A LOT of meetings.

They’re basically corporates deadlines, a way to force feedback.

If prospects need time for extra internal meetings that’s not always bad. It’s normal.


3/ The Art of “Languaging”

The right language makes buy-in easy.

It taps a narrative leadership is already sold on.

So employees learn to frame requests internal phrases that grab attention.

Use them in your materials and forwardable emails.


4/ Non-Committal Feedback

You won’t always know where you are in the sales cycle.

Your buyers probably don’t know, either. Their team is non-committal by default.

So ensure your champion has a sharp, written problem statement to socialize.


5/ Social Capital Matters

Be cognizant of WHO pitches your idea — ideas aren't independent of a messenger.

So that deck you spent days writing up and branding?

People won’t even open it if it’s not sent from the right person (and bigger titles aren’t always better.)


6/ Mismatched Urgency

Large companies never have the same urgency sellers do.

And your contact’s personal finances are rarely linked to a deal like yours.

So the importance of any one sales meeting is diluted to them.

Figure out the personal win they’re craving, and speak to it.


7/ Failure Sticks

Long-time employees have lots of informal clout.

They also know all about the deals that didn’t work, and failure just isn’t well tolerated in the enterprise.

If startups say “fail fast,” enterprises say, “we’ll remember if you do.”

Discover what’s been tried, show you’re different.


8/ Approval Bottlenecks Are Real

Senior execs sign big deals. But they don’t have free time. Like, zero.

That creates bottlenecks for everyone — not just you.

Plant seed early in the deal with internal docs your champion shares + direct “no reply required” updates along the way.

If you’re consistent here early, you’ll get prioritized later.


9/ The Top-Down Scramble

e.g. board member reads a WSJ article, forwards to an exec, who forwards to their team.

“What are we doing here?”

If you’re not part of that newly-urgent priority, you’ll be out of mind.

Know the latest news and align w/ what’s top of mind.

content:
You didn't ask, but I'll tell you my take on slide decks vs. docs anyway: the way AE’s use each is kind of like the guy I saw pulling a suitcase through the grocery store as a shopping cart this week. 

Like, yeah, it can get the job done. 

But there's a better way. One that leans into each format’s design and purpose.

→ Slides:

Reps love to load these down with too much distracting text during meetings. Then send them after with an unclear / incomplete talk track, and gaps in their storyline. 

→ Docs:

Shallow and unclear messaging, because they didn't take the time to "edit their thinking," and were planning to just "talk to it."


Here's how I use both instead: 

1/ Before the Meeting
→ Docs 📄

I'll write-out an exec summary to develop my POV on what, exactly, we need to communicate. I'll collab with my champion if it's mid-funnel. 

Then, we attach it to a short meeting invite. Everyone gets context with the benefit of a full narrative, which is easier to follow async. 

(vs. trying to follow incomplete thoughts across multiple slides)


2/ During the Meeting: 
→ Slides 🏞️ + Docs 📄

Slides = visual aids during the convo, with 0 - 7 words on each, max. No more than 3 slides is my style, personally.

Then, docs play a role that's a little less obvious, but no less important:

Once you've written out your message & reviewed it with a champion, your talk track is WAY more crisp and concise live. 

Try it, you'll see. This is what the screenshot here is getting at.


3/ After the Meeting:
→ Docs 📄

Updated version of the doc is sent out with everyone's feedback added + 1 or 2 visuals from the convo, which helps with meeting recall.

content:
One of the highest performing sellers I ever got to "lead" recently passed away, after a years-long battle with cancer.

(I say "lead," because I learned more from her than she did from me.)

I was writing out stories for her eulogy last week, and there's one moment from a decade ago that still sticks with me.

I cut it from my tribute because it’s more about my own learnings, but, I thought I’d share it here, and you'll see why I'm incredibly grateful for her.

Some context:

Rachel had 15+ years of experience on me, and decided IC work vs. sales leadership was for her. She was an early hire on our strategic team — which was new for the company overall — so there was lots of change and chaos while building a new “division.”

Being the genius leader I was…

I decided I’d keep all the noise away from her. Like a pair of internal earmuffs, so she could stay focused on revenue. Stuff like:

- Lead routing conflicts with “lower” segments
- Getting a dedicated PM for enterprise
- Fighting for CSM & services staffing

So one day she goes:

“Nate, you think you’re doing me a favor, but you’re not. You’re cutting me off from the context I need to do my job.”

Woof.

She proceeded to school me on the fact I was leading everyone based on how I worked best — not how everyone else worked.

Which may sound super obvious, but the idea that I should communicate with others based on how *they* work and learn, vs. my own style, was news to me.

I just kind of assumed everyone worked like me. 

(Everyone took the Predictive Index test after that. Way helpful.)

From that point on, anytime I was second guessing myself or feeling blind to something, I’d call Rach.

She always told me what I needed to hear. With straight up feedback delivered in this Jamaican accent I could never stay mad at. 

(“Oh yeah man!”)

So from Rachel’s life, a few notes:

1/ IC's, your leaders want and need to hear where they’re coming up short. That feedback is a gift.

2/ Certain people aren’t just colleagues; you’ll end up writing eulogies for them. Finding those people in your work life is also a huge gift.

3/ What would your team write in your eulogy?

content:
There are really only 4 metrics AE’s need:

- Average contract value

- Close rate

- Close date

- Sales cycle


So becoming a more effective seller is learning to:

1/ Close more valuable deals

2/ Close them more often.

3/ Close them on time.

4/ Close them in less time.


Which is why I look at 4 things that drive these in deal reviews:

1. How much influence do our contacts hold?

2. What types of interactions are we having?

3. How deep in the buying process are they?

4. How much time passes between activities?


Good signs under these 4 points are:

1/ Expanding Reach.

Are we involving execs and key employees early? One exec-level convo can drive more momentum than 10 below-the-line meetings.


2/ Effective Follow-Up.

The amount of sales activity isn’t very meaningful.

It's buying activity that counts — and it’s actually a worse sign to see lots of follow-up activities buyers aren’t engaging with.

(2:1 and 1:1 are healthy ratios: 1 - 2 follow-up notes = 1 response)


3/ Group Buying Process.

Interactions become more valuable in the late stages of the buying process.

But beware deals marked “stage 5” after a few excited contacts agree to commercials… without talking to their exec, procurement, etc.

It's where missed commits come from.

So look at buying behavior across a group — not individuals, who can all be at multiple different stages in the journey.


4/ Shrinking Cycles.

Making more time to engage with a rep, over a shorter period of time, means you've got more momentum to fight off mid-funnel deal stall.

So ask: are we tapped into a priority they’re already sold on — not just a problem?


Anyone got a 5th point they'd add?

content:
Here’s the # 1 trait on my list for sales leadership.

If you’re a rep who's interviewing, test your future boss to see if they're:

1/ Superficial
2/ Detailed

The Tao of Leadership puts it this way:

“The superficial leader cannot see how things happen, even though the evidence is everywhere. This leader is swept up by drama, sensation, and excitement. All this confusion is blinding.”

1/ The Superficial Leader is the majority.

The ones rushing around at EOQ this week leading by broad directives, discounts, and a high-level dashboard.

They'll say wins = their brilliance, losses = “market conditions” (or something equally vague).


2/ The Detailed Leader is the minority.

The ones who know "revenue" is a composite of a lot of individuals’ pipe coverages, ACV, win %, etc — all the way down to account-level scenarios.

Detailed leaders are calm, clear on what needs to change next quarter, and eager to get started.


If you're looking for a new role right now, here's a shortlist of teams hiring ranked by feedback on how their leadership stacks up: 

https://lnkd.in/gzUDYBab

Then in your interviews, test for Detailed Leadership by asking:

“Could you help me understand last quarter’s performance? I’m curious for a break down on what you're seeing drive revenue right now.”

Then, press in, multiple times.

“What do you think caused that? Does that apply across the team, or only in certain cases?”

You’ll learn quite a bit. Plus, you’ll know it when you feel it:

- You leave a Detailed Leader’s presence feeling calm.
- You'll leave a Superficial Leader feeling more chaos.

And we could all use a little more calm, less chaos.

content:
Here's a major shift for CRO's / VP Sales to consider in 2025 planning — a shift that taps the 90% of selling activity most teams miss.

To start, most people believe that:

- Building a business case is an *activity.*
- That activity is one *part* of the sales process.

But that’s wrong, and that way of operating leaves an incredible amount of revenue on the table.

Instead, here’s the way to think about it:

- Building a business case *is* the sales process.
- Every single activity flows from the business case.

So why’s that the case? (yes, a dad joke)

You already know the stat everyone shares: 

90% of selling happens without reps in the room. So it’s the *internal sale* that champions lead which matters most. 

And that's where building a written business case comes in:

→ Your writing can be "in the room" when you can’t be.

Which makes building a business case the *process of building influence in the buying process.* (The whole point of selling.)

(^not an ROI calculation; a simple narrative that connects you to a customer executive's internal priority.)
‍
Which means you can capture every activity & role inside a single page, e.g.:

1/ Deep Discovery:

Do we have a compelling reason to change? How much data vs. fluff is on the page? Writing reveals how much you've discovered — or not.

‍2/ Designing a Value-Based Demo:

Do we know which outcomes matter? Required capabilities? Do our SE's have a written brief that makes that clear?

3/ Coordinating Internal Deal Teams:

Does our own execs have context before joining customer calls? Does CS know what we're expected to deliver? By when?

4/ Multithreading:

Who contributed what points in the write-up? Do we have the “evidence” (edits, comments, etc..) of their engagement in the deal?

5/ Forecasting:

Does finance, procurement, legal, etc… have the strategic context to push this through on time? While keeping deal value intact?
‍

TL;DR: The business case *is* the sales process. It's like an entire enablement program, in 1 page. Guiding every activity and role. 

And if you're still with me... 

Two last questions are:

1/ "What % of deals in pipeline have a written business case?"
2/ "What would happen if we increase that % ?"

content:
Here's a framework for messaging big issues, in a clear and simple way. 

I came across it last week while reading a memo by Snap CEO, Evan Spiegel.

(Originally from the book "Fierce Conversations," with light edits from me.)

If you're an AE working on engaging a buying team exec, try it. 

White page, black font, short and sweet. It'll work 10X better than chucking a 20 slide deck or a landing page with a bunch of branded content at them.

And FWIW, the order most people communicate in is:

4/ Relevant context
5/ What I've done
1/ The issue is
3/ My ideal outcome is
6/ The help I want

Which means: 

- They talk in order of their experience
- Then eventually get to the core issue
- While leaving out (2) "it's significant because..." entirely

Good things come to those who communicate with clear, concise writing.

content:
I feel like I whiffed while working on a solid opportunity in our pipe last week — here’s what I wish I would have asked, but didn’t.

(So you can.)

Some context:

My contact’s leading the committee to shift the GTM in a few $100M ARR company. An exec-level initiative, and a good-fit customer, who's already using our frameworks in their planning.

He’s incredibly thoughtful, we’ve had good momentum, and multiple meetings inside a tight timeline.

And there comes a time in every deal where it’s either a “let’s go” or a “no.”

We’re there.

I know where on their priority list we sit, and I think I did a good job of laying out 3 options in a fairly "neutral" way with questions to think on:

(1) “DIY” (take our frameworks and DIY with internal owners only).

(2) “Land” (small Fluint pilot + hands-on guidance from our team).

(3) “Expand” (b/c sometimes, underinvesting in change is the bigger risk).

I’m truly open to whichever route they want to go.

But what I DIDN’T actually ask, and wish I would have, is:

“What do you want?”

Which sounds really, really simple.

Like… “that’s it?” I read this whole post, and that’s what you give me?! Well… yeah.

Because often, the right questions are the ones you overlook. Because they almost feel too simple for a complex deal.

Here, I was in full on “logic” mode. Structuring out options. Pro’s/con’s of each. Questions to guide their "evaluation."

Then I switched to “troubleshooting” mode. The hassle of unlocking budgets comes up? I see ways to pick the lock.

But through it all:

All my deal "strategy" got in the way of simply asking:

“What do you want?”

So for all you LinkedIn content junkies:

You can get so much sales stuff stuck in your head that you miss the simple stuff. The human stuff. Which is always the "right" way to sell.

Complex deals generally come down to 3 main ingredients. If you've got all 3, I'm ~80% certain you'll get that deal done:

→ Names, numbers, dates.

(1) Names

What's the internal "codename" for the project you're aligned with? 

Don't have a specific, named initiative you're rolled up into? That deal's probably going to stall in a big org without it. 

But if you do, next question:

Can you pull up the names of who's backing that project as contacts in your cell? Do their names show up in recent text threads?


(2) Numbers 

From inside the buying team, detailing the *problem.* 

(Not a "guess" at the ROI.)

To turn something vague like "churn" into something more vivid, e.g: 

"Our customer LTV fell below $1,000/shopper this year, down from $1,350, since only 40% of loyalty members make more than 2 purchases/year..."


(3) Dates

No exec sets a priority without a target date/deadline. 

If it's meaningful, trust me, it's time-bound. 

So what's the date coming from inside the buying team? Did we break it out into a series of milestones? How are we pacing toward each?


Trying focusing the first ~60 seconds of your next deal review here. 

Even better, pull up the exec summary you wrote — you should have a 1-page brief with the names, numbers, dates — in the customer's language.

content:
My teams' close rate when "co-creating" a business case is 68%.

(Blended rate from 3 teams, and very different buying personas.)

It's a fairly universal principle, in other words:

→ When champions build the case with you, you'll win more than lose.

Which makes sense:

When that happens, your *champions* own the deal. (Not just you.)

But that only happens when you're selling *with* buyers. Not to them.

An approach most reps don't have great examples of, or language for.

So here's a quick word picture to illustrate the shift:

Selling to → Selling with

The ancient Greeks had something called the “middle voice.” While we only have two voices: active or passive. Here’s the difference:

- Active voice: I’m selling you.
- Passive voice: I’m being sold by you.
- Middle voice: I’m selling *with* you.

See the difference?

We typically see sales as either an active *or* a passive activity. Active if you’re the rep. Passive if you’re the buyer.

But the ancient Greeks knew what’s up. They knew there's a 3rd way.

Sales can be something we do together.

Kind of like turning a car *with* your power steering (i.e. champion). Which lets you move a big, heavy vehicle (i.e. enterprise account) way more easily.

“Thanks, we’ll talk internally and let you know.”

Classic. Here's a graceful way I've been avoiding that dead-end to my calls.

Towards the end with ~5 mins left, I've been asking:

“To suggest some next steps, no doubt you'll want to sync up with [ revops, enablement — insert your personas here ] internally on feedback. 

But I'm wondering, if we said for just a second this choice was just yours, would you feel confident enough to move forward?”

And then just listen. 

Which will tell you if your prospect's either:

(1) All in, and they need to sell their team.
(2) Skeptical, and using the “team” as an escape route.

The hypothetical lets you find out, so you can dig in:


(1) Yep. They’re all in.

Why do they see a fit? What do they want to make sure others understand? 

This shifts you to an opportunity to shape internal buying conversations.

(e.g. writing a short memo with key points you can’t let them miss)


(2) It’s not an immediate yes.

Why the hedging? If you hear this, you can share:

“If you’re not certain this is the right fit for you, it probably doesn’t make sense to bring the rest of your team into this…”

So you’re able to address the issue together.

There's this point in our careers where, (1) we're interacting with C-level execs more often, but (2) we don't actually know how to work with execs yet.

So a lot of us do this weird thing:

We stop acting like ourselves, and we start talking in long sentences with big words. 

Like a BBC TV show about the 1800’s.

(This is semi-embarrassing to admit... but a CRO, whose third language is English, recently stopped a meeting between him, me, and his CEO because I used the word “analogous,” and he told me straight up, “I have no idea what you’re trying to say.”)

We make things overly complex, because it *seems* like what we bring to the "top" has to match the “weight” of a big title.

But that’s the *opposite* of how execs operate:

- Complexity is a weight. 
- Weights sink to the bottom. 
- *Simplicity* floats up to the top. 

And simplicity's the mark of seasoned sellers and operators:

People who understand a topic so well, they can communicate it with short soundbites, not slides. Like tree sap becoming maple syrup (h/t David Perrell), the outcome’s distilled, sweet, and leaves you wanting more.

I can’t hand you a few decades of operating experience.

content:
If you're an AE, here are 10 ways to punch up any executive summary. 

To make sure it's one your buyers will actually read, love and share:

1/ Lead with internal language referencing an exec priority.

2/ Use a two-sentence TL;DR at the top with the ask + timeline.

3/ Add a short anecdote, to create a visual that supports the data.

4/ Make sure your data points come from inside the customer's org.

5/ Whenever you add data, it's a chance to cut word count.

6/ Count the # of rewrites to your problem statement. If < 3, you've got work.

7/ Include alternative approaches that were ruled out. Always think, "Could this customer solve this problem with another category entirely?"

8/ People read headers, bold, tables, bullets and underlines. Usually in that order. If they like all that, then they'll read again from the top. 

9/ Execs think in "ranges" of possibility. Use scenarios and sensitivities, not a single ROI number.

10/ Show how that range depends on what you need from them. Time, people resources, change management. Not just $ in a contract.

If you use even 3 - 4 of these points, you'll be better off.

Here’s what sticks out to me after seeing Harris’ campaign tagline — in her ads, website, social profiles, etc.. — and what I think you can takeaway.

What’s he saying with this?

- America was once great.
- But it’s no longer great.

Now, compare this to Harris’ positioning.

What’s she saying here?

My point is it's hard to know what Harris stands for here.

I mean, I know who she stands *against* (Trump). And that she wants to win (like all politicians do).

But I don’t know her actual “position," or what comes post election.

One more example:

What was Hillary Clinton’s campaign tagline in 2016? You remember?

Probably not, because it wasn’t very memorable. So here it is:

→ I’m with her.

So, what's that tell you about what Hillary stood for?

Not much.

And that's my point for anyone in marketing/sales:

Everything rises and falls on actually standing for something. Picking a strong point of view, and tying your positioning to it.

Something specific that people can latch onto and think: 

“Yep, I know exactly what they stand for, and I can decide if I’m about it too.”

content:
Here's the fastest way I'm disqualifying deals in my pipeline right now.

Candid talk on call # 1 about the fact we'll be shifting selling behavior, and why that's really hard — but it might be worth it.

Because claiming high impact + no behavior change is... often just not true.

(It’s unrealistic to promise a board / execs big impact to revenue, while only making tiny tweaks to your GTM. Quick "plugins" only get you so far.)

So when a team's up for the shift, here's a framework we lean into:

→The Change Equation.

Which says people stay the same, unless 3 things are true:
 
1/ Deep dissatisfaction with the way things are.
2/ You have a compelling vision of what could be.
3/ You concrete first steps to move from what is → what could be.
 
Otherwise, resistance wins and everything stays the same. 

Written out formula style, it looks like this:
 
C = [ D x V x FS ] > R
 
Where:
 
C = Change
D = Dissatisfaction with Current State
V = Vision of the Future
FS = Clear First Steps
R = Resistance
 
You notice how the variables are multiplied, not added together? That's key. Because if a single variable = 0, the whole thing goes to 0.
 
So the question is, which variable's lowest in your team?
 
Often, it's "FS": clear first steps. 

Reps crave practical, detailed guidance.

Not just a "methodology" in a kickoff reps know is like a pair of jeans: 

A new style that's "in" for a minute, then it'll disappear, and MAYBE make a come back by a handful of people. (Bell bottoms anyone?)

So, tomorrow we're doing a little crash course. 25 mins long. 

It's all about making change stick, with takeaways from dozens of rollouts, for anyone in leadership / revops / enablement.

content:
This ad is killer, because it swaps vague for more "visual" language. 

"Pretty people" → "supermodels"
"Big cities" → "London" 

Harry Dry broke this ad down in a great episode of "How I Write" with David Perell, and I've been sharing it with our customers like crazy lately.

Because this is a fast and easy practice for AE's to sharpen their writing: 

Be way more specific.

Vague <—————X-> Specific
"Pretty"                         "Supermodel"

There's usually a gap between what we see in our minds, and what reality actually is. So to start a new project in B2B, you have to believe:

1/ It’s known
2/ It won’t hurt too much

If you can't picture exactly how something will happen, your mind adds more time and cost and energy and pain, etc... 

It paints a grim picture to keep us away from the unknown.

So, don’t say:

“Setup's a snap with white-glove support and a dedicated customer advocate.”

Instead, say:

“You’ll spend 3 hours over 2 weeks with Juan during data migration. Then, Lucy's your go-to. Email or text her anytime.”

With a picture of Juan and Lucy:

Vague <————————X-> Specific
"White-glove"                  "Juan and Lucy"

When you write something down, picture someone asking you, “Can you be more specific?”

If you can, then say that.

You’d be surprised how often deals are lost because of wild imaginations.

content:
Something all buyers want sales reps to remember:

“I live here, you don’t.”

Here’s how one buyer — who owns $15M worth IT spend for a Fortune 100 — put it to me.

______

“For every new purchase or upgrade we make, I have a bare minimum of 5 people I need to get onboard.

Which means cashing in some of the chips I’ve been saving up.

So I weigh how pressing this thing is against how much convincing I have to do, and how loud anyone against the project will be, to figure out if it’s worth it.

The thing is, long after the rep for this deal leaves, I still live here.

So my concern is less about the dollars in the budget. It’s the other kind of 'chips' I'll be spending along the way.

And I spend those chips at every step in the process. Even if we don't get to a signed agreement where money changes hands.

So if I think I’ll need to make a bigger ask on another project later, or if I’m burning too much goodwill in the process, I’m out.”

______

The big idea?

Buying is risky business for champions. 

*Even if their team doesn't actually buy anything.*

So you can have the perfect-fit product for a genuinely costly problem.

But before you'll ever go live, you have to "de-risk" the buying process itself.

This is my dad. He’s still practicing medicine, and what might be a very strange photo to you, is actually very profound for me.

My mom texted this last week —

He’s a radiologist, reading scans (MRI’s, CT’s, X-rays, etc…) while they’re out on a roadtrip. So he created a little makeshift darkroom to see the images with more contrast, and make a better call. 

It’s not uncommon for him to spend 10 minutes in the middle of the living room reading a case, sending notes to the ER, the missions hospital, or the pregnancy center he helps in his “free time.”

But it was very uncommon for him to miss out on one of our games or school stuff growing up. 

Father of 4, building a radiology practice, and never missing a game. (My mom was a VERY big part of this equation.)

Now here’s what’s so profound about this photo for me:

We launched the first MVP to Fluint a year ago — two weeks after my daughter was born.

And the thing about having kids later on, after already building up my own working style and schedule for a decade+ , is it largely breaks down when kids come along. 

Before my daughter:

I’d spend time setting up the “perfect” work conditions. Long hours uninterrupted, blonde roast brewed at just the right temperature, room heated to a perfect 67 degrees with a touch of sunlight streaming through the windows. 

Now:

I’ll fill the gaps and cracks in my day with 10 minutes of small stuff while sitting sideways in the backseat of my car to avoid a glare from the sun. Parked near a Starbucks because my hotspot sucked that day. 

As heard on a demo last week:

“Are you… in your car right now?”

Why yes, yes I was.

I’m also far more likely to say, “Hey, I’m really excited about our conversation, and at the same time I’m so sorry, but I’m going to have to keep it to 10 minutes — how can I help?”

Overtime, all those little minutes can add up to “productive” time, that buy back an hour with my daughter. 

All that clicked for me this past week when I saw my mom’s text.

So yes, I work very differently now. 

That’s okay by me, because I saw a “forecast” of the person I’m becoming decades in the future, in a photo of my pops, reading scans on a road trip in a makeshift darkroom.

My point for the working parents: 

It’s okay to look at your phone, do a quick email, and step out for a second, when your kids know you’re stealing away minute *from* them, to buy back hours *for* them.

content:
Here’s the single, biggest reason why sellers get ghosted.

You can run a *killer* demo that everyone on the buying team loves... and still get completely ignored at an exec-level. 

Because you never built a point of view that bridges:

Their priority → your product.

Let's take a newly hired CRO as an example.

Let's say her company just raised a Series C. Now, she's got to deliver on the happy ending they promised investors. So the CRO will ask herself: 

“What’s my biggest revenue opportunity?”

Acquiring new logos? Boosting net revenue retention (NRR)?

Let’s say it’s NRR. Investors were talking about that a lot. 

But does she...

...hire more AM's for the enterprise segment?
...find untapped cross-sells for SMB's?
...take an altogether different path?

There are lots of different "drivers" she can focus on.

In fact, if you look at this example “driver tree”, notice that when you sell to execs, who own very high-level metrics, they have lots of choices, trade-offs, and competing priorities.

Turns out, you can “drive revenue” in a lot of ways.

If you haven't seen a driver tree before, it's a way to link an outcome to a series of inputs: 

- On the left, you list a target metric you’d like to impact. 
- On the right, you'll see what "drives" that metric.

Okay, so, this CRO’s got to pick a priority today, which will affect her buying decisions tomorrow.

Now, let's say your product is some type of AI that helps with prospecting. You see this CRO was just hired. She just raised a Series C. Perfect timing to reach out, right? 

Surely she wants more pipeline?

Well, if the CRO’s thesis is that a singular focus on NRR is best — so she’s entirely focused on expanding revenue from customers who already love them, by cross-selling a new product they just launched — you have one of 2 options while designing your deal:
‍
1/ Align with her thesis.

Let’s say you can give her hard-to-find data on customers they don't have.
‍
2/ Reshape her thesis.

How long can she focus on NRR, without landing new logos? Aren’t the seeds for NRR sown early, during the new sales and onboarding process?

In short:

If there’s no logical "bridge" between her priority and your product—an approach that she’s aligned with—it’s not time to sell your product. 

So back to the big reason sellers get ghosted:

You get excited about a problem, you pitch a solution, but you forget to build a bridge back to an exec priority.

content:
It took ~90 days to get our champion's team on the same page. Only to get hit with, "We'll need 3 bids, so we'll start an RFP next week," by Procurement.

(This was "low enterprise", a ~5,000 person media company.)

They had a rule: 

Any new vendor spend > $100K required at least 3 competitive bids (which was equally frustrating for our champion, who just wanted to get rolling).

So our champion sent the exec summary we'd written to Procurement in a meeting invite for later that day.

He started by explaining he didn't have time for an RFP. Then I asked:

"Has there ever been a scenario where a new vendor came in above $100K, but without an RFP?"

Hoping that maybe, just maybe, we'd find an exception.

"Nope, not that I can think of."

Bummer. 

Then our champion goes: 

"Well, what if we split off $90K of the contract into a first PO, we onboard them, then a month after, put everything else into a second PO?"

Procurement goes, "Well technically that'd work, they'd be a current vendor at this point, so the RFP threshold goes up to $1M."

So that's what we did. 

We split the deal into two separate PO's and skipped the RFP 😂

The points here?

1/ It's always better to get creative than get frustrated.

2/ Big companies rarely break rules. But you can find ways to make the rules work for you — like the definition of what a "new vendor" was, in this case.

3/ When you co-create the business case *with* the buying team, vs. sending them your decks, model, etc... they own it now. Which builds up a sense of ownership in *their* deal, and a type of stubborn persistence to get it done. 

PS, I share a whole lot more of my deal stories in the book 'Selling With' if you haven't read/seen it yet: https://lnkd.in/gJVjW2xE

content:
We live in an "Attention Economy."

Which means budget flows where your buyers’ attention goes.

It also means your first (and biggest) competitor is the noisy, distracting, and overwhelming chaos that is work in 2024.

Sometimes, yes, an actual competitor might steal your deal. 

But more often, the people you need to care... don’t. 

They ain't got the time. 

They've got a ‘heckuva lot to oversee, so they keep such a tight filter on what they do and don’t pay attention to. 

Priorities, in other words.

That also means solving a genuine problem with real costs isn’t enough. 

So I think it’s fair to define things this way:

→ Priorities (plural) are mental filters. And how executives survive.

→ A priority (singular) is something specific that executives are already sold on, and actively subordinating other important topics to.

→ Problems are "issues" that get upgraded to true problem status because they're blocking a priority.

We could also plot the relationship between attention (priorities) x win rates like this, including a "Priority Filter."

The single, best way to know you're playing above The Filter? 

- You mapped your deal to a priority the exec's already sold on.
- Using a headline in your exec summary / biz case to "namedrop." 

I don't mean a person. I mean a "named initiative." 

When projects get their own shorthand phrases or insider codename, you know it's a big deal (see what I did there?) 

It's an immediate way to gain mindshare from the exec, to keep your deal from dying a slow, silent death below The Filter.

content:
Most sellers know they should "quantify" problems, but only a handful "frame" problems — which is a big miss. 

Because how you frame a problem will completely change the way buyers look at a solution (yours, or a would-be competitor's).

Here's the most famous example of this: 

It's from HBR’s "Are You Solving the Right Problems?"

______

Let's say you own an office building, and your tenants hate the old and slow elevator. So much they'll cut their leases if you don't fix it.

So, what's the problem here? 

A slow elevator. 

But is it really? That intro framed the problem in a certain way. 

Which sets you up to browse a specific "solution space."

1/ Problem: slow elevator.
2/ Requirement: speed it up.
3/ Solution: new motor, upgraded lift, etc..

BUT, what if the problem is actually the fact people hate waiting?

How would that change the solution?

1/ Problem: bored tenants.
2/ Requirement: entertain them.
3/ Solution: Install mirrors in the elevator. 

A different and far cheaper solution works, because people love to look at themselves. (Which is a real thing. Look for mirrors in old buildings.)

______

So here's the point for sellers:

Problems are entirely subjective. 

So as a buying team expands, so will the number of problems, and 10 buyers can easily come up with 5+ "root causes."

Which means you'll never know if you're on the same page... 

Until you're *literally* on the same page. By:

1/ Framing up the problem *in writing* 
2/ Attaching that problem statement to a pre-read
3/ Making agenda item # 1 "What are we solving for?" 

A "good" meeting is one where we go so deep on the problem, we start to run out of time. Because then I know the rest of the cycle will be fast. 

(Includes inbound, RFP's, and upsells — all times when reps breeze past the problem.)

content:
Classic sales leader: "Sell value, not features!"

AE: "Umm... yes. Value. Got it."

"Sell value" is generally throwaway advice. 

Unless you know *how* to do it. Then it'll change the game for you.

So here are 2 quick practices to sell "value." Starting with a definition of what value actually means:

→ Value = Positive Outcomes (-) Negative Outcomes

It’s the space between two futures. (One that’s good, one that’s not.)

Here's how to dial up both elements in a value-based message:

_______

(1) Negative Outcomes:

Shift from Cost → Consequences

Most people think "cost of inaction" is a 1st order effect.

But you can go deeper to connect it with 2nd / 3rd order effects:

1st Level: “We lost $2M ARR we should’ve won this quarter.”
↓

2nd Level: “Winning less customers with the same Sales/Marketing spend inflated our cost to acquire a customer (CAC).”
↓

3rd Level: “Our GTM efficiency is looking pretty ugly right now, and we’re already raising in a tough market. Hello, dilution.”


(2) Flip the above upside down to find the Positive Outcomes.

If you're measuring the problem with ARR, CAC, and GTM efficiency, then the payoff you enable should use the exact same metrics.

That's because our brains ❤️ contrast.

We can’t see “value” in isolation.

Only when things stand in comparison to each other.

It’s easier to choose between black and white, so keep the same metrics.

_______

So pick an account. Use your discovery for both sides of the equation.

Then you put them together with the classic copywriting formula:

“Get the ________ (positive), without the ________ (negative).”

content:
7 lessons on writing in sales that typically take 10 years to learn:


1/ Write “forwardable” emails.

Internal emails get prioritized over external emails. Send short, crisp emails that are easy for champions to forward. (Write *through,* not to.)


2/ Simplify everything.

Don’t use a PowerPoint if 1 page will do. 
Don’t use 1 page if a paragraph will do.


3/ Small soundbites get big deals done.

Ask an executive what they remember from your last meeting. 90% of the time, it’ll be a 15-second anecdote with a real-life example.


4/ Small things = big things.

e.g. go the “press kit” on a prospect’s website and use their fonts + hex colors. Some people won’t notice. Those who do will love you.


5/ Spend unreasonable amounts of time on the problem.

Writing, re-writing, framing, measuring, layering, and validating a problem statement is the best time you’ll spend during the sales cycle.


6/ Numbers without a narrative are meaningless.

ROI models are not business cases on their own. Business cases = stories tying an exec priority to an approach you can deliver, that others can’t. 

(Numbers do strengthen narratives, however.)


7/ Write down the wrong thing.

If you don’t know, insert a placeholder value then talk about it. People love to correct you, so it’s more effective than just asking a question.

Ever peeked inside an exec's inbox?

Most reps haven't, so YouTube "Walmart on Black Friday." You'll get the idea:

People throwing elbows, pushing up to the front of the line, trying to grab something: "a few minutes," meetings, approvals, decisions, signoff, etc.

So, 3 things to keep in mind while communicating with an exec:


1/ Execs typically read your emails during other meetings. Or, during early morning and late night workblocks. So:

- If you have something longer (e.g. a 1-page exec summary), try sending in the off hours. The chance it's read goes up. Schedule for 5:30am or 8pm.

(And if you're sending a 30-slide deck that's covered in vendor branding? Might as well just go ahead and delete that. It's not getting read.)

- If you’re sending something mid-day, keep it to ~4 sentences. Again, they’ll read it while multitasking.


2/ It’s basic… but asking for time triggers the “I’m so busy” reflex. More likely outcomes are an internal referral, from a forwarded email with a short opinion. 

Craft your CTA's accordingly, example:

You: "Would you want to weigh in first, or ask the team?"
↓
Exec: *FWD* 

interesting, plz look at this.

-Sent from my iPad


3/ Even better, write your champions a forwardable email and have them send it, CC'ing you. Execs prioritize internal senders over external senders.


Any other tips you'd add? 

Either because you're an exec, or, you found a practice that works?

content:
"RFP's are up 200% year-over-year."

Now typically, "up 200%" sounds like a great thing… 

But if you're seeing this in your pipeline, that's not so great.

Getting dropped into an RFP means you’re playing by rules someone else made. If you didn’t write the RFP, there’s a good chance a competitor did.

(win rate + RFP frequency usually move in *opposite* directions)

That stat was dropped in one of my customer calls earlier this morning, with a dozen of their global leaders talking through some changes we made.

They're not the only team seeing this stat, either. 

So if the way your buyers buy has changed — putting you out to RFP way more often — then the big question for you is: 

→ How did you change the way you sell?

Well, here’s a shortlist of what we've done, and reviewed this am:


1/ Created a “pre-discovery” framework to structure a sharp point of view for first meetings. Think of this like a Venn Diagram. A good POV will blend:

- What’s changing in *this* business specifically? 
- How do we approach that change differently/uniquely?


2/ That POV is then built out inside a a simple, 1-page business case draft, along with discovery input from the prospect. 

Right after the first call. 

It's starts early and ugly, then gets refined over time. Because the business case *is* the sales process. It's not a single activity or stage.


3/ While the deal progresses stage-by-stage, business cases are scored against a benchmark that helps highlight gaps / guides reps. 

Scores now live in the SFDC opportunity to show:

- patterns in a reps' deals for leaders to coach to. 
- how healthy each deal going into the forecast actually is.


4/ Which all relates to a "re-write" of their exit criteria we did this summer, tying all stages back to “evidence” of buying behaviors we can test for. 

Using the content document inside the deal, and built with the buying team.


TL;DR

Your ability to shape the buying team’s narrative from the earliest stages in a deal — and in a way that's different from the rest of the field — will either, (1) position you to write the RFP; (2) skip the RFP all together.

What are y'all doing different in your sales process this year, vs. last year?

Any of this list, on your list too?

The strongest buying signal I'm seeing in my deals right now? 

Time-between-meetings. So I’ve been asking this at the end of calls lately:

“Was this important and interesting enough to meet again on [next step]? If you'd rather just sit on this, and come back to it later, that's all good too."

Nothing crazy. 

If we *don’t* set a new time then, I put them into another category. (A lifecycle stage in HubSpot in between lead/demo request & qualified opp.)

Because one of two things are true: 

(1) building a process for business cases isn’t high-priority. 
(2) it is a priority, but our approach isn’t interesting. 

Doesn't mean I write them off completely. Just move to a longer nurture.

______

Two examples: 

(1) You get a chance for more discovery. 

e.g. a VP Sales said last week: ”It’s high on my list, but I don’t think our reps can make the shift to do this. It's too advanced, I need to hit the basics first.” 

I flat out disagreed, but hey, I know where he stands. 

Maybe one day we cross that bridge.


(2) On the flipside, if they say “yep, let’s set a time,” I’ll ask: 

”Is this a ‘tomorrow’ kinda thing? Or more ‘in a few weeks’ kinda thing?” 

Another VP said: ”I have an hour gap in the airport tomorrow, let’s talk then.” 

We met < 24 hours later during her layover.  A very “high-intent” signal. 


The amount of time that passes between meetings says A LOT.

Maybe the whole "signal-led selling" concept is meant for top-of-funnel... but what's your strongest *mid-funnel* signal right now?

The typical account map is always the same shape: triangles △

Because the lines connecting people are a hierarchy / reporting relationship — but that doesn't actually tell you how to influence a buyer's journey. 

You influence deals by designing the right sequence of internal comms:

The right message, delivered by the right person, in the right order. 

So the way I've always built account maps is to connect contacts with a specific type of message (forwardable email, meeting invite, whiteboarding session, etc.) to design the flow + sequence of info. 

I came across a post from 📈 Jeremey Donovan sharing the different "shapes" of account maps from John Kaplan last week, and it's on point.  

I'm re-sharing it below here, to hopefully make sure more people see it, and make their account maps useful. 

(Not just another copy/paste of an org chart.)

_______

W - Start high, go low, check in high, go low, close high. Probably the best.

N - Start low, go high, multi-thread low, close high. Good.

M or ^ - Start low, bounce around but lose low. Bad.

L - Start high, get pushed down and never come back up again. Bad.

_ (underscore) - Stuck low. Terrible.

An add from Katharine Reagan: 

E - starts and stays high, but you also start mid/low to multithread.

_______

If you go look at the last 3 deals you *lost*, what shape were they?

If you go look at the last 3 deals you *won*, what shape were they?

content:
Here's my # 1 skillset for sellers heading into 2025: 

Simplicity.

Because AE's solving big problems with worldclass products get flat-out ignored by buying team execs. All. the. time. 

Their brilliance gets: 

- Buried inside 50-slide decks
- Fumbled in a wandering pitch from the exec's own team
- Drowned out by everyone else needing something “asap” 

In short: brilliance goes unnoticed unless it’s also brief.

Which makes simplicity *the* skillset for every seller to cultivate. The ability to work in a way's that both brief and brilliant, since: 

- Brilliance without brevity is too complex.
- Brevity without brilliance is too shallow. 

This is why I love the painter/sculptor Constantin Brâncuși's definition:

"Simplicity is complexity resolved, not ignored."

Because you can’t just ignore complexity for sake of a shorter word count. That leaves your message way to shallow to make a splash. 

(And you've got to make waves not ripples to grab exec mindshare.)

Plus, let’s be real: 

Big enterprises with billions of revenue, millions of customers, thousands of employees, and dozens of business units are complex. 

You can’t escape that. So you have to find a way to *resolve* it. 

That's what selling with simplicity means.

content:
QBR’s are incredibly expensive meetings for sales team to run — and based on how most run them, they’re also a massive waste.

Just think about the last QBR you sat through. 

It probably went something like:

CRO: “So, bring us through this deal. It’s a big one this quarter.”

AE: *rambles through some play-by-play commentary*

VP: *says something equally designed to impress CRO*

AE: *not sure how to reply, wanders through more detail*

Manager: *defends AE so it doesn’t reflect poorly on them*

CRO: *answers emails*

(I’m exaggerating a little... but not by much.)

Your QBR's don't have to sound like this, though. 

I'll give you an example of the alternative:

Last month, I flew out to join one of our customer’s QBR’s. Their VP Sales, Christian, asked if I could join on-site, since it was their first since making a pretty big change in their process:

Deals can’t move past Stage 3 without a documented business case, built with the customer.

I slid into the back at ~9:00am, two hours after their official start. (East Coasters who went to SF, early start to the day.)

“How’s it going so far?” I whispered to him.

“Surprisingly well,” he said. Which got my attention.

“What do you mean?”

“We’re already done with 4. I thought we’d be running over on # 2 right now.”

They wrapped around 2:30pm — way ahead of schedule — and all went to the driving range for the afternoon. While I caught an earlier flight back to Denver and had dinner with my family. It was awesome.
